Iran's surge in attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz may be an attempt to exploit US restraint ahead of the midterm elections and undermine a recovery in Persian Gulf oil shipments, experts told Iran International.

Iranian mountaineer executed: Tehran puts another political prisoner to death. Iranian authorities executed political prisoner Ali-Sina Mostafavi, a 38-year-old mountaineer and musician from the southeastern city of Kerman, the judiciary’s Mizan News reported on Wednesday.

Nowhere else to go? The puzzle behind Iran’s stock rally. Iran’s stock market is raising eyebrows with a sustained rally even as the country’s economy struggles with dwindling foreign-currency inflows, energy shortages and uncertainty over the war.

Iranian wheat farmers face planting cash crunch as payments lag, rial slides. Iranian wheat farmers told Iran International that delayed government payments for their previous harvest are leaving them short of cash for autumn planting, while inflation and the falling rial erode the value of money they are still owed.

Women’s Basij commander, police officer killed in southeast Iran. A women’s Basij commander and a police officer were killed in separate attacks on Wednesday in Iran’s southeastern Sistan-Baluchestan province, adding to a series of deadly shootings, bombings and armed clashes in the region.

Zarif under fire for dismissing nuclear deterrence before war. A resurfaced video of former foreign minister Mohammad Javad Zarif saying Iran lacked enough enriched uranium to produce a nuclear weapon has ignited a fierce debate after successive wars with Israel and the United States.

Iran police killed brothers celebrating Khamenei’s death, source says. Iranian police fired 36 rounds at a car during a seven-minute chase near Tehran, killing two brothers aged 15 and 19 after its occupants honked their horn while celebrating the death of then-supreme leader Ali Khamenei, a source close to the family told Iran International.

Iranians report months-long waits for unemployment benefits. Iranians receiving unemployment benefits say payments have been delayed by up to two months, leaving some struggling to pay for food and service debts, according to messages sent to Iran International.

Tehran signals escalation in conflict IRGC likens to a ‘world war’. A senior Revolutionary Guards official has compared Iran’s conflict with the United States to a world war that could reshape the global order, reflecting a mindset in Tehran that appears increasingly resistant to backing down despite the risk of renewed US attacks.

Man in Iran International attack plot told police he was paid £2,000 to film. A man accused of plotting an attack on Iran International journalists in Britain told police he had received £2,000 for filming, according to interview transcripts read at Woolwich Crown Court on Wednesday.

How Iran shielded forces over 2022 protest killings. Iran has built impunity for the killing of protesters into its laws and judicial system, Amnesty International said in an investigation detailing how security forces accused of deadly violence can help determine whether their own actions were lawful.

Ignore prices and economy is fine, Iran ex-minister says. A former Iranian labor minister has drawn ridicule after saying the country has no economic problems other than high prices and inflation, remarks that came as official data showed year-on-year inflation approaching 90%.

Shiraz and the wine industry Iran lost after 1979. Nearly five decades after the 1979 Revolution brought an end to Iran's legal wine industry, the country retains vast vineyards and a centuries-old winemaking heritage but remains absent from a global wine export market worth $37.8 billion in 2025.

Iran’s strikes on Persian Gulf water and power were deliberate - Reuters. Iran and its allies hit water plants, airports, refineries and a nuclear power station across the Persian Gulf with a precision that rules out the official story of falling debris, a Reuters investigation has found, showing the civilian damage was the aim, not a side effect.

‘We cannot bring America to its knees,’ former Tehran mayor says. Iran cannot bring the United States to its knees despite inflicting damage on American forces, a former Tehran mayor said in a state television interview, arguing that Iran's military capabilities cannot match Washington's and calling for an end to the war through negotiations.

Tehran hospital locks its main building and treats patients in the courtyard. A Social Security hospital in Tehran has locked its main building and moved treatment into a cramped clinic in its courtyard, a member of the insurer’s healthcare oversight committee said, two months after officials listed it among the capital’s unsafe hospitals.

German court jails two men over spying for Iran's Guards. A German court convicted two men of spying on prominent Jewish figures and preparing attacks against them on behalf of Iran's Revolutionary Guards Quds Force, sentencing both to prison on Thursday.

Armed suspect arrested over alleged plot to kill ex-minister, reformists say. An armed man was arrested over an alleged plot to assassinate a former Iranian minister after a gathering attended by Mohammad Khatami, the former president associated with efforts to reform the Islamic Republic from within, Iran’s Reform Front said.

Statement on a cyberattack targeting an Iran International correspondent. On 10 October 2026, an unauthorized third party gained access to the work account of one of our correspondents. The correspondent was approached by someone posing as a representative of an established think tank and invited to join an online meeting.

Tehran hardline mayor rolls out economic relief: is he eyeing the presidency?. Tehran’s hardline mayor Alireza Zakani has drawn accusations of using municipal resources to prepare for another presidential bid after announcing a freeze on basic food prices and payments to new parents.

US alert puts Iran’s overseas religious finance networks under scrutiny. The US Treasury’s latest warning over Iran’s alleged abuse of religious charities puts renewed attention on religious and charitable organizations outside Iran that have separately faced criminal, regulatory or government scrutiny over financial or institutional links to Tehran.

Suspect in journalist attack plot says UK-based IRGC officer threatened to kill him. A man accused of plotting an attack on Iran International journalists told a London court on Thursday that a man he identified as a Revolutionary Guards officer living in Britain threatened to kill him and his mother unless he obeyed.

Iran touts economic resilience while households struggle to afford basics. Iran’s central bank governor has dismissed claims of economic collapse, while domestic media reports describe wages failing to cover basic living costs and families struggling to afford medicines, housing and car repairs.

Iran speaker says government overstepped on anti-terror finance rules. Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf says part of the government’s anti-terror financing regulations violates Iranian law, adding that decisions on who is designated as terrorist must remain with the Supreme National Security Council.

Iran shipped jet fuel to Myanmar despite US blockade - Reuters. Iran managed to export jet fuel to Myanmar and send several shipments of liquefied petroleum gas out of the region despite a US naval blockade that has largely halted its crude exports, Reuters reported on Friday.

Norwegian teen gets 20-year sentence in UK murder plot linked to Iran. A Norwegian teenager recruited by a Swedish crime group linked by prosecutors to the Iranian government was sentenced to 20 years’ detention in Britain on Friday.

Iran’s rulers face a reckoning with their own people, former US envoy says. Decades of American sanctions strengthened Iran’s Revolutionary Guards by hollowing out the middle class, former US diplomat Joey Hood told Iran International, and once the fighting ends, Tehran will face a reckoning with its own people.

Iran hangs Iraqi man on Saudi spying charge he denied. Iran has executed a 28-year-old Iraqi man convicted of spying for Saudi Arabia, a charge he denied, according to the Oslo-based group Iran Human Rights.

Iranian court sentences woman to 50 lashes for kissing a man in a cafe. A court in the Iranian city of Qom has sentenced a woman to 50 lashes for kissing and hugging a man in a cafe, after her husband filed a complaint and submitted video of the meeting, according to the rights group HRANA. She denies the charge.

Iran raided, summoned and jailed Baha’is in Yazd 34 times in seven months. Iranian security and judicial authorities have taken action against Baha’is in the central city of Yazd at least 34 times in less than seven months, raiding homes, summoning dozens for interrogation and jailing members of the faith, the rights group HRANA reported on Friday.

After the killings, Iran turned on the families of the dead. A bullet is fired once. For the families of those killed in Iran’s Woman, Life, Freedom uprising, the punishment that followed lasted for years: bodies held hostage, false confessions forced on parents, funerals fired upon and killers set free, Amnesty International has found.

Iran cultivated Houthis for years before opening new war front, insider says. Iran spent years building influence in Yemen through Hezbollah recruiters and Revolutionary Guards officers, a former Yemeni pro-democracy activist told Iran International, and is now using the Houthis to carry the war to Saudi Arabia and its Western allies.

Iran giving Houthis targeting intelligence for Saudi attacks - WSJ. Iranian support has helped Yemen’s Houthis carry out their most potent and sophisticated attacks yet on Saudi Arabia and its Yemeni allies, the Wall Street Journal reported, citing people briefed on intelligence from Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s anti-Houthi alliance.

Iran's January crackdown: Snipers at Friday prayer leader's office, dorm. Iran's security forces deployed snipers on the rooftops of the provincial Friday prayer leader's office and a women's student dormitory to fire on protesters during January's deadly crackdown in Semnan, east of Tehran, an Iran International investigation found.

Tehran’s diplomatic paralysis leaves Iran caught between deal and escalation. A growing number of former Iranian officials and political figures are calling for an agreement with the United States, while hardliners and military commanders continue to push for confrontation, exposing a deeper struggle over the direction of Tehran’s foreign policy.

Iran risks losing ground as East-West trade routes expand. Investment in trade routes linking Asia and Europe through Central Asia and the Caucasus is putting pressure on Iran’s ambitions to become a major transit hub, with neighboring countries developing transport and digital networks that bypass Iranian territory.

Who are the Baluch militants taking on Iran rulers, and how far can they go?. A wave of deadly attacks on Iranian security forces in the country’s restive southeast has brought renewed attention to a coalition of Baluch militants seeking to broaden their fight against the Islamic Republic, raising questions about how far the insurgency can spread.

Architect of Guards' missiles becomes Iran's defense minister. Mehrdad Akhlaghi Ketabchi, a sanctioned veteran of Iran's missile industry with ties to the Revolutionary Guards, became defense minister on Sunday, following his predecessor's killing in the war with the United States and Israel.

Iran signals possible nuclear policy shift, threatens US retaliation. Iranian officials raised the possibility of a shift in nuclear policy and threatened retaliation against further US-Israeli attacks, while Tehran outlined its conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday.

Trump says US may ‘soon finish the job’ on Iran, Netanyahu vows to topple regime. US President Donald Trump on Sunday warned Washington could “soon finish the job” against Iran unless Tehran changed course, as Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Israel was prepared to strike Iran without US support and vowed to bring down Tehran’s government.

Iran rolls out regional Data Authority amid threats to Mideast tech infrastructure. Iran's parliament speaker said a "Persian Gulf Data Authority" was coming and urged regional governments and investors to withhold resources from AI companies involved in military operations, amid Tehran threats against digital infrastructure across the region.

Retirees protest across Iran over economic hardship, repression. Retirees staged protests in several Iranian cities on Sunday over soaring living costs, inadequate pensions and healthcare problems, with some demonstrators also chanting against government corruption, repression and executions.

US and Israel threaten renewed Iran strikes, Tehran warns of response. US President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu escalated threats against Iran on Sunday, and Tehran warned of retaliation even as diplomatic efforts continued over the Strait of Hormuz and the wider conflict.

Iranians report soaring medical costs, staff shortages at hospitals. People in Iran have described deteriorating hospital services, rising treatment costs, shortages of medical staff and equipment, and long waits for care, as healthcare workers struggle with low wages and growing workloads, according to accounts shared with Iran International.

Iranians report mass security warnings over social media activity. Iran's police intelligence agency has sent threatening text messages warning citizens of possible prosecution over online activity, including people who do not use social media, according to accounts shared with Iran International.

Teenager killed by gunshot to eye after arrest in Iran, source says. An 18-year-old mechanic was killed by a gunshot to his right eye after being wounded and detained on January 9, according to information obtained by Iran International from a source close to his family.

Au Sénégal, pourquoi Pastef se heurte à répétition à la censure du Conseil constitutionnel. Depuis les législatives de 2024, pas moins de dix textes de loi émanant du parti d’Ousmane Sonko ont été censurés par les « sages ». Décryptage d’un bras de fer institutionnel qui vient encore de rebondir.

En Centrafrique, qui sont les activistes arrêtés après la journée ville morte ?. Cinq responsables de la société civile centrafricaine ont été arrêtés le 15 octobre à Bangui, alors qu’ils s’apprêtaient à s’exprimer sur les suites du mouvement contre la vie chère. L’opposition dénonce une atteinte à l’État de droit.

Cameroun : Samuel Mvondo Ayolo dément de nouvelles rumeurs sur la mort de Paul Biya. Une rumeur annonçant la mort du président Biya a circulé sur les réseaux sociaux. Contacté par Jeune Afrique, Samuel Mvondo Ayolo, le directeur du cabinet civil de la présidence, dément.

Souleymane Diarrassouba : « Avec son nouveau Plan national de développement, la Côte d’Ivoire change d’échelle ». Industrialisation, TGV, recul de la pauvreté : le PND 2026-2030 de la Côte d’Ivoire voit grand. Et le ministre chargé de sa concrétisation défend un programme de 175 milliards d’euros, dont le succès repose largement sur les investisseurs privés.

RDC : ce que l’on sait des perquisitions visant l’entourage de Félix Tshisekedi en Belgique. Plusieurs perquisitions ont été menées en Belgique mercredi 14 octobre, en lien avec une plainte déposée en 2025 contre neuf personnes proches du président congolais. Cette procédure fragilise la relation congolo-belge.

Comment la BDEAC a réussi son pari des marchés internationaux malgré ses fragilités. En mobilisant 222 millions de dollars sur les marchés internationaux de capitaux, la banque régionale entend élargir ses ressources et soutenir le financement des économies de la Cemac. Mais le coût de cette opération et les fragilités financières de l’institution soulignent l’ampleur du chantier qui reste à accomplir.

BGFI : Henri-Claude Oyima réussit son pari de l’introduction en Bourse en deux temps. L’introduction en Bourse de BGFI Holding Corporation franchit un cap avec une deuxième phase largement sursouscrite. Après l’ouverture timide au grand public, les investisseurs professionnels ont accueilli l’opération avec plus d’enthousiasme.

Au Kenya, l’annulation du deal Vodafone-Safaricom menace de peser sur les finances du pays. Le Kenya fait face à une grave crise budgétaire et réglementaire après l’annulation de la vente d’une participation de 15 % de Safaricom à Vodacom. L’État risque de devoir rembourser 1,9 milliard de dollars.

Cameroun : le renseignement d’État, entre guerre des clans et business privé. Officiellement destinés à protéger l’État, les services de renseignement camerounais, affaiblis par la guerre des clans autour de Paul Biya et par la précarité de leurs agents, se mettent régulièrement au service d’intérêts privés. Décryptage en vidéo.

RDC : Joseph Kabila, rebelle après tout. L’ancien président a pris la tête d’une nouvelle rébellion le 12 octobre. Il s’est donné pour mission de renverser Félix Tshisekedi mais court le risque, en faisant le choix des armes, de s’isoler un peu plus.

En Côte d’Ivoire, le PPA-CI et le PDCI face au rouleau compresseur de la justice. Alors que le pouvoir avait promis de « recréer la confiance » avec l’opposition, les convocations devant la justice antiterroriste se multiplient dans l’entourage de Laurent Gbagbo et de Tidjane Thiam, interrogeant la possibilité d’une décrispation politique.

Au Maroc, piliers reconduits et nouveaux entrants : le gouvernement El Mansouri enfin dévoilé. Les principaux arbitrages du nouveau gouvernement nommé ce 16 octobre dessinent une équation familière au sommet de l’État, avec des piliers reconduits, des surprises et une majorité désormais articulée autour de quatre partis.

Au Mali, les dessous de la bataille pour le contrôle de la Maison de la presse. Alors que son second mandat touche à sa fin, Bandiougou Danté se prépare à se représenter à la présidence de la Maison de la presse. Un début de fronde s’organise contre ce proche d’Assimi Goïta, promoteur d’un « traitement patriotique de l’information ».

Cameroun anglophone – Felix Agbor Balla : « Le gouvernement doit comprendre que dialoguer n’est pas une faiblesse ». Dix ans après le déclenchement du conflit dans les régions du Nord-Ouest et du Sud-Ouest (Noso), l’avocat et activiste des droits de l’homme Felix Agbor Balla continue de militer pour « l’autodétermination » des peuples de l’ancien Southern Cameroon, tout en défendant un retour au fédéralisme.

Le Grand Prix d’Afrique au Rwanda, le retour de Joseph Kabila en RDC, le président tchadien à Paris… Les 5 infos qu’il ne fallait pas manquer. Cette semaine, le Brief de Jeune Afrique revient sur le retour de Joseph Kabila en RDC, dresse le portrait du nouveau président de la Chambre des représentants au Maroc, fait le point sur les relations entre le Tchad et la France, s’interroge sur l’opération F1 du président rwandais et décrypte la montée au capital d’Eramet de Paris.

Lounès Magramane, un diplomate choisi pour succéder à Boualem Boualem au cabinet de la présidence algérienne. Sa nomination a surpris, d’autant que lui-même se voyait plutôt ambassadeur à Paris. C’est pourtant bien Lounès Magramane qui a été choisi pour travailler au plus près du président Tebboune, devenant ainsi un nouvel acteur clé du pouvoir algérien.

Secrétariat général de l’ONU : la menace d’un veto plane sur la candidature de Macky Sall. Lors du sixième tour de scrutin au sein du Conseil de sécurité, tous les candidats, dont l’ex-président sénégalais, se sont retrouvés sous la menace d’un possible veto de la part de plusieurs des cinq membres permanents.

Course à l’hydrogène vert au Maghreb : le Maroc garde-t-il une longueur d’avance ?. Entre les partenariats industriels, les promesses de développement et les milliards d’euros en jeu, la ruée vers le « carburant du futur » s’est-elle vraiment traduite par des projets concrets au Maghreb ? État des lieux en infographies.
Secrétariat général de l’ONU : Macky Sall jette l’éponge. Au lendemain du sixième vote indicatif au sein du Conseil de sécurité, l’ex-président sénégalais a décidé de retirer sa candidature.

Entre Sahara et océan, la petite ville marocaine de Lagouira attise l’intérêt de la Mauritanie. Alors que les négociations sur le Sahara occidental se poursuivent, la Mauritanie souhaite faire reconnaître sa souveraineté sur la ville marocaine de Lagouira. Éclairage historique sur un enjeu territorial majeur.

Cameroun : ces femmes qui font l’économie. Banque, BTP, cacao : six Camerounaises brisent les plafonds de verre et dynamisent l’économie locale. Elles racontent leurs réussites, mais aussi les freins majeurs à l’entrepreneuriat féminin.

En Ouganda, comment Muhoozi Kainerugaba étend son influence de l’armée à la politique. Depuis la réélection de Yoweri Museveni en janvier 2026, l’emprise du chef d’état-major de l’armée sur son pays ne cesse de croître. Du Parlement au gouvernement en passant par la sphère économique, il a continué à étendre son réseau, se positionnant plus que jamais comme le successeur de son père.

Cameroun : sur la route Douala-Yaoundé, sept heures pour parcourir 230 kilomètres. Le délabrement de la route Douala-Yaoundé exaspère les usagers et inquiète jusqu’aux cadres du parti au pouvoir. Alors que le gouvernement annonce de nouveaux travaux, le financement et les délais de reconstruction restent des défis majeurs.

Touadéra et les rebelles : en Centrafrique, l’interminable bras de fer entre le président et les groupes armés. Le gouvernement centrafricain s’active pour signer, en novembre à Bangui, un nouvel accord consacrant la réhabilitation de certains chefs rebelles, parmi lesquels Mahamat al-Khatim, Ali Darassa et Sembé Bobo. Mais l’est du pays reste menacé par un ancien allié de ces derniers, Noureddine Adam.

Au Mali, les compagnies minières prises entre étau fiscal et casse-tête logistique. Confrontées à la hausse des redevances, à la dégradation des conditions sécuritaires ou encore à des différends juridiques avec la junte au pouvoir, les sociétés minières naviguent dans un environnement de plus en plus incertain.

RDC : la discrète médiation finlandaise entre l’opposition et le pouvoir. Des représentants de la majorité et de l’opposition ont été invités en septembre pour un séjour de trois jours à Helsinki. Objectif : favoriser le dialogue avec un cadre plus informel et détendu.

AES-Cedeao : les deux blocs annoncent vouloir travailler à un « accord-cadre ». Dans un communiqué conjoint samedi soir, les deux parties se « sont félicitées de l’esprit de fraternité » des discussions et ont affiché l’ambition de parvenir à un accord-cadre de coopération.

Érythrée-Éthiopie : entre Issayas Afewerki et Abiy Ahmed, le retour de la guerre. La reprise de la guerre dans le Tigré fait planer la menace d’un conflit ouvert entre l’Éthiopie et l’Érythrée. Issayas Afewerki et Abiy Ahmed, un temps alliés, se livrent une bataille des ambitions sur fond de retournements d’alliances inédits.

Joseph Kabila, « proxy » de Paul Kagame ?. En prenant les rênes du mouvement rebelle FRN, Joseph Kabila bouscule l’échiquier politique et militaire congolais. Décryptage d’une alliance opportuniste avec le Rwanda.

Cameroun : Tiriane Noah à la tête du MRC, entre fidélité à Maurice Kamto et défis internes. L’opposante a été élue à la tête du Mouvement pour la renaissance du Cameroun, principal parti d’opposition camerounais. Elle succède à Maurice Kamto, déjà annoncé comme le candidat du parti à la prochaine présidentielle.

Pour la « gen Z » de Madagascar, un an après le putsch militaire, les lendemains qui déchantent. « Madagascar, un an après le coup d’Etat » (1/4). Lancé en septembre 2025, le mouvement de protestation de la jeunesse malgache, qui a conduit au renversement du président Andry Rajoelina, se heurte aux promesses d’une « refondation » du pouvoir par la junte restée lettre morte.

Le Maroc désapprouve en silence la visite du roi d’Espagne, Felipe VI, à Ceuta et à Melilla. Mohammed VI n’a pas publiquement condamné le déplacement du monarque espagnol dans les enclaves d’Afrique du Nord, mais les signes du mécontentement royal sont là.

A l’île Maurice, un couvre-feu décrété après plusieurs jours de manifestations et de violences, déclenchées par un tir policier. Un policier a grièvement blessé par balle une femme, vendredi, à Camp-Levieux, au sud de Port-Louis. Selon la police, 84 personnes ont été interpellées mardi. Les faits recensés comprennent des pillages, des incendies, des actes de violence et des infractions au couvre-feu.

Navanethem Pillay, Prix Nobel de la paix : sur Gaza, « on nous a accusés d’antisémitisme et de partialité. Mais je sais ce qui est constitutif du crime de génocide ». La juriste sud-africaine a présidé la commission d’enquête du Conseil des droits de l’homme des Nations unies, qui a estimé qu’un génocide se déroulait à Gaza. Dans un entretien au « Monde », elle revient sur son travail, récompensé le 9 octobre par le prix Nobel de la paix.

« Les Damnés de la donnée » : les travailleurs du Sud, invisibilisés et pourtant indispensables au développement de l’IA. Au fil d’une enquête menée auprès d’annotateurs de données à Madagascar, le sociologue Clément Le Ludec met en lumière la centralité du travail de cette main-d’œuvre précarisée et invisibilisée, indispensable au bon fonctionnement des systèmes d’intelligence artificielle.

Ceuta : des ONG accusent l’armée espagnole de « cruauté » à l’égard des migrants et dénoncent le non-respect de leurs droits fondamentaux. Au moment où le roi Felipe VI visitait la ville nord-africaine, mardi, huit ONG ont annoncé la saisine du défenseur du peuple espagnol pour dénoncer l’opacité entourant les retours prétendument volontaires vers le Maroc.

A Madagascar, l’ascension de l’ambitieux colonel Michaël Randrianirina. « Madagascar, un an après le coup d’Etat » (2/4). Depuis son arrivée au pouvoir, le « colonel Michaël » tente de rassurer ses partenaires et multiplie les promesses aux Malgaches, dans l’optique du scrutin présidentiel attendu d’ici à novembre 2027. Des observateurs indépendants alertent toutefois sur une opposition et une justice muselées.

Huit ans après la sortie de « Rafiki », la Cour suprême kényane se prononce sur l’interdiction du film pour « promotion du lesbianisme ». Le long-métrage, qui raconte l’histoire d’amour de deux jeunes femmes à Nairobi, n’avait été autorisé en 2018 que pendant une seule semaine sur décision de justice et avait battu des records au box-office.

En Ethiopie, la fête ancestrale d’Irreecha connaît un regain de popularité après des décennies de répression. Longtemps caisse de résonance de la résistance du peuple oromo contre le pouvoir, le rassemblement culturel est désormais mis en avant par le gouvernement comme un symbole de renouveau national.

Ethiopie : au Tigré, une administration intérimaire mise en place par le gouvernement fédéral. La région, en proie aux combats depuis plusieurs semaines, était dirigée jusque-là par les rebelles du Front de libération du peuple du Tigré.

A l’île Maurice, une colère qui dépasse la crise de l’eau dans une société « très inégalitaire ». Depuis qu’un policier a grièvement blessé une jeune femme, vendredi 9 octobre, des émeutes ont lieu dans plusieurs régions de l’île, où la pénurie d’eau s’ajoute au désarroi d’une jeunesse touchée par l’austérité.

Crânes sénégalais : pourquoi la restitution de restes humains pose-t-elle question ?. Au Sénégal, un député réclame le retour de plusieurs crânes, collectés durant la colonisation française. Il rouvre ainsi le débat sur la question de la restitution des restes humains.

Hyron Andrews, joueur de rugby sud-africain des Lions de Johannesburg, retrouvé mort à la veille d’un match en France. Une minute de silence sera respectée sur tous les terrains de rugby européens ce week-end. Le match de Champions Cup contre La Rochelle samedi est maintenu « en son honneur ».

Au Burkina Faso, le président Ibrahim Traoré crée une « ligue de la souveraineté » de football après une lourde défaite de l’équipe nationale. Le chef de la junte au pouvoir n’a pas digéré la déroute de la sélection nationale (0-7) face à l’Argentine et veut étendre sa « révolution » au ballon rond.

Au Maroc, un nouveau gouvernement formé, mais peu de changement, sauf pour les femmes. Trente-deux ministres ont prêté serment devant le roi du pays, Mohammed VI, vendredi 16 octobre, mais 40 % d’entre eux étaient déjà en poste. Les femmes, elles, reculent dans la hiérarchie gouvernementale.

Entre la RDC et la Belgique, des tensions après des perquisitions menées dans la famille du président congolais. La première dame et huit autres proches de Félix Tshisekedi sont au cœur d’une instruction pour blanchiment d’argent, ouverte par la justice belge en 2025. Après des perquisitions menées dans le plat pays, mercredi 14 octobre, le chef de l’Etat congolais a interdit à son gouvernement « tout contact » avec l’ambassade de Belgique.

« Dès qu’une tête dépasse, il la coupe » : Muhoozi Kainerugaba, héritier brutal et fantasque du président ougandais. Le fils du chef de l’Etat, déjà à la tête des forces armées et successeur présumé de son père à la présidence, est accusé de multiples violations des droits humains et enchaîne, sur les réseaux sociaux, les tirades aussi baroques que terrifiantes.

A Madagascar, un an après avoir été renversé, l’ex-président Andry Rajoelina rêve encore d’un retour sur la Grande Ile. « Madagascar, un an après le coup d’Etat » (3/4). Vivant en exil depuis octobre 2025, l’ancien chef de l’Etat s’efforce de mobiliser son réseau diplomatique loin de son pays, même si ses leviers d’action demeurent limités.

En Tunisie, plusieurs milliers de personnes ont manifesté samedi dans les rues de la capitale, malgré la répression du régime de Kaïs Saïed. Depuis le coup de force du président tunisien, il y a cinq ans, une chape de plomb s’est abattue sur le pays. 'Beirut Fragments' captures the horror Israel keeps inflicting on Lebanon Submitted by Belen Fernandez on Tue, 10/13/2026 - 07:16 Jean Said Makdisi's reissued memoir recounts bombardment, siege and civilian resistance in scenes painfully familiar from Gaza and Israel's renewed assault on Lebanon Two women walk through a West Beirut street devastated by Israeli shelling during the siege of the city on 24 July 1982 (Dominique Faget/AFP) Off Sometime in the autumn of 2000, when I was a sophomore at Columbia University in New York, I was browsing the shelves of the university bookstore and came across Edward Said's The Question of Palestine , published in 1979, the year after Orientalism . At the time, I had no idea who Said was or, really, what Palestine even was, raising the question, perhaps, of how I had managed to make it this far in my educational trajectory in such a state of cluelessness. In my defence, the education system in the United States doesn't exactly encourage an interest in understanding the world and how it works, since that would no doubt produce a whole lot of graduates with a negative view of the US itself and its habit of tormenting people at home and abroad. I bought the book and read it, wide-eyed, over the winter break. I'd never had an opinion one way or the other about Israel either, but it had not occurred to me that the state might owe its entire existence to the mass killing and dispossession of Palestinians. My real education began in 2003, when I abandoned the US after finishing university and set off to travel. In Greece, I met a young Polish woman named Amelia, and together we developed an obsession with hitchhiking that would take us across countries and continents for years. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); In the summer of 2006, having already traversed Turkey and Syria, we planned to thumb our way through Lebanon , but the trip had to be postponed slightly on account of Israel's 34-day war on the country. The assault killed approximately 1,200 people, with the help of rush-shipped bombs from the US, and left swathes of territory saturated in unexploded ordnance. Neighbourhoods and villages were reduced to rubble. I returned to Lebanon countless times after 2006, but that first visit remains one of the defining episodes in the formation of my political consciousness Amelia and I arrived in Lebanon in September, one month after the war's end, and spent two months on the receiving end of relentless hospitality from Lebanese of all sects as well as Palestinians. Our hosts not only picked us up on the side of the road but also carted us home to be stuffed with food and given free accommodation, often with an invitation to stay for as long as we liked. Along the southern border with Israel, we stayed in various villages that have now been more or less obliterated by the Israeli military, which, after launching its genocide in the Gaza Strip in 2023, once again expanded its manic destruction to Lebanon. I returned to Lebanon countless times after 2006, but that first visit remains one of the defining episodes in the formation of my political consciousness. I found myself thinking a lot about it when I recently reread Beirut Fragments : A War Memoir by the Palestinian writer and scholar Jean Said Makdisi, sister of Edward Said. Born in Jerusalem, died in Beirut Originally published in 1990, at the end of Lebanon's 15-year civil war, which, like many a "civil" conflict, boasted plenty of outside participation, most notably by Israel, Beirut Fragments was rereleased this year. A sort of homage to Lebanon's capital and its inhabitants, the text is a collection of memories, anecdotes and analyses - political, societal and psychological - by a woman who lived a war intimately rather than just hitchhiking through its aftermath. Makdisi writes: "I was born in Jerusalem, grew up in Cairo, aged in America, and died in Beirut." Although her extended family was directly affected by the Nakba , resulting in the "broken lives" of all of her relatives in Palestine, Makdisi recognises that her own privileged upbringing is not representative of the Palestinian condition, and at times seems to consider herself almost unworthy of identifying as Palestinian. She is an amalgam of various identities and international experiences, including a stint at the Cairo English School. There, students are "trained not only in the fine art of playing cricket but in the even finer art of applauding it" and inculcated with "good English manners, sometimes with uproarious results such as occurred when we were required, against all custom and reason, to eat dates with knife and fork". US campus protests: Edward Said would have treasured this moment Read More » In the late 1950s she travels to the United States for college, where, to her astonished dismay, an invitation to take part in a panel discussion on the place of women in the Arab world ends with a hounding by the audience: "Why do you hate Jews?" "Why do you want to throw all the Jews into the sea?" Armed with nothing but an awareness of the clear distinction between Zionism and Judaism, and the knowledge that Jews are under no circumstances the "victims" in Palestine, Makdisi admits that she "had no dates, no names, no maps, no newspaper clippings" with which to back up her convictions. "I was in fact very ignorant of politics and would probably have remained so had this episode and a thousand like it never occurred." Instead, she heads to the library to read up so that she can "argue a case that, the greater the blind opposition to it, the clearer it became to me and therefore the more compelling". Unfortunately, she soon finds that no wealth of dates, names, logic and history can counteract the stubborn hallucinations of Israel's American defenders. Roots in a city at war Makdisi marries a Lebanese man, Samir, who is "firmly rooted in Arab culture", and after living in the US for a spell, they move to Beirut: "I thought that in going with him I could attach myself to his firm roots." He is a professor at the American University of Beirut, she teaches a class here and there, and they raise their young children. Then the war starts - the booming artillery, the ubiquitous shattered glass, the endless trips to the garage shelter, the end of sleep. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Makdisi begins to write "as a witness to the common experiences of common people, feeling that in the trial of history there should be a record, a vindication, of their pain… Sharing that pain, and writing about it, I came to love the place." In the end she puts down her own roots, and after 15 years of war feels "more committed to Beirut than ever, even dependent on it in a strange sort of way", a commitment that is partly "based in anger, in a kind of furious defense of the collective humanity so outraged in Beirut". In describing the "lingering magic" of the city, Makdisi never succumbs to the trite nostalgia for the so-called "Paris of the Middle East" that has afflicted so many of her contemporaries, as well as younger generations of observers. Under no illusion that pre-war Beirut was some sort of cosmopolitan paradise where beautiful women lounged in bikinis and no one had a worry in the world, Makdisi addresses the role of acute socioeconomic inequality in fuelling the civil war, a conflict that is often erroneously reduced to "Christian versus Muslim" and otherwise oversimplified. In the book's prologue, Makdisi reflects: "Outsiders look at Beirut from a wary distance, as though it had nothing to do with them; as though, through a protective glass partition, they were watching with immunity a patient thrash about in mortal agony, suffering a ghastly virus contracted in forbidden and faraway places." The outside world, though, has much to do with perpetuating that agony. At one point, Makdisi finds herself pondering, "for the ten thousandth time since this damnable war began, on the happiness of the manufacturers and salesmen of arms and ammunition. Every roar, whistle, and crash translates itself in my mind to the sound of a cash register, the tinkle of champagne glasses." Yet another Israeli air raid The Israeli invasion of Lebanon in 1982 occupies a full chapter of Beirut Fragments , since it is this event that finally, halfway through the civil war, provides Makdisi with a prolonged moment of macabre clarity. Of course, Israel has been bombing the country from the get-go, not to mention performing its signature move from the psychological terror playbook: the sonic boom. Early in the war, Makdisi recalls, she wrote "more than one piece entitled 'The Morning After an Israeli Air-Raid'", then modified the title to "The Morning After Another Israeli Air-Raid" and then to "The Morning After Yet Another Israeli Air-Raid - Five Years Later". 'There was no doubt in my mind that the Israelis wished… to stamp something out entirely: principally, the idea of Palestine in the minds of Palestinians and their supporters' Without fail, the Israelis claim they are hitting "Palestinian targets" or "terrorist bases" (sound familiar?), and yet "the pictures in the papers were always the same: babies and old men, Palestinian and Lebanese, lying dead or dying; bits of bodies, shops, and cars; houses reduced to unrecognizable rubble; an old woman, wiping away her tears, picking her way through the ruins of her home, holding up a picture, perhaps, a saucepan, a bent and twisted vase - items that had once been part of her life and now had lost all meaning." Although Makdisi criticises many aspects of the conduct of the Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO) in Lebanon, these criticisms are summarily dispelled in 1982. "Until this point, perhaps, the war that began in 1975 had never been clear, had never been pure; now, in the confrontation I felt something akin to a sublimely clear revelation… Out of the muddy waters of the last seven years had emerged the true evil: Israel had presented itself thus at last, in open, undisguised, unpardonable ferocity." Tens of thousands of people are killed in the invasion, "the sky orange with the unnatural light of exploding phosphorus bombs", and Makdisi muses that "the accusatory word genocide no longer seemed exaggerated". "There was no doubt in my mind that the Israelis wished to destroy not just an organization or just an army but to stamp something out entirely: principally, the idea of Palestine in the minds of Palestinians and their supporters." It bears recalling that the US gave Israel the green light for the 1982 operation, a subject into which Makdisi does not delve. The cosmic stink At the start of the invasion, Israel announces that its aim is to create a 40km "security zone" to protect its citizens against "terrorists". This, again, might sound familiar to the present-day news consumer. As the invasion gives way to an apocalyptic siege of the Lebanese capital, however, it becomes "less clear that the Israelis were only after the PLO and not Beirut", as Makdisi puts it. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); It has never been in Israel's interest to have a thriving multi-sectarian society right next door, and an Arab one at that. The shelling eventually gets so intense that Beirutis are unable to make it to the cemetery to bury their dead, and instead have to throw bodies into the sea. It is during this time that Makdisi focuses on "the necessity of resistance, which became to me the most meaningful political act of my life", and which in her case simply entails surviving in place and refusing to abide by Israeli orders to leave. The morning after the Lebanon 'agreement' Read More » Residents of Beirut assert their humanity through weeks under Israeli bombardment without water, food or electricity, and feel "a kind of closeness, a kind of unity that in normal times would have been unthinkable". The "grand climax" of the Israeli assault takes place on 12 August 1982, coincidentally after the PLO has already agreed to withdraw from Lebanon. Makdisi has taken her children to her brother-in-law's house in Mansourieh, in the hills just above Beirut, where she stands on the balcony and watches "as wave after wave of bombing continued". "It was as though the Israelis had gone stark raving mad; as though they had achieved a paroxysm of violent hatred; a lunatic, destructive urge to kill, to blot out every living thing, to leave nothing standing, to eradicate the city." Yet the "most extraordinary aspect of the occupation" is discovered only when the Israelis pull out of Beirut, leaving behind a "great heap of excrement". The soldiers have literally defecated everywhere they have been, on school desks, in bathtubs, in shop windows, making their olfactory mark on the city in the form of a "cosmic stink". Fast forward half a century from the start of the Lebanese civil war, and Makdisi's war memoir reads at times like current events. The "accusatory word genocide " is as far from an exaggeration as ever in the Gaza Strip. Israel is once again engaged in lunatic urges to eradicate sections of Lebanon, pulverising entire villages in the south of the country under the age-old pretext of maintaining a " security zone " to protect itself against the "terrorists". Now, of course, the appointed "terrorists" in Lebanon are no longer the PLO but Hezbollah, which formed as a direct result of none other than the 1982 Israeli invasion. Fancy that. If history is anything to go by, people generally resist their own destruction, meaning that Israel's ongoing paroxysms of violent hatred will likely only breed more violent resistance and more war. The UK Green Party is simply stating historical fact Submitted by Joseph Massad on Fri, 10/16/2026 - 17:15 Despite objections to the label from some of Israel's own critics, the movement was founded on Palestinian dispossession and Jewish supremacy Green Party supporters march across Westminster Bridge during the National March for Palestine in London on 10 October 2026 (Vuk Valcic/Zuma Press Wire) Off On 4 October 2026, the Green Party of England and Wales officially adopted a motion titled "Zionism is Racism". Swift condemnations followed from pro- Israel groups, which declared the policy antisemitic. The equation of Zionism with racism, however, is not a new proposition. In 1975, the United Nations General Assembly adopted a resolution determining that Zionism is a form of racism, which the US insisted on revoking in 1991, during the last days of the USSR. Many countries that had voted for it reversed their positions in line with US instructions. Perhaps more curious is that objections to describing Zionism as racist have also come from Israel's critics. That too is not new. Noam Chomsky , long a critic of Israel, was appalled at what he labelled the "notorious" 1975 UN resolution, which he condemned "for profound hypocrisy, given the nature of the states that backed it (including the Arab states), and (arguably) for referring to Zionism as such rather than the policies of the State of Israel, but restricted to these policies, the resolution cannot be criticized as inaccurate". It is unclear whether, for Chomsky, the pro-Israel states that opposed the resolution also deserved condemnation for their endorsement of Zionist racism. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Today, Norman Finkelstein is among Israel's critics who have objected to the Green Party motion. Invoking his investment in "the precision of language", he has surprisingly claimed that "Zionism is a nebulous term". The Zionist movement's literature, its policies and the pronouncements of its leaders provide ample evidence of that racism Some critics argue that condemning Zionism, an ideology and political movement, as racist is abstract and meaningless, whereas condemning the State of Israel identifies racism in the concrete form of its institutions, laws and practices. While this may be partly true, there are many ideologies that are castigated as racist without reservations, including white nationalism and white supremacy, not to mention a whole panoply of nationalisms, especially of the European variety. If this is the principal objection, it is not clear why some of these critics have such a visceral reaction to describing Zionism and the political movement bearing its name as racist. The movement's literature, its policies and the pronouncements of its leaders provide ample evidence of that racism. Surely, none of this is in question for someone like Chomsky or his minor disciples. Colonial origins The word "Zionism" was coined in 1890 by the Austrian Jewish journalist Nathan Birnbaum (1864-1937), whose family came from Galicia - the part of Poland annexed by Austria in 1772. He founded the group Zion: Union of Austrian Societies for the Colonization of Palestine and Syria. Birnbaum later supported Theodor Herzl, who founded the Zionist Organization in 1897, only to break with him in 1898 and advocate national-cultural autonomy for Jews in the diaspora. He abandoned Zionism altogether in 1900 and became an advocate of Yiddish. He later became a leader of the non-Zionist religious group Agudas Yisrael. Revisiting the genesis of the term makes clear that, contrary to some of its stubborn but ignorant defenders, Zionism has always been a colonialist ideology and movement. Its central project has always been the colonisation of Palestine by European Jews. UK Green motion on Zionism: Why we need to change the conversation Read More » From the beginning, Herzl and his followers conceived of it as necessitating the expulsion of the indigenous Palestinians, whom they regarded as inferior to Jews and an obstacle to its realisation. A few examples from the movement's history suffice. Herzl insisted that the Jewish colonists must "try to spirit the penniless [Indigenous] population across the border by procuring employment for it in the transit countries, while denying it any employment in our own country". There were minor variants at the beginning of the 20th century, such as the racist Englishman Israel Zangwill's Territorialist movement, which sought a Jewish homeland outside Palestine. That, too, was racist. Zangwill himself called for the expulsion of the Palestinians in 1905. In 1930, Chaim Weizmann , the head of the Zionist Organization, rejected Palestinian demands for self-determination while endorsing it for world Jewry. The movement had not yet been able to expel the Palestinians. He wrote to a British official that the "rights that the Jewish people has been adjudged in Palestine [by the British Mandate] do not depend on the consent, and cannot be subject to the will, of the majority of its present inhabitants". Citing the alleged "unique[ness]" of the Jewish "connection" to Palestine, he stressed that when Britain promised a Jewish national home, "the agreement of the Palestinian Arabs was not asked". He insisted that Arab self-determination elsewhere, such as in Iraq , precluded Palestinian claims in Palestine that conflicted with Jewish colonial aspirations. Racial hierarchy For Weizmann, the inferior Palestinians could not "be considered as owning the country in the sense in which the inhabitants of Iraq or of Egypt possess their respective countries". To grant them self-determination, self-government or a legislative assembly, he argued, "would be to assign the country to its present inhabitants" and cancel the Balfour Declaration "in an underhand manner". He insisted on a different occasion, however, that "we wish to spare the Arabs as much as we can of the sufferings which every backward race has gone through on the coming of another, more advanced nation". When the Palestinians revolted against their colonisers, Weizmann called it a struggle between the "forces of civilization and building" and "the forces of destruction", declaring it "the old war of the desert against civilization" and vowing, "we will not be stopped". In 1938, David Ben-Gurion declared: "I support compulsory transfer [of the Indigenous Palestinians]. I do not see anything immoral in it." His statement reflected the policy of the Jewish Agency, which had established its first "Population Transfer Committee" in November 1937 to expel the inferior Palestinians. By the 1970s, Israeli Foreign Minister Abba Eban did not mince words when he said that "Israeli self-determination should take moral and historical precedence over Palestinian self-determination, though it does not rule it out entirely". Even as it asserted Jewish supremacy, the movement was changing how it described itself. As early as the 1930s, amid growing global anti-colonialism and the major Palestinian anti-colonial revolt, Jewish colonists in Palestine and the Zionist Organization began to recognise the liability of describing themselves as colonialists. They sought to alter the project's vocabulary - what might today be called rebranding - although they continued to use explicitly colonial terms for years to come. After the Second World War, the Zionists sought to capitalise on burgeoning decolonisation and the growing prominence of "self-determination" by claiming that their racist settler-colonial movement was, in fact, a movement for the "self-determination" of the Jewish people. This was an odd reconfiguration. Neither Herzl's writings nor the Zionist Organization's congresses nor the speeches of its delegation to the Paris Peace Conference after the First World War had invoked " self-determination " as the principle underpinning the project. The term was also absent from the 1917 Balfour Declaration, the 1922 League of Nations Mandate for Palestine, which guaranteed Jewish colonisation, and the 1947 UN Partition Plan. Claiming rights Neither the Balfour Declaration nor the League of Nations Mandate recognised a Jewish right to establish a state in Palestine. The British and the League recognised only the dubious idea of "the historical connection of the Jewish people with Palestine" as the basis for sponsoring their alleged "return". (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); The Partition Plan proposed Arab and Jewish states as a "solution" to the "problem of Palestine"; it did not proclaim an inherent Jewish right to statehood. Zionist leader Chaim Weizmann listens to the Arab Higher Committee’s case against partition at the UN in New York on 18 October 1947 (Acme Newspictures/AFP) In May 1948, 58 years after the term "Zionism" was coined, the movement invoked such a right for the first time in its " Declaration of the Establishment of the State of Israel", propagating the outright fabrication that "this right was recognized" in the Balfour Declaration, reaffirmed in the Mandate and acknowledged by the Partition Plan. None of them had done so. Continuing attempts to reframe Zionism alchemically as the Jewish people's "national liberation movement", rather than the colonial project it had always proudly proclaimed, were popularised in the mid-1960s by the anti-Palestinian Tunisian Zionist Albert Memmi , who remarkably appropriated the language of the colonised. His statement comes a week after the Centre imposed governor’s rule and emergency in KP, citing the provincial government’s “deliberate disengagement” from the fight against terrorism. The move also followed a mobilisation drive and protest march by the PTI, which was in power in KP and in opposition in the Centre, to demand the release of its jailed founder, Imran Khan. “If they really want to fight terrorists, and if they want that emergency and governor’s rule in KP to end, they should engage with the federal government and politicians and discuss a united policy regarding the fight against terrorism,” Bilawal said on Sunday, referring to the PTI-led opposition. He added that if the opposition was ready to fight terrorism and “we agree on a plan” to do so, the emergency and governor’s rule in KP could end. “If the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa chief minister (Sohail Afridi) is a coward, if he is not ready to defend his homeland, if he is not ready to fight those terrorists, then the PPP is ready to fight them,” Bilawal said. “That is why we supported the government’s decision to impose governor’s rule in KP.” He stressed that the party would “join forces with everyone to fight these terrorists”. In his media talk, the Bhutto scion said the country had reached a point where “terrorist attacks are taking place from Khyber to Khuzdar”. He regretted that when the Taliban came to power in Kabul in 2021, the Pakistani government at that time “also decided to invite the terrorists who were in Afghanistan to come back and live in our Swat, our Malakand, our former tribal areas”. He was seemingly referring to then-prime minister Imran’s plans to resettle members of the Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan in the country. Bilawal went on to say that terrorists who were in jail in Pakistan were also freed. “Today, Pakistan is suffering the losses from these wrong decisions,” he lamented. He added that the country had now once again reached the point where “some forces want to take down Pakistan’s flag in Swat” and there was a fight against terrorism ongoing across the entire country, while security forces, law enforcers and the public were being targeted. However, he claimed, in the province where the highest number of terrorist incidents were taking place — KP — its chief minister had pledged that he would not face the terrorists. In response to a question about the Karsaz bombing, the PPP chairman remarked that the greatest loss was caused when terrorist incidents were not taken seriously. He said that the PPP had “prepared entire society” to fight terrorism by creating an environment for counterterrorism operations in 2008, when the party was in power. After that, he said, when the National Action Plan was introduced, the PPP adopted a holistic approach towards bringing changes in institutions to assist with combatting terrorism. He emphasised that success was achieved when “every citizen” of Pakistan joined the fight against terrorism, saying, “Today as well, we will make efforts to create an environment where we are all united, and will fight the terrorists together.” Answering further questions, he said Pakistan was facing a “historic economic crisis”. “It appears that the situation will worsen. Our priority is to address this economic crisis, and to do that, we will have to fight terrorism as well,” he added. He said efforts should also be made to improve the democratic and electoral system in Pakistan. For this reason, he said, the PPP had highlighted the need for a new NAP and consensus on the fight against terrorism, while also extending an invitation to the opposition to play a part in this. He said the PPP also made an effort to improve the democratic system by pushing for electoral reforms. To this end, the federal government had decided to establish an electoral reforms committee in the National Assembly, adding that he had invited the opposition to play their part in that committee as well. “If they say that democracy is weak in this country, they should help us to strengthen it,” the PPP chairman said. He added, “If we can create such an environment, we will be in a better position to fight terrorists.” Bilawal also said KP Governor Faisal Karim Kundi had been nominated by the PPP for the office of governor, but “constitutionally, he is now a representative of the federal government”. He said Kundi reported to the federal government, but “I will keep talking to him and keep advising him; in principle, though, he is now working together with the federal government”. Responding to a question regarding a potential “compromise” with the opposition, Bilawal said, “You say ‘compromise’ like it’s a bad word […] Compromise and politics go hand in hand.” He stressed that ex-PM Benazir had always strived for compromises during her political career, adding that she knew that one could reach “extremes” if they remained a revolutionary or an activist who only protested rather than working for their cause. “We had to solve our issues and lift the public and our workers out of difficulty,” Bilawal said about the PPP’s past tenures in government. He asserted that it was the result of the PPP’s “compromises” that led to the end of Gen Pervez Musharraf’s dictatorship, as well as the passage of the 1973 Constitution and the 18th Amendment. “We (the PPP) are not in the federal government. Nor do we have a majority in Parliament,” he said. “But [we have to see] how we can conduct politics in the space we have.” New provinces Answering a question regarding the creation of new provinces, Bilawal stated that Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi knew “clearly” what the PPP and President Asif Ali Zardari’s policy was regarding new provinces or administrative units, and that this was “not possible without the president’s signature”. Naqvi’s July remarks calling for new provinces and reforms in the current governance system had ignited an animated debate across the country. The PPP, which rules Sindh, has strongly opposed any possible division of the province. Bilawal stressed that the PPP’s position was clear: that they could be created in accordance with the Constitution and law if the provincial assembly agreed. The Sindh Assembly, amid a boycott by the opposition, adopted a resolution last month rejecting all attempts to divide the province or create new administrative units. “Where there is consensus and it is not a political stunt, if there is no other purpose behind it … why aren’t provinces being made there?” the PPP chairman said, giving the example of Gilgit-Baltistan. “If we really want this to be implemented, it must only be implemented where the provinces want this,” he stressed, noting that the entire GB Legislative Assembly had passed a resolution with consensus for the region’s constitutional rights. Bilawal requested politicians, whether on the treasury or opposition benches, not to politicise the issue of terrorism or create controversy out of steps taken to combat it, but rather to play their role in fighting it. Bilawal also spoke about Jamiat Ulema-i-Islam (JUI-F) chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman, saying he had the right to criticise the government’s policies, and that there should certainly be room for difference of opinion in the country. He said the PPP had always imposed emergency through constitutional and legal means. “In fact, during the 2008–2013 government, when emergency rule was imposed in Balochistan, it was also because of the terrorism situation, and governor’s rule was imposed there against the PPP’s own government. “If the PPP thought only of itself, how would it have removed its own government?“ He said Fazl’s party has also been affected by terrorist attacks, so he hoped the JUI-F chief would criticise the PPP politically as much as he wished, but also condemn the terrorists. Bilawal added that if Fazl made an effort, harmony between the government and the opposition could be achieved.

Cotton arrivals jump 7.5pc as textile crisis deepens. • Industry says 500 ginning factories, over 150 textile mills closed • Ginners allege imported inputs meant for re-export are being sold locally LAHORE: Cotton arrivals at ginning factories rose 7.53 per cent year-on-year to 4.08 million bales by Oct 15, but the domestic cotton and textile industries are facing a deepening crisis, with around 500 ginning factories, over 150 textile mills and nearly half of the country’s power looms reportedly lying idle. Industry representatives have attributed the crisis to rising production costs and alleged misuse of the Export Facilitation Scheme (EFS), under which imported yarn and fabric are reportedly being sold in the domestic market instead of being re-exported. According to the Pakistan Cotton Ginners Association (PCGA), arrivals reached 4,081,265 bales by Oct 15, up 285,628 bales from 3,795,637 bales a year earlier. Punjab recorded arrivals of 1.64m bales, up 7.79pc, while Sindh’s arrivals increased 7.35pc to 2.44m bales. Bahawalnagar led Punjab with 418,750 bales, followed by Bahawalpur with 294,606, Dera Ghazi Khan 236,514, Rahim Yar Khan 169,949 and Layyah 122,327. In Sindh, Sanghar topped the list with 1.14m bales, followed by Sukkur with 264,500 bales, Naushehro Feroze 223,200 and Khairpur 213,900. A total of 471 ginning factories were operational nationwide. Textile mills had purchased around 3.45m bales and exporters 97,000 bales, leaving 531,530 bales unsold. Arrivals during the preceding fortnight totalled 872,863 bales. However, Cotton Ginners Forum Chairman Ihsanul Haq warned that adverse weather could leave national production below initial estimates. He also pointed to a discrepancy between PCGA figures and those of the Punjab Crop Reporting Service, which put provincial production at 2.983m bales against the PCGA’s 1.638m bales in arrivals by Oct 15. Mr Haq said the alleged misuse of the EFS, coupled with rising production costs, had undermined the domestic industry. He cited estimates that 40m to 50m metres of fabric had been imported from China alone under the scheme, while exports had shown little corresponding growth. Figures released by the All Pakistan Textile Mills Association (Aptma) showed man-made yarn imports rising from 3,056 tonnes in the first quarter of 2025-26 to 12,773 tonnes in the corresponding quarter of 2026-27. Man-made fabric imports increased from 660 tonnes to 8,628 tonnes over the same period. Mr Haq alleged that some imports intended for re-export were instead being sold locally, where an 18pc sales tax applied, putting domestic manufacturers at a disadvantage. Aptma has welcomed Customs action against alleged misuse of the scheme and called for restrictions on imports of man-made yarn and fabric under the EFS. It said around 500 ginning factories and more than 150 textile mills had closed, while nearly half of the country’s power looms were inactive. Sajid Mahmood, head of the Transfer of Technology Department at the Central Cotton Research Institute (CCRI), Multan, said cotton revival required policies focused not only on production but also on farmers’ profitability, production costs, market access and lint quality. If cotton continued to offer lower returns than competing crops, farmers could reduce acreage in the next season, he warned. With 15 to 20 days of picking remaining, he urged farmers to follow agricultural experts’ advice to protect yields and quality. The CCRI has recommended a spray containing 2kg of urea per 100 litres of water in fields with eight to 10 green bolls per plant to encourage boll opening. Farmers should also monitor pink bollworm infestation, pick mature bolls promptly and harvest in dry weather to prevent contamination. Mr Mahmood said the success of cotton revival should be measured by farmers’ net income per acre, not merely the volume of arrivals at ginning factories. Karachi Cotton Brokers Forum leader Naseem Usman urged the government not only to announce a cotton support price but also to devise a procurement mechanism in case market prices fell below the support level. He hoped that the undocumented cotton business would see a decline this year due to strict government measures and might lead to some increase in the overall cotton production. 18 marble workers abducted in Khuzdar. QUETTA: As many as 18 labourers working at a marble mine in the Naal area, about 40 kilometres from Khuzdar city, were kidnapped on Sunday, police said. A large group of armed men entered the mine premises, held the labourers at gunpoint and abducted 18 of them, along with the son of a mine factory’s owner, officials said. The abductors also opened fire on a worker when he attempted to flee, they added. The abducted labourers are locals from the Wadh and Naal areas. The mine belongs to Sardar Alam Khan Bizenjo, son of Sardar Aslam Bizenjo, the tribal chief of the Bizenjo tribe. Aslam Bizenjo is affiliated with the National Party and has served as a minister in several Balochistan governments. While fleeing the scene, the armed men also took away a loader and two vehicles, officials said. Officials said security forces had launched a search operation in the area to trace the abd­u­cted labourers. No group has so far claimed res­ponsibility for the kidnapping. Land dispute between railways and KMC over road construction erupts into street fighting. KARACHI: A road project promising to bring relief to the city’s traffic problems has become the centre of a tense confrontation, with a clash between Pakistan Railways (PR) police and Karachi Metropolitan Corporation (KMC) City Wardens, threatening to derail construction just weeks before its scheduled completion. It began with an objection over alleged “unauthorised construction” on the railway land. The dispute soon escalated into a physical scuffle, with the railway police taking the chief of KMC City Wardens to a police station. The controversy centres on the dual carriageway linking Natha Khan Bridge with Pehlwan Goth and Habib University, running parallel to Chakor Nullah. The road is intended to provide an alternative route for commuters travelling through Gulistan-i-Jauhar and adjoining areas. Valued at around Rs780 million, the project is expected to ease pressure on Sharea Faisal, Rashid Minhas Road, Dalmia Road and Gulistan-i-Jauhar. Railway police claim ownership of land where municipal authorities are constructing dual carriageway With Oct 30 project completion deadline looming, the railway police’s objection over land ownership and permissions has raised questions about why the issue surfaced at such a critical stage. The confrontation also threatens to acquire a wider political dimension, with an already strained relationship between the Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz-led federal government and the Pakistan Peoples Party, which governs Sindh and Karachi’s municipal administration. The railways, a federal government enterprise, maintained that the road project encroaches on land belonging to the Karachi Circular Railway (KCR) and that the construction on its land was without authorisation. The KMC officials said railways never raised the objection before. The incident unfolded on Sunday afternoon when the railways police officials intervened at the construction site and stopped the work, prompting the chief of KMC City Wardens to arrive with their contingent. The two sides initially engaged in a heated exchange over the construction, which soon escalated into a physical scuffle. The KMC alleged that the railways police personnel severely beat City Wardens Director Saim Imran before taking him to a Pakistan Railways police station. “The land where the road was being constructed belonged to the KCR and that the dispute arose over construction activity on the railways land,” a PR official said. He said railway authorities were currently collecting information about the incident and would determine the next course of action in accordance with the law once all relevant details had been gathered. The KMC, meanwhile, expressed strong resentment, questioning why the PR had raised objections so late, putting a multi-million-rupee public welfare project at risk just weeks before its completion. The KMC spokesman rejected the PR’s claim and said that the municipal body had fulfilled all legal requirements before launching the project more than two months ago. “This is not correct,” he said responding to the railways’ claim over land ownership. “This is a major project in terms of benefits it will bring to the people and any move to undermine its potential or put it at risk would be detrimental to the interests of Karachi’s residents.” He said senior KMC officials were in contact with the railways authorities and expressed the hope that the matter would be resolved soon. Pakistan stresses diplomacy as Iran rejects US ‘threats’. • Dar discusses evolving regional situation in call with Araghchi • Iranian FM says Tehran rejects intimidation but remains open to dialogue • Insists seven-day Hormuz reopening proposal remains on table • Pakistani, Egyptian FMs condemn Houthi attacks, discuss R-4 coordination • Iran’s new defence minister threatens ‘enormous damage’ to US if attacks renewed ISLAMABAD: Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar on Sunday stressed the need for continued dialogue and diplomacy in a telephone conversation with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi as regional tensions persisted amid the US-Iran conflict and renewed fighting in Yemen. The Foreign Office said the two ministers discussed the evolving regional situation as well as the ongoing meeting of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation’s (OIC) Council of Foreign Ministers in Baghdad. Mr Dar “underscored the importance of continued dialogue and diplomacy in addressing regional challenges”, the FO said, adding that the two sides agreed to remain in close contact. Mr Dar also held a telephone conversation with Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty and exchanged views on recent regional developments. The ministers strongly condemned Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia and reaffirmed their solidarity with the kingdom as well as support for its sovereignty, territorial integrity and security. They also discussed cooperation under the Regional Four (R-4) framework comprising Pakistan, Egypt, Turkiye and Saudi Arabia. The two ministers looked forward to the next R-4 meeting to coordinate further on regional issues. Iran rejects ‘threats’ Meanwhile, Mr Arag­hchi told the OIC meeting in Baghdad that Iran “does not accept coercion, threats, or intimidation” by the US and “will not relinquish its sovereign rights under pressure”. “But it remains ready for dialogue based on mutual respect and credible guarantees,” he added. Speaking to the media in Baghdad, Mr Araghchi said Iran’s offer to reopen the strategic waterway within seven days remained on the table. “Our situation is clear and based on the seven-day proposal presented to the US. They shared comments which we are reviewing, but our proposal is still on the table,” Mr Araghchi said. He said that if the US showed “honesty”, the path towards reopening the Strait of Hormuz was clear. Iran’s conditions incl­ude lifting the US blockade on its ports, removing sanctions on its oil exports and ending hostilities across regional fronts. Mr Araghchi added that if Washington accepted Tehran’s conditions, the strait could reopen within six days, followed by the resumption of talks the next day. US warned Iran’s newly appointed defence minister Mehrdad Akhlaghi warned that any renewed US military attack would cause “enormous damage” to Washington and its regional allies. “People can rest assured that they will most likely not dare to attack us,” Mr Akhlaghi told reporters shortly after securing parliament’s vote of confidence. “If they do, they themselves and the region will suffer enormous damage,” he said.
