Recriminations grow over failure of PTI protest plan. • Salman Akram Raja tries to quell talk of ‘disagreement’ among core committee members • Insiders say march date was announced without consultation; protest plans kept under wraps, even from party leaders ISLAMABAD: Controversy over its failure to hold a protest march continues to plague the PTI, with the fallout suggesting differences within its leadership over who is to blame for the botched mobilisation , even as party leaders continued to publicly deny any disarray. With questions mounting, PTI Secretary General Salman Akram Raja turned to social media on Sunday to play down talk of a “disagreement” during a meeting of the party’s core committee and to answer the allegations made against Sohail Afridi, the non-functional chief minister of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. “There should be no ambiguity,” Mr Raja wrote on X, calling Mr Afridi “a brave young man” who has stayed steadfast with the ideology of PTI founder Imran Khan. He said, however, that the administrative aspects of the protest march needed to be critically reviewed to counter the “narratives” being propagated against Mr Afridi. He accused critics of presenting core committee discussions “out of context” and distorting them as part of “conspiratorial narratives”. Meanwhile, a senior party leader who attended the meeting and spoke to Dawn on condition of anonymity, painted a less rosy picture. The leader said the party’s core committee meetings had started to discuss why the protest march failed and that the discussion was still ongoing. “On Saturday night, the meeting started after 10pm and ended after 2am. As many as 16 members of the committee got an opportunity to speak, and the remaining will speak in upcoming sessions,” he said. “At the outset, PTI Chairman Barrister Gohar said the meeting was called to discuss the current situation and the way forward. However, Raja suggested that they first discuss how the date for the protest march, Sept 27, was announced,” the leader added. “During the meeting, it was revealed that in August, Afridi had called a meeting in KP which was attended by Gohar, Raja, Asad Qaiser, Shafiullah Jan, Mina Khan, Shahid Khatak and Taimur Jhagra,” he said. Afridi had announced that the march would be held on Sept 27 , but this information was leaked to some vloggers subsequently. When criticism started that it had not been discussed in the political committee and core committee, the meetings of both committees were called on the same day, and in the evening Afridi made the announcement at a public meeting. The insider further disclosed that the leadership was kept in the dark regarding the operational strategy for the protest and the party’s broader negotiation tactics. “It was also revealed that Afridi was asked a number of times what the plan was, but he kept his cards close to his chest,” he said. “The meeting also heard that the PTI team had decided to walk out over the issue of terrorism, and when they realised it could trigger criticism, it was decided to use the name of Imran Khan and a meeting with him.” The leader said that during the meeting, Raja asked Ali Asghar Khan, son of the late Air Marshal Asghar Khan, why the party did not hold the protest march after Afridi’s arrest. Ali Asghar Khan, who is PTI secretary general in KP and head of the coordination committee for the protest march, said he was not aware of any such plans. “Asghar claimed that he had asked Afridi and Junaid Akbar many times, but they said details would be shared soon,” the leader said. “It annoyed many members of the core committee, as they said more than 1,400 workers and leaders were arrested under the Maintenance of Public Order law, but PTI in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa did not have any plan.” Another leader said Haleem Adil Sheikh confessed that the opposition was 70 per cent responsible and the government 30pc responsible for the failure of talks. “The agreement was finalised as Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi brought an amended agreement that both sides agreed to without meeting Imran Khan,” he said. “Soon after that, a call also came from Afridi to say that the meeting could not be held without first consulting Imran Khan.” The committee also discussed reports claiming that Barrister Gohar had given approval to establish offices of TTAP at the district level, the leader claimed. “Raoof Hasan objected and asked how it was possible, and Barrister Gohar said that he did not give any such approval.” The source further claimed that during the meeting, Seemabia Tahir suggested that the party should go for another protest march, but a majority of the members said that it was not possible during the current circumstances. When contacted for a response, PTI Central Information Secretary Sheikh Waqas Akram declined to comment on the matter. Published in Dawn, October 19th, 2026

LPG stakeholders seek daily pricing amid soaring rates. ISLAMABAD: As liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) prices surge following the closure of the Rahimdad-250 border post, market stakeholders on Sunday urged the government to shift from monthly to weekly or daily pricing, in line with petroleum products, and delink rates from Saudi Aramco’s Contract Price (CP). The demand comes ahead of winter, when LPG consumption traditionally rises, increasing the risk of hoarding, blackmarketing and artificial price hikes, particularly in remote and hilly areas. Stakeholders say the LPG policy, unchanged for over a decade, no longer reflects market realities. Although prices are benchmarked to Saudi CP, supplies largely come from Iran, Oman, the UAE and Iraq, including Iranian LPG allegedly routed through alternative sea channels. They argue that advance monthly prices notified by the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) discourage major state-owned enterprises (SOEs) from importing LPG, leaving the market vulnerable to private importers and land-route suppliers amid weak enforcement. Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik and ministry spokesman Zafar Abbas did not respond to written queries. Border closures, outdated pricing and weak oversight fuel LPG market crisis The Ministry of Commerce’s October 16 memorandums withdrawing electronic import form (EIF) exemptions for Iranian imports and shipments to Central Asian Republics (CARs) and Azerbaijan via Iran have further disrupted supplies. More than 4,500 tonnes of LPG are reportedly stranded on the Iranian side. Pakistan consumes nearly two million tonnes of LPG annually, of which 30 per cent is produced domestically and 70pc imported. Of the 1.2 million tonnes imported, around 250,000 tonnes arrive through Port Qasim and nearly one million tonnes through Iranian routes, including Taftan, Mand and Rahimdad-250. Taftan has remained closed for nearly six months over security concerns, while Mand faces intermittent disruptions, increasing reliance on Rahimdad-250. Mohammad Ali Haider, vice chairman of the LPG Marketing Association, representing over 200 companies, said prices rose by Rs100 per kilogram over the weekend following withdrawal of the trade exemption and could climb further without immediate intervention. He said no imports were currently arriving at Saudi CP-based prices. Before the war, Iranian auctioned LPG reached the border at $100-150 per tonne below Saudi CP. War-related insurance and freight premiums have since pushed costs to around $300 per tonne above CP, making Ogra’s benchmark increasingly unrealistic. Mr Haider said oil prices had shifted to daily adjustments after the war began, while LPG remained tied to advance monthly notifications disconnected from actual costs. Consequently, major players, including SSGC, SNGPL and Pak-Arab Refinery, avoid imports at notified rates, fearing accountability investigations. Border disruptions have also shifted pressure to Gwadar, pushing freight costs from $60-80 to as high as $380 per tonne. Mr Haider alleged that manipulated freight arrangements, questionable import declarations and the absence of digital tracking of tankers, transporters and distributors facilitated profiteering and tax evasion. He also criticised a petroleum division directive requiring SOEs to auction LPG against signature bonuses, arguing that the mechanism favoured cash-rich companies. Pakistan Petroleum Limited had previously allocated production through transparent bidding, offering 25 tonnes monthly to each successful bidder. A relatively obscure company reportedly offered a Rs220 million signature bonus for a five-tonne quota, prompting allegations of money laundering and consumer exploitation. Litigation has stalled the process. Mr Haider urged the government to review the LPG policy with stakeholders, revise the Rs35,000-per-tonne marketing margin fixed in 2016, digitally track imports and distribution, and publish daily prices on Ogra’s website. He also questioned the use of a Rs4,690-per-tonne petroleum levy introduced in 2016 to cushion consumers against price shocks, saying it was not serving its intended purpose. Mangrove loss raises flood, erosion risks along Karachi coast. Satellite images from 2000 and 2025 show mangroves near Mai Kolachi replaced by reclaimed land.—Courtesy Suparco ISLAMABAD: New satellite images from 2000 and 2025 released by the country’s space agency show a fundamental shift in land cover along Karachi’s coastal zone near the Mai Kolachi Bypass, where mangrove stands and natural tidal creeks have increasingly given way to reclaimed land and urban development. In a note on the development, the Space and Upper Atmosphere Research Comm­ission (Suparco) said areas once characterised by continuous mangrove cover and natural tidal creeks had progressively been converted into reclaimed land and urban plots. “This transformation refle­cts a transition from ecosystem-based coastal protection to hard, land-intensive development. Mangrove removal directly weakens the coastal system’s ability to respond to climate stress,” the agency said. Suparco observed that mangroves played a key role in regulating coastal temperatures, trapping sediments and absorbing atmospheric carbon. Their clearance not only eliminated an important blue-carbon reservoir but also disrupted hydrological connectivity, increasing surface runoff and altering tidal flows, it said. “Over time, this raises the likelihood of localised flooding, shoreline instability and long-term land subsidence. From a climate perspective, the conversion of mangrove wetlands into built-up land represents a loss of natural resilience at a time when sea-level rise and extreme weather events are accelerating,” it said. Unlike engineered structures, mangroves adapt and regenerate, offering protection that strengthens over time. Their replacement with static infrastructure transfers climate risk directly to urban assets and populations, the agency observed. Satellite images from 2000 and 2025 show mangroves near Mai Kolachi replaced by reclaimed land.—Courtesy Suparco When contacted, Senator Sherry Rehman, chairperson of the Senate Standing Committee on Climate Change, declined to comment. Karachi Mayor Murtaza Wahab did not respond to messages. Climate policy specialist Mohammad Saleem Shaikh warned that Pakistan must protect its mangrove forests and natural tidal creeks, stressing that their destruction threatened coastal communities, livelihoods and economic stability. Referring to Suparco’s satellite evidence showing changes along Karachi’s coast near Mai Kolachi Bypass between 2000 and 2025, Mr Shaikh called for urgent measures to prevent further environmental degradation. He said mangroves stored carbon, reduced coastal erosion, weakened storm surges and sustained fisheries and biodiversity. Their loss could increase Pakistan’s vulnerability to rising sea levels, cyclones and other climate-related threats, particularly along Karachi’s coastline and the Indus Delta, he warned. Mr Shaikh urged the federal and Sindh governments to strengthen environmental enforcement, prevent encroachment and ensure that coastal development projects underwent comprehensive environmental assessments. He also called for transparent satellite monitoring, community participation and scientifically planned restoration using native species. He said mangroves should be treated as natural climate infrastructure essential for disaster resilience and future generations. Meanwhile, satellite imagery acquired between 2019 and 2026 and posted on Suparco’s Spa­ce4Cli­mate webpage showed a substantial mangrove afforestation event in the Shah Bandar region of Sujawal. Comparative analysis of 19 Areas of Interest showed a 115pc increase in mangrove forest cover relative to 2019 baseline area of 116.46 hectares. Newly established mangrove vegetation of 151.24 hectares accounted for around 6.5pc of the total 2,321.8-hectare study area. Published in Dawn, October 19th, 2026

Oil-rich Alberta vote to determine next step towards possible separation from Canada. Alberta decides Monday if it wants to pursue a binding referendum on leaving Canada, with Prime Minister Mark Carney warning a separatist win would bring dangerous uncertainty during a trade war with the United States. Polls indicate less than a quarter of people in the western Canadian province support independence. But attention has focused on turnout in the days before the vote, and whether a motivated separatist camp could defy the polls, helped by complacent federalists. “Don’t let anyone tell you this is already decided. Turnout will determine the outcome,” Carney told a rally on Thursday. Carney, who grew up in Alberta, has called the referendum “a dangerous bluff” as US President Donald Trump imposes punishing tariffs and levels annexation threats aimed — the prime minister says — at breaking Canadian resolve. “Vote like Canada depends on it, because it does,” Carney said. Alberta has the world’s fourth-largest proven oil reserves and separatist momentum has been driven by anger over Ottawa’s management of the sector. Many Albertans loathed Carney’s predecessor, Justin Trudeau, who they accused of trying to suppress oil production to advance his pro-climate agenda. “If you want me to pinpoint who is responsible for the separatist sentiment, I think it’s Justin Trudeau,” Alberta Premier Danielle Smith told the Canadaland podcast this month. At a separatist rally in Edmonton on Saturday, 61-year-old Sandy Martel said people connected to the oil industry feel “robbed, cheated (and) mistreated.” “It’s time to stand up and say stop,” she told AFP. The vote comes days after a fire at a military base in the province left at least four soldiers dead and wounded dozens, prompting a national outpouring of condolences. ‘Huge uncertainty’ Smith, a conservative, says she wants Alberta to remain in Canada but called the referendum to settle the divisive issue. If a majority votes to separate, she has pledged to move forward with a binding referendum. If the federalists win, Smith says the secession question should be considered closed. Analysts have compared Smith’s tactics to those of former UK prime minister David Cameron, who had hoped to resolve the debate over Britain’s European Union membership with a vote. Carney led the Bank of England through the turmoil that surrounded Brexit, and issued a warning to Albertans about that experience on Thursday. “It wasn’t clear what ‘Brexit’ meant at the time,” he told a Calgary television station. “For the next few years, while that was being determined, there was huge uncertainty, investments stopped, the economy started to underperform,” he added, cautioning over unintended economic consequences. AI influence Monday’s referendum features 10 questions, including several related to immigration, but focus is on question 10, which asks: “Should Alberta remain a province of Canada?” or should the province take the legal steps required for a definitive independence vote? Alberta’s election authority says ballots for question 10 will be counted first, with results expected in the early hours Tuesday. The pre-referendum period was clouded by avalanches of manipulated AI content. Carney has urged “a decisive result,” but experts are concerned about a contested outcome no matter the numbers. “A very likely result of this referendum is going to be a community that sees this election as stolen or at least unfair,” said Aengus Bridgman, director of the Media Ecosystem Observatory at McGill University. Close Trump allies have also inserted themselves into the discussion, including Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who in January described Alberta as a “natural partner” for the United States. After a separatist party won Quebec’s provincial election on October 5, tech billionaire Elon Musk posted that “they would be better off” if they seceded. “Alberta and Saskatchewan should separate too,” he added. Asked about alleged foreign interference, Carney said Thursday that foreign governments, including the US, should not “get themselves involved in our elections.”

Traffic accident on Multan’s Bosan Road kills 5 men in their 20s. A road accident on Multan’s Bosan Road claimed the lives of five men in their 20s early on Monday after their speeding Toyota Corolla hit a road divider before crashing into the wall of a nearby plot and catching fire, Rescue 1122 said. All five occupants, who were residents of Shujaabad, died at the scene. “As a result of the accident, five individuals traveling in the car sustained severe injuries and died on the spot,” Rescue 1122 said. According to the police report, the accident occurred at 4am, and a passerby informed the control room about it at 4:15am. Rescue 1122 identified three of the five victims as men aged 22, 23 and 28. The ages of the two unidentified men were estimated to be around 24 or 25 years. All five victims had sustained head injuries, Rescue 1122 said. The spokesperson added that firefighters had brought the fire under control following the mishap. Rescue personnel shifted the bodies to Multan’s Nishtar Hospital. Rescue 1122 reported 43,160 road traffic crashes, resulting in 23,013 serious injuries and 434 deaths during the month of May across Punjab. The department secretary had expressed concerns at the large number of road accidents.

Covering Karachi's Nehr-i-Khayyam poses risk of urban flooding: experts. • Clifton residents, environmentalists stage rally to protest construction at key waterway • Demand suspension of work until EIA is conducted and project details are made public KARACHI: Expressing concern over construction at Nehr-i-Khayyam, an open drain in Clifton’s Block 5, residents and environmentalists from across the city held an awareness walk on Sunday, fearing that covering the drain would reduce its width and pave the way for “commercial activity”. Holding placards with messages such as “Commercial use of Nehr-i-Khayyam not accepted” and “Stop concreting drains, restore Nehr-i-Khayyam”,“Save Nehr-i-Khayyam and stop urban flooding”, the participants gathered near the construction site and said trees had previously been present on both sides of the drain, but now remained on only one side, with just a few left along the stretch where construction was under way. Dawn visited the site and observed that construction was underway on one side of the drain, where two columns had been built. Half of the columns had been plastered with cement, while T-shaped concrete blocks lay nearby. Standing behind a banner bearing the words “Save Nehr-i-Khayyam”, Rasha Tarek, a protester and member of the Karachi Residents’ Community (District South), questioned the practice of discharging sewage into the waterway and then using its pollution to justify covering more than half of it. “Where in the world do people discharge sewage into a waterway, then claim that its water is polluted and proceed to cover over half of it?” she asked. She added that they had stood up for the city and urged everyone to unite to save the waterway. She also demanded an environmental impact assessment (EIA) and said residents should be informed about the project. Masood Lohar, founder and CEO of the Clifton Urban Forest and an environmentalist, claimed that the project had been approved by the Sindh cabinet in 2019 for “recreational purposes”. He alleged that the construction was intended for commercial activity. He said that if an EIA hearing had been held, its details should be made public and the authorities should disclose which civil society representatives or residents had been invited to attend. Expressing concern, he said the authorities were blocking a major intertidal channel between two creeks, adding that the city had already been choked. He termed the matter a “national security issue”. He warned that if Karachi received 250mm of rainfall, the port and important security installations could become dysfunctional. Another environmentalist, Yasir Husain, said he had joined the protest to show solidarity with the community. He added that under the law, every government project should undergo an environmental assessment. He said the purpose of the project remained unclear, as its details had not yet been shared. Mr Husain said that a one-kilometre stretch of the drain, from Ocean Mall to Boat Basin, had suddenly been taken up for construction and a platform had now been built over it. He added he would file a right-to-information request to obtain details of the project. Meanwhile, he added, the protest would continue every weekend. He said he had only been able to obtain information that the project fell under the local government department and was titled “Rehabilitation of Nehr-i-Khayyam, including diversion of sewerage water, district South”. “This project is not about cleaning sewage,” he said, adding that “it is a commercial project, and the sewage will end up in the sea”. Actor Tipu Sharif, who stood alongside other protesters, said he had been a resident of the area for the past 25 years. He claimed that over the past four years, he had witnessed rapid commercialisation in the area. He questioned why the waterway could not be allowed to remain in its original form, asking, “If it was built as a waterway, why not let it remain one? Why is it necessary to cover everything with cement?” He warned that the waterway had helped prevent rainwater from accumulating during heavy rainfall in the area. However, if it was covered, blocked or narrowed, garbage could obstruct the flow of rainwater and create problems during the rainy season. In a press statement, residents of the area demanded the suspension of construction until the required environmental assessment had been conducted and approval obtained from the Sindh Environmental Protection Agency. They also demanded the disclosure of project documents, including the design, and the preservation of the channel’s full original width and banks as open public land. The statement further called for an end to the discharge of untreated sewage into the channel and demanded that wastewater be treated before reaching Boat Basin and the sea. Published in Dawn, October 19th, 2026

UN agency to end monthly aid to 500,000 people in Gaza over funding shortfall. The World Food Programme said Monday it would end monthly assistance to 500,000 people in Gaza due to a funding shortfall, despite acute needs in the war-battered Palestinian territory. With the cutbacks, 1.1 million Palestinians in Gaza — still about half the population — will be receiving either food or cash assistance each month from the UN agency, in reduced amounts. The World Food Programme (WFP) said its efforts had mitigated the effects during a famine last year in Gaza and warned that conditions had not improved to the point that it can take away aid. “People are not safe. Airstrikes continue on a daily basis. People continue to be displaced,” Shaun Hughes, the WFP country director, told AFP at the agency’s office in east Jerusalem. “Almost everybody remains without a permanent home to live in. And the humanitarian conditions are brutal,” he said. According to the latest assessments, 1.4 million people — or two-thirds of Gaza’s population — are still “acutely food insecure” and need humanitarian assistance to survive, he said. In August last year, the UN’s Integrated Food Security Phase Classification said that Gaza was suffering famine conditions. The famine classification was lifted in December, two months after a US-brokered ceasefire was announced in Gaza. Israel has kept striking Gaza since then, vowing to kill anyone involved in the October 7 attack. Since the ceasefire, the WFP has been able to step up assistance and had been reaching between 1.5 million and 1.8 million people every month. “This has been a lifeline. But now, rather than being able to sustain and scale up that assistance, we’re actually having to reduce it,” Hughes said. “And that’s not because we don’t have humanitarian access to deliver food; that’s because we don’t have funding.” Less aid to each recipient In addition to reducing the number of people who receive rations, the WFP has been forced to shrink the content. Families receiving food assistance will now get only one food parcel instead of two and a smaller bag of wheat flour, the WFP said in an operational note. The 75,000 families who receive assistance in cash will see the amount reduced from 1,250 to 750 shekels ($400 to $240) per month. The WFP is funded by governments as well as private donors. It has seen a sharp drop in resources, including after President Donald Trump returned to power in the United States and drastically slashed contributions to UN agencies as well as bilateral aid. The agency says it needs about $450 million over the next six months for its operations in Gaza and the West Bank, but in 2026 it has only received about half the usual financing for the Palestinian territories. In September, the agency also reduced by half the number of aid recipients in the West Bank, which Israel has occupied since 1967, from 400,000 to 200,000. “Now is not the time in the history of Palestine and Gaza to turn away from what is happening in Gaza,” Hughes said. The WFP says that conditions have moderately improved in Gaza but noted that needs could rise again with the onset of winter. Israel has allowed more goods into Gaza under the terms of the Trump ceasefire but still imposes heavy restrictions, turning away shipments of anything that is seen as having potential military use — a policy that has included blocking even prosthetic limbs, according to the United Nations. Israel has ramped up longstanding criticism of the United Nations since the Gaza war, accusing the world body of bias and perpetuating dependency among Palestinians.

We were ready with our tax filings, was the FBR?. “Wherever law ends, tyranny begins” — John Locke A few years after my resignation from the Income Tax Service, I happened to visit the offices in Lahore as a representative of a corporate client. A female officer made a remark that left me somewhat bewildered. According to her, laws were binding on taxpayers, not on those administering them. Having spent nineteen years within the department, I had thought I had understood the relationship between law and administration reasonably well. Her statement appeared astonishing then. However, as I watch the annual ritual surrounding income tax returns unfold today , I sometimes wonder whether she was merely articulating an institutional philosophy that the rest of us had failed to recognise. For individuals and associations of persons (AOPs), the statutory date is on or before September 30 following the end of the tax year. In the case of companies, section 118 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 prescribes December 31 where the tax year ends between January 1 and June 30, and September 30 in other cases. The words “ on or before ” are important. A normal tax year ends on June 30, which corresponds to the financial year (July to June) adopted by the state. Nothing in the statutory formulation suggests that a taxpayer who is ready to comply should have to wait until September merely because the administration has not yet made its prescribed return operational. It stipulates the last date by which the obligation must be discharged but there is one rather substantial difficulty. While the taxpayer may be ready, the FBR may not. Income tax returns in Pakistan are now overwhelmingly filed electronically through the online portal named IRIS (Inland Revenue Information System) . Taxpayers cannot invent their own return form. They cannot prepare an Excel sheet containing what they consider adequate information and declare that they have complied with section 114. They must use the prescribed electronic return made available by the FBR. The state, therefore, controls the only doorway through which compliance is possible. Compliance cannot be a one-way street. Once the state makes itself the exclusive gatekeeper of compliance, its own preparedness ceases to be an internal administrative matter. It becomes part of the taxpayer’s ability to obey the law. This becomes particularly important because every Finance Bill, once passed an Act of Parliament, introduces amendments affecting rates, exemptions, deductions, credits, withholding provisions, declarations and sometimes the very manner in which income is to be reported. Naturally, the return form has to accommodate those changes. Nobody disputes that software requires modification in the light of these amendments. What is difficult to understand is why this annual phenomenon continues to be treated as an unforeseen emergency. body{margin:0;padding:0;font-family:system-ui,-apple-system,sans-serif;overflow-wrap:anywhere;} The filing window that shrank Timeline of Tax Year 2026 income tax returns. The FBR issued draft returns on 6 May. The Finance Act took effect on 1 July but the final return was not ready. The final return was notified on 2 September, leaving 28 days before the 30 September deadline. The deadline was extended to 15 October and again to 31 October. The writer proposes building the return alongside the Finance Bill, having it live on 1 July, a legal minimum of 90 days to file from the day it goes live, and automatic deadline shifts for any delay. The budgetary exercise begins months earlier. Proposed amendments are available through the Finance Bill. The FBR itself participates intimately in the legislative exercise. Its policy officers know what changes are being contemplated and its information-technology teams should be working simultaneously on alternative versions of the return. Tax Year 2026 provides a particularly revealing example. The FBR issued draft electronic returns for individuals, SMEs, AOPs and companies on May 6, 2026. Yet the final electronic returns for Tax Year 2026 were notified only at the beginning of September — SRO 1495(I)/2026 dated September 2. In other words, although the taxpayer’s statutory deadline remained September 30, the final return itself arrived when nearly two-thirds of the presumed compliance period had already vanished. Consider what this means. The statutory deadline remained September 30, but taxpayers and practitioners were effectively given certainty about the final prescribed electronic return only when September had already begun. Millions of returns then had to be prepared, checked, reconciled with wealth statements and submitted through a single electronic system within a dramatically compressed period. Inevitably, tax bars and trade organisations sought an extension. The original September 30, 2026, deadline was first extended to October 15, 2026 and, on October 15, the FBR extended it again to October 31, 2026 , expressly referring to requests received from trade bodies and tax bar associations. And here lies the irony. The FBR calls this an extension. Taxpayers may reasonably regard part of it as restitution. The extension is presented as a concession to taxpayers but is it really so? If an authority takes a substantial portion of the statutory filing period to make the final compliance mechanism available, the additional time subsequently granted cannot honestly be regarded entirely as administrative generosity. Part of it merely restores time which taxpayers never effectively possessed. We have somehow reversed the relationship between citizen and state. The taxpayer is admonished to comply punctually. Failure attracts consequences. Late filing affects status and can invite statutory penalties and other disadvantages. Notices, payments, appeals and responses carry dates. The taxpayer lives by the calendar. Yet the institution that determines whether electronic compliance is even possible appears to face no comparable clock. When it delays, taxpayers must petition that very institution for additional time. Administrative default is thus converted into administrative discretion. This is not merely an issue of convenience. It raises a basic question of administrative fairness . A government cannot reasonably demand punctual compliance with an obligation while withholding, until late in the prescribed period, the instrument through which that obligation must be performed. Imagine a court requiring an appeal to be filed by September 30 but refusing to provide the prescribed appeal form until September 2. Would we seriously congratulate the court for subsequently extending the deadline? Digitalisation was supposed to facilitate compliance. It should not convert administrative preparedness into a condition precedent to the taxpayer’s ability to obey the law. Nor is the answer complicated. The return for the following tax year should be substantially designed alongside the Finance Bill. Drafts can be programmed and tested before June. Once Parliament enacts the Finance Act, final changes can immediately be incorporated. The electronic form should ordinarily be operational from July 1 , or as close to that date as technically unavoidable. More importantly, the law itself should guarantee a minimum effective compliance period — say ninety days — beginning only when the final prescribed electronic return is fully operational. Every day of administrative delay should automatically move the statutory deadline by an equivalent period. If the prescribed electronic return is not available by July 1, the statutory filing date should automatically move by the corresponding period. Better still, legislation could provide that no taxpayer shall have fewer than, say, ninety days from the date on which the final electronic return becomes fully operational. Then nobody would need to plead for extensions. There would be no annual suspense. No last-minute circulars. No ritual exchanges between FBR and tax bars. In addition, no pretense that restoration of lost compliance time amounts to benevolence. The FBR rightly expects taxpayers to organise their affairs, maintain records, understand amendments and respect statutory deadlines. Taxpayers are equally entitled to expect their tax administration to anticipate legislation, prepare its systems and provide the prescribed mechanism in good time. The rule of law does not mean that citizens obey while administrators improvise. It requires the State itself to organise its conduct around the law it enforces. Perhaps that officer’s remark from many years ago deserves to be remembered — but as a warning, not a principle. Laws are not made merely for those upon whom the state imposes obligations. They bind the institutions entrusted with administering them as well. Until that elementary proposition enters our tax culture, the ritual will continue: The FBR will provide the instrument late, taxpayers will plead for more time, and the restoration of lost days will be announced as facilitation. That is not taxpayer facilitation. It is compliance by endurance.

Kidnapping, torture case registered against railway police officials amid dispute with KMC over road project. KARACHI: A kidnapping and torture case has been registered against Railway Police officials on the complaint of Karachi Metropolitan Corporation (KMC) City Wardens Director Saim Imran, who has accused them of abducting him and taking him to an undisclosed location, where he was allegedly tortured. The development comes amid a dispute between Pakistan Railways (PR) police and KMC City Wardens over a road project aimed at easing traffic congestion in the city. The confrontation threatens to disrupt construction weeks before its scheduled completion. The controversy centres on a dual carriageway linking Natha Khan Bridge with Pehlwan Goth and Habib University, running parallel to Chakor Nullah. Valued at around Rs780 million, the project is expected to ease pressure on Sharea Faisal, Rashid Minhas Road, Dalmia Road and Gulistan-i-Jauhar. According to the FIR, Imran said a road had been under construction from Natha Khan to Pehlwan Goth for the past four months and that he was on traffic management duty at the site on the day of the incident. He alleged that Cantt police station SHO Ahsan Rasheed arrived at the site with other police personnel and assaulted him. The complainant further alleged that he was taken to an undisclosed location, where he was tortured. He claimed that he was asked to hold the feet of senior officers and lick their shoes on their instructions. He was subjected to further torture after refusing to comply, according to the FIR. Imran added that he lost consciousness due to the alleged torture and regained consciousness at Abbasi Shaheed Hospital. According to the information provided, the case was registered at Shahrah-i-Faisal police station on the KMC’s complaint. The incident unfolded on Sunday afternoon when railway police officials intervened at the construction site and stopped the work, prompting the chief of KMC City Wardens to arrive at the site. The two sides initially engaged in a heated exchange over the construction, which soon escalated into a physical scuffle. The KMC alleged that the railways police personnel severely beat the City Wardens director before taking him to a Pakistan Railways police station. “The land where the road was being constructed belonged to the KCR and that the dispute arose over construction activity on the railway land,” a PR official said. He added railway authorities were collecting information about the incident and would determine the next course of action in accordance with the law once all relevant details had been gathered. The KMC, meanwhile, expressed strong resentment, questioning why the PR had raised objections so late, putting a multi-million-rupee public welfare project at risk just weeks before its completion. The KMC spokesman rejected the PR’s claim and said that the municipal body had fulfilled all legal requirements before launching the project more than two months ago. “This is not correct,” he said responding to the railways’ claim over land ownership. “This is a major project in terms of benefits it will bring to the people and any move to undermine its potential or put it at risk would be detrimental to the interests of Karachi’s residents.” He said senior KMC officials were in contact with the railways authorities and expressed the hope that the matter would be resolved soon.

Army major martyred, 4 terrorists killed in Balochistan IBOs: ISPR. An army major was martyred and four terrorists were killed during intelligence-based operations (IBOs) in Balochistan, the military’s media wing said on Monday. The Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) said in a statement that security forces conducted a series of operations in areas of Shadi Kaur and Pasni in Gwadar, and Jattakabad in Kalat district, on the reported presence of multiple hideouts of Fitna al Hindustan. The state has designated Balochistan-based groups as Fitna al Hindustan to highlight India’s role in terrorism and destabilisation across Pakistan. In the first operation on October 18, security forces conducted an IBO in the general area of Jattakabad, during which four terrorists were eliminated. “A large cache of arms and ammunition was also recovered,” it added. In the second operation, ISPR added that security forces conducted a series of clearance operations in the general area of Shadi Kaur, Pasni, in Gwadar. It added that 34-year-old Major Wajahat Waheed, a Lahore resident who was leading the operation, was martyred in an improvised explosive device (IED) attack. “Sanitisation operations will continue to eliminate any other terrorists found in the area. The relentless counterterrorism campaign under the vision of ‘ Azm-e-Istehkam ’, as approved by the Federal Apex Committee on the National Action Plan, will continue at full pace.” “Security forces and law enforcement agencies remain committed to eliminating the menace of foreign-sponsored and supported terrorism from the country,” ISPR added. President Asif Ali Zardari and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Monday, in separate statements, commended security forces for the successful operations. They also paid tribute to Major Wajahat Waheed, extending their condolences to his family. President Zardari, in a statement posted on X, reaffirmed that conspiracies of “the terrorists’ foreign patrons and their local facilitators will be thwarted”. PM Shehbaz reiterated the resolve to continue the fight against foreign-sponsored terrorism until its complete eradication, state media reported . Intensified operations Balochistan has witnessed an increase in terrorist activities in recent years, prompting security forces to intensify counter-terrorism operations. A day earlier, security forces killed eight “India-sponsored” terrorists during IBOs conducted in the Quetta, Nushki and Khuzdar districts of Balochistan. On the night of Oct 12/13, security forces busted a terrorist hideout and killed five terrorists during an IBO in Washuk, ISPR said . Days later, Balochistan government officials said that six terrorists affiliated with the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), two would-be female suicide bombers, and two commanders of a banned organisation had been arrested during IBOs across the province. They said around 90 arrested terrorists were being held at a centre where investigations and legal proceedings were under way. Earlier this month, five terrorists were eliminated in Balochistan’s Mastung district, state media reported . The number of terrorist attacks in the province increased by seven per cent from 83 in July to 89 in August , according to data compiled by the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies (PICSS). As per the report, Balochistan was declared the province “most affected” by terrorism.

Musk says will give SpaceX share to 'every kid in America'. Tech billionaire Elon Musk said on Monday that he would give every child in the United States a share in his SpaceX rocket company. “Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America,” Musk, the richest man in the world, said on X. “This will be the first of many,” he said, without providing details about how the scheme would work. There are around 73 million children under the age of 18 in the United States, according to 2024 data from the US Census Bureau. Musk owns 38 per cent of SpaceX, according to Forbes . His announcement comes after US President Donald Trump promised last month to give every American adult $5,000 if his Republican party retains control of Congress in November’s midterm elections. SpaceX set the record for the largest initial public offering in history, raising $85.7 billion in June. The company’s Starship megarocket reached orbit for the first time in September, a milestone for the rocket central to Musk’s Mars ambitions.

DPM Dar arrives in Tajikistan for high-level SCO moot. Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar arrived in Tajikistan’s capital Dushanbe on Monday to lead Pakistan’s delegation at a Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) meeting. Upon arrival, he was received by Tajikistan’s Minister of Energy and Water Resources Daler Juma, Pakistan’s Ambassador to Tajikistan Irfan Ahmed and Pakistan’s national coordinator for the SCO, Khalil Hashmi, along with senior Tajik government officials. Dar is visiting Dushanbe at the invitation of Tajik Prime Minister Qohir Rasulzoda to attend the SCO’s Council of Heads of Government (CHG) meeting being held from Oct 19-20, according to the Foreign Office (FO). The CHG is the SCO’s second-highest decision-making body and provides guidance on economic, financial, trade, connectivity and socio-economic cooperation, as well as the organisation’s budgetary matters, FO noted. “The prime ministers of Belarus, China, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Russia, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan, Iran’s vice president and India’s external affairs minister will also represent their respective countries at the meeting.” During his visit, Dar will also call on Tajikistan’s president and prime minister and hold bilateral meetings with his counterparts from SCO member states on the sidelines of the meeting, the FO added. Pakistan assumed the chairmanship of the SCO Council of Heads of State (CHS) for 2027 during an annual summit held in Kyrgyzstan in September. On Oct 1, Dar chaired a follow-up meeting to review preparations for the SCO CHS summit, which Islamabad is scheduled to host in 2027. In July, Pakistan hosted the 12th meeting of the Heads of Border Services of the Competent Authorities of the SCO. Islamabad also chairs SCO’s Reg­ional Anti-Terrorist Structure (SCO-RATS), a role it assumed last September. The country last hosted the SCO CHG meeting in Islamabad in October 2024.

Pakistan providing 'whatever support' Saudi Arabia needs for its defence: DG ISPR. Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) Director General Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry has said Pakistan is providing “whatever support is needed” to defend Saudi Arabia amid attacks by Yemen’s Houthi rebels against the kingdom. The military spokesperson’s remarks — made during an interview with Independent Arabia aired on Sunday — come as Saudi Arabia has been facing deadly attacks by Houthis in recent weeks . Islamabad and Riyadh have signed two defence pacts aimed at collective deterrence, the Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement between the two and the Makkah Joint Defence Alliance that also includes Turkiye. Responding to a query about the military support Pakistan was providing to the kingdom amid attacks by Houthis, the DG ISPR said Saudi Arabia’s “sovereignty, territorial integrity, and the security, and foremost the security of the Two Holy Mosques, is paramount”. “It’s non-negotiable; it’s absolute as far as Pakistan is concerned […] So whatever support is needed to do that is being provided and will be provided,” he affirmed, adding that no alliance makes public the specifics and the quantification of the support provided. Commenting on Pakistan’s reaction to the Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia, the military spokesman said, “Our reaction in Pakistan, on the streets, from a young boy and girl up to our political and military leadership, is one of anger.” He remarked, “Our reaction is that why would anyone in his right mind attack or threaten Saudi Arabia or the holy places or even give an impression of threatening the holy places.” He declared there could be no “ifs and buts” on the security of the holy sites. On whether Pakistan’s support to Saudi Arabia will strictly remain defensive if the Houthi attacks continue, the the military spokesperson said all three members of the alliance were “absolutely clear […] that this alliance has no offensive intent; it is purely defensive”. Citing Article 51 of the United Nations Charter that provides collective deterrence, he said such a mechanism “gives a very strong and clear message to those elements of instability, of chaos, in the region that if you directly or indirectly wage this war against any of these three countries, then the response will be collective”. “If that deterrence doesn’t work, then that deterrence has to be re-established by all means that are available to the three countries,” he added. Asked whether Islamabad had issued any “warning” to Tehran regarding Houthis as the Saudi deputy foreign minister linked the two, the DG ISPR stressed that Pakistan had been engaging with all parties involved, including Iran, “with the singular intent of restraint and to reduce the temperatures”. The military spokesperson reiterated that “all interactions and all conversations with the parties are based on dialling down the escalation”. Speaking further about the ongoing tensions in the Middle East, Lt Gen Chaudhry noted, “You have seen a sinusoidal sort of pattern in this conflict, that it does down and then the agent of chaos starts and they come into play and take the entity up.” He contended that such escalations will not “resolve this conflict”. “Whether you expand it to Houthis, whether you expand it to other places, it doesn’t serve anything. It only serves those who are interested in chaos in the region.” The DG ISPR added: “But at the same time, […] Pakistan is giving very strong signals that this collective deterrence is at play, has already been actualised and we will take all necessary steps for the security and territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and the Haramain Sharifain (The Two Holy Mosques).” He remarked that the “message is going to everyone, whether he is in front or he is behind” the escalation. Regarding reports linking the alliance’s formation to the need to deter Iran or Israel, Lt Gen Chaudhry said the pact was not “country-specific” and did not have any “offensive intent”. However, he added: “It is [formed] to have peace, stability and security in the region. So any actor which threatens that peace, stability and security, it automatically interacts with this collective deterrence mechanism.” Regarding the threats to maritime navigation in the Bab al-Mandeb Strait and the Strait of Hormuz, the DG ISPR noted that Riyadh had established a multinational maritime defence coalition, with a Pakistani naval officer serving as its deputy commander. ‘We need to stop attacking each other’ Asked about his message to Saudi Arabia and the Muslim world, Lt Gen Chaudhry said Muslims “need to unite”. He emphasised that there was no advantage “to these countries, any country, by vertically or horizontally escalating these conflicts”. “We need to stop attacking each other,” he maintained, highlighting that Pakistan had been trying to convey the same to all parties since the US-Iran war erupted. “If we are unable to come to a negotiated outcome and we turn into a military conflict, then this instrument of collective deterrence of the Makkah alliance will definitely come into play, as it is coming into play,” Lt Gen Chaudhry said. On scepticism raised about the Makkah pact, the DG ISPR remarked that the sceptics were “only those who have a problem with this alliance, so it’s their job to do this criticism”. “It’s not suddenly out of the blue that they have decided. The relations go way back,” he stressed. He further termed it “phenomenal” how the alliance has evolved “in a very short period of time”. Regarding the expansion of the alliance, the military spokesperson maintained that the door remains open to other countries that believe in the principle of collective deterrence and share the member states’ goals related to regional security and stability. Asked about reports of Egypt and Syria’s interest in joining, he stated such decisions rest with the political, strategic and military leadership of the three countries. Earlier this month, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye convened an emergency meeting under the Makkah Defence Alliance and agreed to deploy military forces and capabilities rapidly in the kingdom. While the statement did not specifically name any threat, the development came against the backdrop of Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia. The Makkah defence pact , signed on Aug 7, aims to strengthen collective deterrence and empower its signatory states to treat an attack against one of them as an attack against all of them. On Sept 18, the DG ISPR said Pakistan would go to “any extent” to defend Saudi Arabia, adding that Islamabad’s commitment to the kingdom’s security is “unconditional”. At the same time, Pakistan also stresses that the alliance is intended for collective deterrence and is defensive in nature.

IHC takes up Imaan, Hadi’s appeals against framing of charges in security breach case. ISLAMABAD: The Islamabad High Court (IHC) on Monday took up appeals filed by human rights lawyer Imaan Mazari and her husband, Hadi Ali Chattha, against an anti-terrorism court (ATC) order rejecting their petitions challenging the framing of charges and the inclusion of terrorism-related provisions in the security breach case . The case pertains to the alleged disruption of the security route of an international cricket team and incitement to public unrest. A division bench comprising Justice Inaam Ameen Minhas and Justice Shahrukh Arjumand heard the matter on Monday, with Riasat Ali Azad, Zainab Janjua and other lawyers appearing before the court. At the outset, Justice Minhas asked whether the accused had received copies of the relevant documents. Counsel Riasat Ali Azad replied in the negative and said he wanted to examine how the charges had been framed. The counsel argued that the ATC had passed the impugned order without the requisite authority to do so. He said the case had remained pending before the court of Judge Abual Hasanat Mohammad Zulqarnain from March 12, 2025, until recently. Citing the precedent in the Zulfikar Ali Bhutto case, Azad argued that the court in which the challan was submitted was the one authorised to hear the case. He further contended that the accused had not been provided with copies of the relevant documents and that the charges had not been read out in their presence, as they were not physically present in the courtroom at the time. “Legal proceedings cannot move forward in the absence of the accused,” the counsel argued, adding that the charge must be framed in the presence of the accused. He also alleged a violation of a decision of the National Judicial Policy Making Committee. Describing the charge as the foundation of a trial, Azad maintained that any defect in its framing would undermine the legality of the subsequent proceedings. Justice Minhas asked whether the trial was being conducted through a video link. The counsel replied that the proceedings had initially taken place through a video link but had shifted to a jail trial at the most recent hearing. The judge also inquired whose signatures appeared on the charge document. Azad said the document bore his signature, but lacked those of the accused, which, according to him, were legally required. Justice Minhas questioned whether the proceedings could not be conducted through a video link, observing that the accused had been connected through the facility and that their attendance had been recorded when the charges were framed. The counsel, however, insisted that the accused were not present when he signed the documents and requested the court to summon the video recording of the proceedings. He also said the copies had not been delivered to the accused in jail and that an affidavit had been submitted to this effect. Justice Minhas remarked that it appeared the defence had not intended to accept the copies. Azad responded that every application filed by the defence before the ATC had been rejected. He said the defence had requested both the case record and the video recording of the proceedings. The judge subsequently asked where it was stipulated that the accused must be physically produced for the framing of charges. Azad reiterated that the appeals also challenged the inclusion of anti-terrorism provisions in the case and repeatedly urged the high court to halt the trial. “We shall see; we will let you know,” Justice Minhas remarked. Justice Minhas said the court would issue an order and inform the parties accordingly. He concluded that notices had been issued and the court would decide how to proceed once the responses were received. ATC hearing adjourned Meanwhile, ATC Judge Tahir Abbas Sipra conducted the proceedings of the security breach case against Imaan and Hadi at the Adiala jail, where they are incarcerated. Advocate Janjua, representing the accused, withdrew her vakalatnama (authorisation to represent them). Subsequently, the hearing was adjourned until 10am tomorrow (Tuesday). No prosecution witnesses’ statements could be recorded during the hearing. Imaan and Hadi were indicted in the case on Oct 7, when both accused were produced via video link. Hadi had objected to the framing of charges, arguing that he had not yet been provided copies of the case documents and that charges could not be framed before completion of all legal formalities. Advocate Janjua also opposed the indictment, submitting that neither of them had been provided copies of the case record. She further contended that neither of the accused had been allowed to meet their lawyers, and therefore, the requirements for framing charges had not been fulfilled. Imaan and Hadi’s rearrest The lawyer couple has been in jail since their arrest on Jan 23 in a case registered against them for protesting outside the IHC and allegedly manhandling the IHC Bar Association (IHCBA) president. The arrest prompted criticism by rights bodies, politicians and journalists, who stressed the couple’s right to a fair trial. Just a day later, a sessions court sentenced them to 17 years on multiple charges under the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act (Peca) in a case pertaining to controversial social media posts. The convictions were widely condemned by lawyers and United Nations (UN) experts . On Sept 17, following months of litigation before the courts , the Supreme Court suspended their sentences in the case. The SC ordered their release pending the IHC’s final verdict on their appeals against the trial court’s decision. However, the reprieve was short-lived as hours later, Islamabad police arrested the couple again in connection with another case and produced them before an ATC, which sent them to jail on judicial remand. The case in which the two were arrested was registered at the federal capital’s Kohsar police station on March 22 last year on the complaint of City Magistrate Ghulam Murtaza Chandio. Imaan and her husband were accused of chanting anti-government slogans and blocking roads and were nominated by name in the FIR. However, at the time of registration of the case, no section of the Anti-Terrorism Act (ATA) had been added. The FIR included sections 188 (disobedience of an order lawfully promulgated by a public servant), 341 (wrongful restraint), 506 (punishment for criminal intimidation), 353 (assault or use of criminal force to deter a public servant from discharging their official duty) and 186 (obstructing a public servant in the performance of official duties).

French prime minister calls for curfews as govt grapples with unrest. French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu called for localised curfews on Monday, as protesters blocked the entrance to the Louvre in Paris and authorities scrambled to stem public discontent that over the weekend saw mass cost-of-living demonstrations spill over into some of the worst street violence in recent years. Lecornu huddled with ministers in a crisis meeting after the interior minister said the police “had lost control” during the weekend’s unrest . With the Yellow Vests movement, which organised the weekend’s rallies, calling for a new round of protests next Saturday, Lecornu called for regional authorities to impose “partial” and “localised” curfews to protect businesses after hundreds of shops were damaged and looted. “I’m absolutely determined to restore public order,” he vowed, adding that the government was ready to impose a state of emergency “if needed”. Saturday’s demonstrations saw some half a million people turn out across France to protest the cost of living, but morphed into some of the worst violence to rock the country in years, with town halls and shops looted and set ablaze. French President Emmanuel Macron also refused Interior Minister Laurent Nunez’s resignation even as he acknowledged security and intelligence failures in the government response. More than 2,500 people were arrested, while almost 1,000 members of the security forces were injured. Injuries were also reported among protesters, with one demonstrator’s hand blown off by a police crowd-control grenade. “On Saturday, in some major cities, you couldn’t look shopkeepers in the eye after hundreds of shops had been looted and tell them we hadn’t lost control,” Nunez said. Nunez acknowledged a “lack of anticipation” in the deployment of security forces on Saturday, whose numbers were insufficient to deal with the large crowds of rioters and looters on the fringes of the demonstrations. He estimated that some 60,000 law enforcement personnel had been deployed across the country that day. “Given the damage that has been caused, it was only right that I should hand in my resignation,” Nunez said. The presidency said in a statement that Macron had rejected the resignation, however, citing “the necessity for continued leadership of law enforcement”. Instead, Macron ordered Nunez to “take all necessary steps to ensure transparency over the failures in planning and intelligence that led to the violence”. To end the “barricades and looting, he also requested that the interior minister promptly implement new operational methods for security forces to use on the ground in combating rioters,” the statement added. Looting continued on Sunday, with Paris Mayor Emmanuel Gregoire saying Monday that around 30 shops had been targeted in the capital the previous day, describing the scenes as “unbearable”. CCTV footage shows a masked group breaking into a jewellery shop in Lyon, France, October 17, 2026, in this screengrab obtained from a handout video. — Reuters Nunez said some 350 people had been arrested in Paris on Sunday and overnight. Nationwide, more than 2,330 people were taken into police custody over the weekend — 70 per cent of whom were adults — and many of whom were already known to authorities, Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin said on Monday. More than 2,000 shops were expected to have been affected by the weekend’s violence across France, with damage running into “hundreds of millions of euros”, according to chamber of commerce president Alain Di Crescenzo. In an address to the nation on Sunday, Macron slammed the “unbridled” violence and said local authorities would be able to ban some rallies, but stopped short of imposing more drastic measures. City authorities in Marseille said on Monday they had banned public gatherings from noon to 08:00 pm (1000-1800 GMT). The European Union slammed the weekend violence as “unacceptable” but warned that the right to peaceful protest “must be protected” in France. Germany condemned the violence and updated its travel advice for France, saying “further demonstrations and, in some cases, further outbreaks of violence in the coming days cannot be ruled out”. The United Kingdom said the right to protest “can never excuse violence”. Louvre blocked Public discontent showed no signs of subsiding on Monday, with demonstrators blocking the entrance to Paris’s iconic Louvre Museum, the most visited in the world. Rising prices have fuelled anger in France, where diesel prices have jumped nearly 40pc and petrol by 25pc since March, and where food prices have risen by 25pc since 2021. The unrest has flared just months before a key presidential election where centrist Macron cannot stand again and Marine Le Pen, the far-right presidential candidate for the National Rally party, is riding high in the polls. Protesters and students from art and culture schools block the entrance to the Louvre Museum during a demonstration in support of a high school student movement demanding better school conditions and government action, in Paris, France, October 19, 2026. — Reuters Ministers and Le Pen have accused ultra-left groups of stoking the violence to boost the chances of the far-left firebrand Jean-Luc Melenchon in the presidential polls. On Monday, Lecornu blamed the “ultra-left movement” for seeking to “orchestrate deep unrest across the country”. “There is a whole network that could be mobilised to even call into question the timetable for the presidential election and the holding of the presidential election itself,” Lecornu told reporters. Europe Similar demonstrations have broken out in other countries. During the weekend, clashes broke out on the sidelines of a cost-of-living demonstration in Milan, with Mayor Giuseppe Sala warning: “I’m very worried because it’s a new phenomenon, which also originates from an international scenario and therefore feeds itself.” In Belgium, police fired tear gas and water cannons to disperse protesters in Brussels and Liege. In Spain, hundreds of tents have occupied Madrid’s central Puerta del Sol square since September, when the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her lifelong flat sparked nationwide protests in a country with soaring housing costs. Protesters have also set up tents in Portugal’s main cities of Lisbon and Porto over rising costs of housing.

SHC dismisses state appeal against Mahrang's 2025 acquittal in sedition case. The Sindh High Court (SHC) on Monday dismissed an appeal filed by the provincial government through the prosecutor general against the acquittal of Baloch Yakjehti Committee (BYC) leader Mahrang Baloch in a sedition case, declaring it non-maintainable. Mahrang had been booked on terrorism and sedition charges by Malir district’s Quaidabad police on Oct 11, 2024 for allegedly inciting people by levelling “allegations against security institutions”. Over a year later, she was acquitted by a Karachi anti-terrorism court (ATC). Subsequently, acting prosecutor general Muntazir Mehdi, on behalf of the state, had challenged the acquittal before the SHC in December 2025. On Monday, a two-judge SHC bench, headed by Justice Shamsuddin Abbasi and including Justice Miran Muhammad Shah, heard the appeal. Advocate Jibran Nasir appeared before the court to represent Mahrang and advanced his arguments. The court observed that the complainant in the first information report (FIR) was a private individual and questioned how the prosecution could file an appeal against the acquittal instead of the complainant. The prosecution claimed that the ATC had ignored facts while accepting Mahrang’s acquittal application. It highlighted that the public prosecutor had informed the ATC that there was clear evidence against Mahrang and that such evidence was supposed to be presented during trial. The prosecution further argued that deciding the acquittal application before the framing of charges was inappropriate. Mahrang, who is in Quetta prison in connection with other cases, had filed an acquittal application under Section 265-K of the Code of Criminal Procedure before ATC-V, which the court allowed. The FIR was registered on the complaint of a resident named Asad Ali Shams, who claimed that Mahrang was inciting violence in his area. The FIR invoked Section 7 (punishment for acts of terrorism) of the Anti-Terrorism Act (ATA) 1997 as well as sections 124-A (sedition), 148 (rioting, armed with deadly weapon), 149 (every member of unlawful assembly guilty of offence committed in prosecution of common object), 153-A (promotion of enmity between groups), 500 (punishment for defamation) and 505 (statement conducing to public mischief) of the Pakistan Penal Code. In June, a Quetta ATC handed two life sentences to Mahrang and another BYC leader in a case involving the death of a security personnel during a 2024 protest in Gwadar. Mahrang’s challenge against her conviction is pending before the Balochistan High Court (BHC).

Kremlin says Putin, Trump and Xi could hold a three-way meeting in China next month. The Kremlin said on Monday that Russian President Vladimir Putin, US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping could hold a three-way meeting on the sidelines of next month’s APEC summit in China and that a potential meeting had come up in talks. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov commented after being asked about a report in The Wall Street Journal which said that Putin had proposed such a meeting to discuss how to end the conflict in Ukraine. “Given that all three heads of state may potentially take part in the summit in China, the subject of such a hypothetical meeting was indeed raised. It was raised, but no specific proposals or agreements were discussed or put forward by anyone, either regarding the meeting itself or the possible agenda and content of that meeting,” said Peskov. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha criticised the idea of such a summit. “A trilateral meeting between the leaders of Ukraine, the US, and Russia could help end the war sooner. A trilateral meeting between the leaders of Russia, China, and the US would do only the opposite: encourage Putin to continue this war,” he said on X. Peskov, who told reporters on a daily conference call that the US was continuing its mediation efforts to resolve the conflict and that Russia appreciated those efforts, said it was obvious that Ukraine would need to be involved in any final peace deal. “Of course, a final settlement is impossible without the participation of someone in Kyiv who is prepared to take responsibility,” he said. The last US-mediated peace talks took place in February before the United States and Israel launched a war on Iran. Ukraine and Russia remain as far apart as ever when it comes to the terms of any possible peace deal.

Climate exodus. SOUTH Asia may see a vast movement of people as climate change makes parts of the region harder to live in. According to the International Organisation for Migration, as many as 40.5m people could be forced to move by 2050. The warning deserves attention for what such displacement could mean for a region already struggling with poverty, overcrowded cities, unemployment, and competition for resources. From the sinking coastlines of Bangladesh to the drought-hit districts of Pakistan , climate pressures are threatening millions of livelihoods. But it is not just the communities directly affected that will feel the impact. As farmers abandon unproductive land and families leave disaster-prone areas, towns and cities will have to accommodate growing populations. Competition for housing, employment, water and public services could make life harder for poorer communities and generate social tensions. Countries with limited resources may struggle to provide for both established residents and newcomers. The danger is particularly acute in South Asia, where weak regional cooperation could hinder a coordinated response. Climate displacement could then become another source of instability unless governments prepare for it together. The warning raises questions about how Pakistan intends to accommodate people whose homes and livelihoods become impossible to sustain. Our urban centres already struggle with inadequate housing, sanitation, transport, and job opportunities. An influx of climate-displaced families could deepen these problems. Yet migration need not mean destitution. As the IOM chief has pointed out, moving can itself be a means of adapting to climate change. Pakistan must, therefore, recognise climate mobility as a permanent consideration in development planning. Provincial and local governments need reliable information about communities likely to leave, destinations likely to receive them, and services required to support their transition. Land-use policies, affordable housing, vocational training, and access to schools and healthcare must reflect changing population patterns. Equally important is protecting the rights of displaced families, who should not lose access to documentation, education or public assistance simply because they have moved. Regional cooperation on forecasting, disaster preparedness and population movements could help countries anticipate shared pressures. The challenge is to ensure that people forced to move by climate change can rebuild their lives. Published in Dawn, October 19th, 2026

SOCIETY: BALOCHISTAN’S UNENDING CYCLES OF POVERTY. Farm workers in Balochistan often work more than the stipulated eight hour daily, while often earning less than the minimum wage. Some even work for food | Photo by Zaheer Baloch Mian Dad has spent much of his life ploughing fields on a tractor. He started as a young boy, helping drive a tractor that tilled land for a local landlord in his village in Tamboo, Nasirabad district, Balochistan. Now, Mian drives the tractor himself, earns just Rs14,000 per month — a little over a third of the provincial minimum wage of Rs37,000. During peak cultivation season, he tells Eos , the work-day can stretch up to 16 hours — double the standard eight hours. But Mian isn’t complaining. He now makes “a lot more” than what he earned as a tractor helper. It is still not enough, however, to feed his family, including his 11 children. “We look for odd jobs or work for food during the off-season,” he says. “When that doesn’t work, we have to beg.” For agricultural workers in Balochistan, a lifetime of labour may still not be enough to escape poverty. Debt, unequal sharecropping arrangements and climate shocks can trap entire families in a vicious cycle of dependence THE BOTTOM RUNG Mian’s situation is not unusual in a province where poverty remains widespread. An estimated 47 percent of the population in Balochistan lives in poverty, compared with a national average of 28.9 percent, according to the Pakistan Economic Survey 2025-26. Poverty is particularly acute in rural districts, where livelihoods depend mostly on agriculture. In a 2025 study by the global not-for-profit Population Council, District Vulnerability Index for Pakistan, 17 Balochistan districts were listed among the 20 most-vulnerable districts in the country. Nasirabad was towards the bottom in both provincial and national lists, ranking 11th most vulnerable out of 31 districts in Balochistan and 13th most vulnerable among the 129 districts assessed nationwide. Agriculture is the main source of livelihood in Tamboo, Mian’s hometown, which has a population of around 130,000. As elsewhere in Balochistan, agricultural production in Tamboo involves a network of tribal chieftains, landlords, intermediaries known as bothars , farmers, tractor drivers, technicians and sharecroppers. Workers like Mian Dad occupy the lower rungs of this hierarchy, often putting in long hours to cultivate the land. Locally, they are also referred to as begaar — which refers to a historical practice of forced, unpaid labour that was widely practised during the British era, including in princely states. In today’s Balochistan, unpaid labour may arise from a lack of alternative employment, obligations linked to debt or, in some cases, pressure arising from tribal and social relationships. INHERITED DEBT It can take decades for those starting work as peasants to move up in this hierarchy. Qadir Naseeb, whose family worked as peasants for generations in the Chattar area of Nasirabad, says his family didn’t have access to clean drinking water. He recently installed a tubewell near his hut. “Before [installing] the tubewell, the women in my family had to filter the water through a cloth to make it drinkable,” he tells Eos . One of the reasons why upward mobility can take peasants decades, explains local researcher Muhammad Nawaz Khosa, is because they are often caught up in a cycle of debt . “Households often have to rely on interest-based loans to meet everyday expenses as well as the costs associated with cultivating the very land on which they work,” he explains. In his book Balochistan Ki Nehri Zaraat [Canal-Irrigated Agriculture in Balochistan], Khosa writes that peasants often work as sharecroppers. In such cases, the peasants are responsible for managing production and handling expenses — often financed in the form of loans acquired from the landlord’s bothar. The eventual harvest is then divided between the landowners and the peasant, with the peasant using his share of the harvest to pay off the loan. If the harvest fails to return a profit, the loss has to be borne by the peasant, leaving him mired in a vicious debt trap. Such agreements also don’t factor in force majeure — whether it’s a pest attack or floods. In the case of a loss of harvest, the sharecropper has to pay off his debt to the landlord. In some instances, writes Khosa, peasants are also expected to bear the expenses associated with the landlord’s hujra [guest area], a system rooted in longstanding feudal traditions of the region. This is something that Mian Dad and many others have experienced. Mian had to borrow Rs200,000 following the floods in 2022. The amount equals more than 14 months of his pay. While Mian was repaying the debt, a medical emergency forced him to take on another loan. He says he is now trapped in a cycle of that debt, worried that his future generations will have to work to pay it off. Parts of Balochistan continue to exhibit forms of bonded labour, particularly within the households and estates of tribal and feudal elites, says Asad Baloch, a researcher who hails from a tribal family. Baloch says this practice has “considerably decreased” in Nasirabad as compared to previous generations. “But yes, remnants of such practices can be found in parts of the province,” he tells Eos . In rural and remote parts of the province, he explains, the tribal chiefs function not just as cultural leaders, but as economic masters. Impoverished tribesmen often rely on their chiefs for basic survival, protection and mediation. In some villages, there is a custom where one child from every household has to be in service of the tribal chief. In some cases, individuals work as guards or domestic workers, for minimal wages. Over time, limited economic opportunities and restricted access to education and alternative livelihoods continue to make it difficult for some individuals to pursue other means of earning a living. RESETTING THE CLOCK The 2022 floods that pushed Mian Dad into debt were not the first to disrupt the relationship between landlords and agricultural workers in Nasirabad. Dr Abid Mir, a lecturer at Government Degree College, Quetta, says the 2010 floods weakened some landlords’ hold over the families who worked for them. “Widespread agricultural losses weakened some landlords’ ability to retain regular workers, prompting many peasant families to seek employment elsewhere,” he tells Eos . For some, this opened up the possibility of finding work on their own terms and seeking better education, healthcare and basic amenities for their families. But the effects of climate-related disasters have been uneven. Families who remained in rural areas continued to face crop losses, declining incomes and mounting debts, Mir explains. For those already struggling to make ends meet, another failed harvest or flood could mean borrowing again simply to survive. The same disaster that may loosen one family’s dependence on a landlord can deepen another’s debt to one. For agricultural workers such as Mian Dad, recovering from a disaster is not simply a matter of rebuilding a home or returning to the fields. It can mean years of repayment — and the fear that their children will inherit the debt. The writer is a journalist and researcher. X: @ImtiazBaluch Additional input and editing by Hussain Dada.
