AFP. Q&A / Africa 08 October 2026 11 minutes Niger Wrestles with the Aftermath of a Military Revolt A mutiny by Niger’s special forces in late August morphed into a coup attempt. In this Q&A, Crisis Group experts explain how the unrest exposed growing discontent within the military’s ranks. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Related Tags Niger What is happening? Niger’s military leadership continues to reel from a coup attempt that exposed serious divides within the defence and security forces. On 28-29 August, soldiers from Niger’s Special Forces began shooting in their barracks at Air Base 101, which lies within the compound of Niamey’s international airport and houses most of the country’s military aircraft, as well as army units and foreign troops. Unrest quickly spread: groups of soldiers attacked the state broadcaster and the presidential palace, both in the city centre. Whether the incident began as a mutiny or whether it was meant from the start to oust General Abdourahamane Tiani, who seized power in a July 2023 coup, remains unclear. But the ramification of an uprising by a group of well-trained soldiers unhappy with their conditions of service and recent battlefield setbacks could be significant – particularly if it deepens divisions within the armed forces and disrupts their operations at a time when jihadist threats are looming large across several parts of the country. Members of the Special Reconnaissance Battalion for Special Operations Command, known by the French acronym BSR-COS, appear to have been behind the coup attempt, although a small number of soldiers from other units may have joined. Loyalist forces, particularly the presidential guard that Tiani commanded from 2011 to 2023, fought back as gunfire and detonations shook the capital, while national radio and television temporarily stopped broadcasting. By midday on 29 August, the mutineers withdrew to Air Base 101, where they unsuccessfully sought to rally other units to join them in toppling the government. Their stand did not last long, however. By the evening, national TV was up and running again, broadcasting images of loyalist forces arresting dozens, including at least one female soldier. A few days later, the government organised a national funeral for three members of the presidential guard forces who died in the clashes, while media reported that at least 27 mutineers were killed. The clashes further unsettled civilians in the capital, where heavy gunfire and explosions had already jolted residents twice this year, in January and June, when jihadists attacked the international airport, leaving many increasingly anxious about their safety. Why did the soldiers rebel? Tensions had been building within the BSR-COS for some time. In the days leading up to the revolt some soldiers had reportedly refused to go on a mission, citing a lack of adequate equipment. The battalion’s commander, Major Boubacar Maïhatchi, was detained soon after in the town of Tera as he returned from a mission escorting supply trucks from neighbouring Burkina Faso. Social media platforms have portrayed Maïhatchi as popular among younger officers, who respect his bravery and concern for his troops. His arrest may have prompted the soldiers’ decision to turn against the military leadership. The BSR-COS is part of Niger’s elite special forces, trained and equipped to work specifically in high-danger zones. As jihadist violence intensified in western Niger starting in the mid-2010s, the government expanded these forces, creating additional battalions, often with training and equipment from Western partners such as the U.S., France, and Germany. Today, there are more than a dozen battalions of roughly 500 to 600 soldiers each. The BSR-COS is among the most recently established units, with its members receiving training in Morocco. These battalions are leading the fight against jihadist insurgencies in Niger, including Islamic State Sahel Province and Jama’ at Nusratul Islam wal Muslimin (JNIM) in the west. From its headquarters at Air Base 101, the BSR-COS has frequently assisted units under attack from jihadists or escorted convoys travelling through dangerous areas. In November 2025, for instance, Niger sent 82 fuel tankers to Mali to ease shortages caused by a JNIM blockade on the city. Members of the battalion led the military escort that protected the vehicles during the 1,400 km journey. While special forces battalions are valuable to the fight against jihadists, they are also capable of posing a serious threat to the military regime. Since winning independence from France in 1960, Niger has experienced five coups and several failed coup attempts. The army has long held sway in politics. Seven of its eleven presidents have been military officers. Given that history, Niger’s leaders are understandably wary of powerful military units. Where to deploy the special forces often presents the authorities with a dilemma. As the jihadist threat draws closer to the capital, their presence is increasingly indispensable to protect strategic localities and sites. At the same time, their proximity to the seat of power also fuels concerns within the military regime about the risk of yet another coup. The BSR-COS was initially expected to deploy to Ayorou, a jihadist hotspot near the Malian border where the government is building a large dam crucial for electricity and irrigation. That deployment was delayed in part because of militant attacks on Air Base 101 in January and again in June 2026. Why are soldiers unhappy with Niger’s top military leaders? The incident revealed a widening gap between the military leadership and the rank and file. The July 2023 coup brought senior officers from various components of the defence and security forces to power, ranging from the presidential guard and the army to the gendarmerie and the national guard. Together, these senior figures formed the National Council for Safeguarding the Homeland, which shapes government policy and military strategy. Four generals wielded the most influence in the council: Abdourahmane Tiani, who had himself sworn in for a five-year presidential term in 2025; Defence Minister Salifou Mody, his second-in-command; Mohamed Toumba, who heads the interior and security ministry; and armed forces chief of staff Moussa Salao Barmou, who has since been removed. Yet beneath the military brass that had seized control of the country, discontent has been simmering in the lower ranks. The senior officers justified their power grab partly by accusing the civilian government they toppled of failing to tackle the jihadist threat. Three years on, insecurity has grown and spread to more parts of the country; the opening of new fronts has stretched the defence and security forces thin. Troops are deployed to the front line more frequently and remain there longer. Foot soldiers complain that they lack adequate weapons and equipment. They allege air or ground reinforcements are slow to arrive when needed, if they arrive at all. Combat vehicles and pickup trucks are often in poor shape and the government has been slow to replace them, which makes working in high-risk zones hazardous. Conditions in military barracks have added to soldiers’ frustrations. Some have posted images on social media of the poor-quality meals they are served; others pool their money and buy condiments to improve their rations. On top of that, a recent wave of jihadist attacks – in Diffa, Dosso, Tillabery and Niamey – has killed dozens, draining troop morale. Senior command seems aware of the rumblings. The defence minister, the chief of army staff and other generals have made multiple visits to military bases to listen to soldiers’ concerns. They often blame sanctions imposed by foreign powers after the July 2023 coup for hampering their ability to procure arms. Most of these sanctions have since been lifted, however, and many soldiers appear unconvinced by the senior leadership’s explanation for the lack of equipment. In several instances soldiers’ frustration has manifested in defiance. The August revolt was Niger’s fourth episode of military unrest in less than two years. In June 2025, after an attack in Banibangou in northern Tillabery killed over 70 military personnel, soldiers assigned to retake the position protested and beat the officer in charge, who was later evacuated for medical treatment. A few days later, soldiers in the Zinder region mutinied and tried to kill their superior. In August 2025, soldiers in Ayorou rebelled and opened fire on their commander. As one officer puts it, “A mutiny is first and foremost a failure of leadership”. What did the coup attempt and its aftermath reveal about military divisions? The incident broke an unwritten rule that has long guided Niger’s military: namely, it is essential to avoid internal confrontations between different branches of the armed forces. In 2023, various military units opposed Tiani’s move to detain then-President Mohamed Bazoum in order to remove him from office, but senior commanders ultimately decided to avert an open conflict and rally behind Tiani’s power grab. This time around, the mutineers fought the presidential guard, while the government asked Russia’s Africa Corps to help quell the revolt. Hours after the August revolt had subsided, Russia’s ambassador to Niger, Viktor Voropayev, told reporters that Russian forces had helped subdue the dissidents. Around 200 men from Africa Corps, the expeditionary force controlled by Russia’s defence ministry, have been deployed in Niger, including at Air Base 101, since 2024. They have assisted the regime with intelligence gathering, training on drone use, and operating air-defence systems. Russian forces reportedly used kamikaze drones that explode upon impact to force the mutineers to surrender. Some within the military found the involvement of foreigners in an internal confrontation particularly grating. Rumours have it that armed forces chief of staff Barmou may have been among those who voiced reservations about the Africa Corps’ intervention against the mutineers. In any event, on 11 September Tiani replaced Barmou with General Mamane Sani Kiaou, a move observers interpreted as aimed at reasserting control over the army. Barmou was also among the first generation of Nigerien special forces officers trained by the U.S. in the 2000s; he had reportedly threatened to resign previously over the army’s lack of equipment and his limited influence over military decision-making. Regime authorities, meanwhile, arrested over a hundred soldiers, while dozens of others, including special forces members, remain unaccounted for. Several civilians were also arrested, including two former ministers and a prominent journalist. The coup attempt could accentuate the resentment many troops feel vis-à-vis the presidential guard. The elite unit has long had access to the best equipment and the most talented recruits. It also foiled several coup attempts in the 2010s and early 2020s, leading some in the armed forces to perceive the guard as preoccupied with policing the military and protecting the regime rather than national security. Finally, the failed coup demonstrated that public support for the military regime is declining. The generals’ promises to restore security, overhaul governance, and assert Niger’s sovereignty on the international stage won a degree of sympathy from the public early on. But much of that enthusiasm has evaporated amid repeated security setbacks and an economic slowdown, partly attributable to the departure of Western donors and the closing of many NGOs by the government. On the afternoon of the coup attempt, regime supporters called on Niamey residents to turn out in support of the military leadership; notably, only a few dozen people did so. How did the incident reverberate in the region? The unrest had major diplomatic repercussions. The following day, a Nigerien officer speaking on national television alleged that he had received calls and messages from contacts in Chad, France, Belgium and the United Arab Emirates (UAE), informing him that several foreign countries – including Chad, Benin, Côte d’Ivoire and France – were prepared to intervene in support of those who had seized Air Base 101. He said they were operating with the blessing of the Economic Community of West Africa, the regional bloc from which Niger – alongside Burkina Faso and Mali – withdrew in 2025. On 3 September, the government spokesperson accused France of orchestrating the mutiny and alleged that “other African countries” had supported Paris. Some of these accusations were unsurprising. Tiani has repeatedly accused Benin, Côte d’Ivoire and France of conspiring against him, allegations the countries have rejected. But the regime’s claims that Chad was somehow also intent on destabilising Niger were new. Niger’s relations with Chad have soured in recent months. Niger’s authorities and their counterparts in Chad have traded accusations of tolerating, or even supporting, armed opposition groups active in their common border zones. Chadian officials did not respond to the allegations, although President Mahamat Idriss Déby later posted Quranic verse on social media warning against mixing truth with falsehoods. At the same time, the failed coup brought northern neighbour Algeria closer to the Nigerien authorities. Algeria condemned the incident and sent its chief of army staff to Niamey along with four fighter jets and a refuelling aircraft. The deployment of the fighter jets was apparently aimed at sending a strong message of support and to deter any attempt by foreign interests to dislodge the regime. The gesture also reinforced a diplomatic thaw already under way between the two countries. Relations had deteriorated last year after Algeria shot down a Malian drone near its border, prompting Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger – the three members of the Alliance of Sahel States (AES) – to recall their ambassadors from Algiers. Niger and Algeria have since taken several steps toward rapprochement, culminating in President Tiani’s visit to Algiers in February. The episode has also reinforced Niger’s relationship with Russia. Moscow’s intervention demonstrated the growing importance of Russian security support to the authorities in Niamey. In turn, the episode could deepen the regime’s dependence on Moscow for its survival. Since the coup, most Western forces have left Niger, including U.S. and French troops, as well as German, Belgian and Canadian personnel involved in training the Nigerien armed forces. Today, only a few hundred Italian troops remain, making Italy the last Western country with a military presence in Niger. What should the authorities do next? The Nigerien authorities should exercise restraint during their ongoing post-coup crackdown. While those within the BSR-COS who instigated the mutiny will likely face sanctions, the authorities should spare the rank and file who simply followed commanders’ orders. Thus far, over a hundred soldiers have been arrested. A sweeping purge risks further weakening the armed forces, deepening mistrust between ranks and damaging troop morale at a time when Niger is under enormous pressure from jihadists and rebel groups. Restraint will not address the grievances that helped fuel the revolt, however. The authorities should tackle soldiers’ concerns about inadequate equipment, housing and food. A leaked 2020 defence audit exposed widespread corruption in procurement practices. In February 2024, however, Niger’s military authorities issued an ordinance exempting defence and security procurement from ordinary state contracting and public accounting oversight. Without compromising legitimate security concerns, the authorities could adopt a stronger approach to rooting out wrongdoing in the acquisition of military equipment, as well as improve living conditions in the barracks. The authorities should also tread carefully in order not to deepen divisions between different wings of the defence and security forces. Even symbolic decisions matter. The national funeral held for three presidential guard soldiers reinforced perceptions of double standards: regular soldiers who are killed in the line of duty are often buried quietly and rarely honoured publicly. A more equitable recognition of soldiers’ sacrifices could help reduce resentment across the ranks. More fundamentally, Niamey needs to reduce the mounting burden on its armed forces. The authorities should develop a comprehensive strategy for dealing with the proliferation of conflict fronts, giving greater weight to non-military approaches. Where possible, dialogue and diplomacy could help pacify restive areas. Even if such approaches do not produce sustainable peace, they could help demobilise combatants, achieve temporary ceasefires, and possibly reduce the number of simultaneous conflicts, providing relief to armed forces that show growing signs of fatigue. Finally, the authorities should recognise that military discontent is unfolding in an increasingly closed political environment. With political parties dissolved and civic space severely restricted, peaceful avenues for expressing dissatisfaction with the government have narrowed considerably. In such an environment, the armed forces risk becoming one of the few remaining channels through which opposition to the regime can erupt, and potentially in its most dangerous form. Reopening political and civic space would allow grievances to be expressed through less destabilising channels, even if doing so exposes the authorities to greater public criticism. On Our Radar eschelhaas Fri, 10/09/2026 - 00:00 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Special Coverage / Global 09 October 2026 20+ minutes On Our Radar On Our Radar scans conflicts and crises around the globe every week and features some of the hotspots Crisis Group’s analysts are closely watching. Whether an under-reported trend or a headline-grabbing development, our field experts explain why it matters or what should be done. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print 9 October 2026 HAITI Haiti’s electoral council announced changes to the country’s voting rules Tuesday. The new law, which will likely result in delays to polls presently scheduled for 13 December, will remove provisions that would have disqualified individuals subject to bilateral sanctions imposed by third countries from running for office. Those subject to UN sanctions remain barred from candidacy. The move comes as the UN Panel of Experts on Haiti, which makes private recommendations to the Security Council regarding who should be sanctioned, denounced several high-profile politicians for using gangs to fuel violence. Some UN Security Council members worry that sanctioning public figures could interfere with Haiti’s political process. Crisis Group expert Diego Da Rin says the risk of inaction is greater, however: those who have collaborated with gangs could return to power, further delaying resolution of the Haitian conflict. MALI On Tuesday, the Malian army recaptured Kidal, a strategically important city in the country’s north that had been held by the separatist Front for the Liberation of Azawad (FLA) since April. The FLA said it had decided to temporarily withdraw from Kidal as the army, backed by Russian Africa Corps paramilitaries, launched a large-scale offensive. Crisis Group expert Ibrahim Maïga says the recapture of Kidal is a significant military development. But without a political process to build on these gains, the takeover alone is unlikely to bring this conflict closer to a lasting resolution. UKRAINE A Russian attack on Kramatorsk in Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region killed at least 33 people on a public bus Thursday. Previous Russian strikes across the country Wednesday killed at least 28 others, including 22 when a missile hit a residential building. Kramatorsk – one of the cities Russia has been unable to capture in Donetsk – has become an important supply hub for the Ukrainian army. The attack came as Kyiv struck a data centre belonging to Russia’s largest technology company, Yandex, in the central Ryazan region, south east of Moscow. Crisis Group expert Lucian Kim says both sides are using long-range strikes to put pressure on their adversaries, though Russia’s aerial campaign is far more devastating, raising the number of casualties among the civilian population and upending daily life for millions. 2 October 2026 MYANMAR Military airstrikes on a market in Kyauktaw, Rakhine State, on Monday reportedly killed at least 50 people. The UN described the attack as one of the deadliest in the state since the 2021 coup. The Arakan Army, an ethnic Rakhine group, vowed on Tuesday to take “retaliatory measures” against those responsible. The strikes came amid a military counter-offensive launched in early September on several fronts in and around Rakhine to retake territory from the Arakan Army. It has made little headway, says Crisis Group expert Thomas Kean. The market raid was likely intended to punish civilians and disrupt trade and governance in Arakan Army-held areas of Rakhine. U.S. - IRAN U.S. and Iranian negotiators held indirect talks on the UN General Assembly’s sidelines to end a conflict now in its eighth month. On 26 September, U.S. President Donald Trump said he had rejected an Iranian ceasefire proposal but continued to make counteroffers. On Wednesday, Trump warned of further military action, saying: “We blow them up or make a deal”. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says prospects for a breakthrough appear slim: Tehran proposes reopening the Strait of Hormuz in exchange for the U.S. lifting its blockade of Iranian ports and releasing Iranian assets. Washington believes it has overcome Iran’s efforts to restrict shipping while continuing to weaken the Iranian economy. Tehran also wants to defer nuclear issues to subsequent talks; Washington seeks concessions up front. Fear of escalation could keep the door to engagement open, but significant gaps over substance and sequencing remain. YEMEN Fighting between the Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces and their allies intensified this week, including around Taiz, a city in the middle of the country, where the rebels have been seeking to cut the road link with Aden on the southern coast. Taiz is home to more than 2 million people, many of whom have been displaced from other parts of Yemen. Meanwhile, the World Health Organization warned that Yemen’s health system was nearing “breaking point” amid mounting casualties. Crisis Group expert Ahmed Nagi says Houthi success around Taiz could help consolidate the group’s gains along the Red Sea coast. Diplomacy faces substantial obstacles: the Houthis are unlikely to accept de-escalation without tangible concessions from Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s government, while Riyadh may seek limited battlefield gains before mediation. 25 September 2026 SOUTH SUDAN President Salva Kiir dissolved South Sudan’s transitional unity government Tuesday, three months before elections scheduled for 22 December, dismantling key power-sharing institutions established under the 2018 peace agreement. Following a hurriedly passed amendment to the National Elections Act, Kiir dismissed all five vice presidents, including his long-time rival First Vice President Riek Machar, and installed a caretaker government composed entirely of loyalists. Crisis Group expert Daniel Akech says the changes allow Kiir to concentrate authority in his hands. Greater control of state institutions could help him retain power, through either a stage-managed election or a delay that prolongs his administration. The resulting political exclusion risks provoking greater conflict in an already deeply fractured country. UNITED NATIONS World leaders met this week in New York for the UN General Assembly’s annual high-level session. Crisis Group expert Daniel Forti says the week’s events proved that states still value the UN as a forum for discussing global concerns, even if common ground between them remains elusive. Some countries expect the next Secretary-General to single-handedly get the UN back on track and provide solutions for crises around the world. That attitude is short-sighted. The UN needs the conviction of its members to tackle global risks from deadly conflict to artificial intelligence. Whether states choose to work together – or continue down the path of international fragmentation – will determine whether the next decade at the UN is defined by diplomacy or disorder. U.S. - CHINA President Donald Trump hosted Chinese leader Xi Jinping for a state visit in Washington this week. Xi touted their personal rapport, called for “healthy” bilateral competition “within bounds” and argued that U.S.-China cooperation is needed to address most global challenges. Crisis Group expert Ali Wyne says the summit’s outcome was modest: the two leaders agreed to extend by two months the trade truce that they blessed in Busan, South Korea last October; it was due to expire on 10 November. They do not appear to have made a breakthrough on managing cross-strait ties, spurring diplomacy to end the U.S.-Iran war or erecting guardrails around artificial intelligence. China’s readout called on the U.S. to “adhere to the correct position of opposing ‘Taiwan independence’”, incorrectly but provocatively implying that the U.S. had changed its longstanding position (that it “does not support” that outcome). 18 September 2026 DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO Protesters streamed into the streets of Kinshasa Tuesday to decry the government’s proposals to change the constitution by popular referendum. One person was killed in clashes with police who intervened to stop the marchers from reaching parliament. Crisis Group expert Richard Moncrieff says the government’s main aim in trying to alter the constitution is to revise the clause imposing a two-term limit on presidents, thereby allowing the incumbent Félix Tshisekedi to stand for a third term. Tshisekedi is keen to hold the referendum soon, despite the opposition, because he senses that the country’s political balance has tilted in his favour. Going ahead with this vote may prove unwise, however, even if it comes off fairly smoothly. It may produce an illusion of political stability that, in turn, deflects attention from urgent tasks like reducing poverty among ordinary Congolese and taming the interlinked wars raging in the eastern provinces. MALI Algerian Prime Minister Sifi Ghrieb visited Bamako Monday in the latest sign of rapprochement between Algeria and Mali, whose relations had deteriorated badly in recent years. Crisis Group expert Jean-Hervé Jezequel says the thaw is welcome news for the Malian authorities. Bamako has been struggling to contain an insurgency linked to al-Qaeda, Jamaat Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM), which killed 50 Malian soldiers in its latest attack on an army base last week. JNIM has lately allied with northern separatists who have also been fighting the Malian army. Historically, Algiers has been an important mediator between Bamako and northern armed groups. The warming of Algeria-Mali relations raises hopes that it might again play such a role, though maybe a more limited one given the Malian authorities’ increasingly sovereignist mindset. It could nevertheless help mitigate the conflict that has torn at Mali since 2012. PHILIPPINES Regional parliamentary elections took place on Monday in the Bangsamoro, the swathe of the southern Philippines that won autonomy in 2019 as part of a 2014 peace agreement between Manila and the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF). At least five people were killed and twenty injured during the vote, though violence was less widespread than feared, with incidents concentrated in a few locations. No party secured an absolute majority, meaning that politicians will likely need to form a coalition. Crisis Group expert Georgi Engelbrecht says the incoming government, slated for inauguration by 30 October, will likely pair former MILF rebels with representatives of the region’s traditional political clans, unless the ex-insurgents, who have split into two factions, can reunite. The elections were a big step forward for the Bangsamoro peace process, with all eyes now on a crucial meeting between national government and MILF delegations to discuss gaps in fulfilling the 2014 accord’s terms. 11 September 2026 IRAN The International Atomic Energy Agency referred Iran to the UN Security Council Wednesday for breaching its nuclear non-proliferation obligations, marking the first time in twenty years the organisation has taken such a step. Tehran condemned the decision, blaming U.S. and Israeli strikes on its nuclear facilities for disrupting the agency’s inspections. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says concerns about Iran’s lacklustre cooperation with the UN watchdog have been mounting for years, capped by over a year of blocked access to key sites bombed by the U.S. and Israel in June 2025. Given that UN sanctions were already reinstated last year, and the expectation that China and Russia will shield it from additional punitive measures at the Security Council, the referral may harden Iran’s obduracy rather than cajole it into overdue cooperation. LEBANON Israel stepped up its attacks in southern Lebanon over the weekend with strikes that killed nearly 30 people and wounded dozens more. While Israel claimed that it had targeted Hizbollah arms caches and military installations, the assaults killed several children and medical staff. Crisis Group expert David Wood says Israel’s lethal escalation could continue, unless it faces strong pressure from the U.S., its most important ally, to desist. Washington sponsored a Lebanon-Israel ceasefire struck in late June but, over two months later, the deal remains largely unfulfilled, with Israeli military action continuing and Hizbollah refusing to disarm. SOMALIA Somali piracy has seen an uptick this year, with at least six hijackings of cargo ships and smaller vessels since April. The turmoil resulting from the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran has created opportune conditions for pirates, with fewer naval patrols off the Somali coast and more commercial traffic in nearby waters as ships are diverted from the Bab al-Mandab and the Strait of Hormuz. Crisis Group expert Omar Mahmood says the number of pirate attacks is far below what it was during the heyday of Red Sea piracy fifteen years ago. The current trajectory is concerning, however, and more raids are bound to occur, absent international and local measures both offshore and on land to combat the phenomenon. 4 September 2026 HAITI Armed gang members stormed the commune of Kenscoff, overlooking Port-au-Prince, overnight on 23-24 August, killing at least 47 people and abducting more than 50, whom they threatened to kill if security forces go after the gang in that area. At least thirteen abductees have subsequently been released. Briefing the UN Security Council on 28 August, UN envoy Carlos Ruiz Massieu said the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF) would beef up its presence in the capital, while Haitian units would send reinforcements to Kenscoff. He also urged the GSF, which remains far short of its planned 5,500-person strength, to deploy in full without delay. Crisis Group expert Diego Da Rin says the Kenscoff massacre is the latest indication that gangs are on the offensive as the GSF assembles. U.S. - IRAN After a month-long lull, the U.S. resumed attacks on Iranian soil over the weekend, first striking rocket launchers on Larak island that Washington said were preparing to deploy sea mines, then hitting dozens of military targets along Iran’s southern coast. Tehran responded with missile and drone fire at bases hosting U.S. forces in the Gulf. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says the uptick comes as the Trump administration tries to isolate Tehran financially through increased sanctions and a naval blockade, while in parallel undermining Iranian efforts to control the Strait of Hormuz by escorting vessels through the waterway. While Washington's approach is to squeeze wherever possible and strike whenever it deems necessary – for example, in response to Iranian strikes or efforts to rebuild its military capabilities – the Islamic Republic could counter with additional strikes of its own on U.S. assets and allies, along with further attacks on shipping. THAILAND Overnight on 22 August, militants in Thailand’s three southernmost provinces staged over 50 attacks in four hours, including bombings and arson attempts at local administrative offices, shops and other buildings. Three passersby were injured. Further incidents followed on 23 and 29 August despite tightened security. Authorities blamed Barisan Revolusi Nasional Patani Melayu (Patani-Malay National Revolutionary Front, BRN), which has fought Bangkok’s rule since 2004. Such coordinated attacks are routine, says Crisis Group expert Matt Wheeler, but the scale of this campaign was unusual. It was likely intended to discredit the state, demonstrate insurgents’ reach and heighten pressure on the government to resume peace talks that have occurred intermittently since 2013. Thailand’s chief negotiator has reportedly proposed bringing technical-level talks with BRN forward from October to this month, in part to determine the reasons for the attacks. 21 August 2026 CHINA - SOUTH KOREA Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi paid a two-day visit to South Korea this week to discuss bilateral ties, Korean peninsula tensions and broader Asian affairs. The trip came three days after U.S. President Donald Trump ordered the Pentagon to scale back joint military exercises with South Korea. Trump also said he is willing to meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, as he did during his first term. These two unilateral announcements in turn prompted South Korean President Lee Jae-myung to reiterate his call for Seoul to bolster its own defences, for instance by acquiring nuclear-powered submarines and regaining independent control of its military in the event of hostilities. (Its forces would now be under U.S. command in a wartime contingency.) Crisis Group expert William Yang says the U.S.-South Korean friction has given Beijing an opening to deepen its own engagement with Seoul. It may now seek to present itself as the main mediator on the Korean peninsula, given its links with Pyongyang. ISRAEL - SYRIA Israeli warplanes bombed the Abu al-Duhur air base in northern Syria early Tuesday morning, in what Israel said was a warning against “deployment” of Turkish military personnel at the site. No casualties were reported. In remarks protesting the strike, Syrian Foreign Minister Assad al-Shaibani said Turkish officers had visited the base three days previously, but only for “training” purposes as Syrian forces refurbish the base. Tom Barrack, the U.S. ambassador to Türkiye who doubles as envoy for Syria, described Israel’s action as “unnecessary”. The backdrop, says Crisis Group expert Noah Bonsey, is an impasse in Israeli-Syrian talks about a bilateral security agreement. In these U.S.-mediated negotiations, under way since last summer, the Syrian government is seeking Israel’s withdrawal from parts of southern Syria it has occupied since December 2024, while Israel presses for limits on Turkish support for the Syrian military, among other security guarantees. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has pledged to retain a “buffer zone” in Syria as he campaigns for re-election in October. SOMALIA Local paramilitaries clashed with federal forces Monday in Baidoa, capital of Southwest state, leaving 30 dead, according to the Somali government. The militia is loyal to Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed “Lafta-Gareen”, a former state president whom Mogadishu forcibly removed in March after a disagreement over state elections. Lafta-Gareen fled to the Kenyan capital Nairobi, but his followers have been seeking to reinstate him, making regular incursions into Baidoa from a base on its northern outskirts. They reject the new state president who took office after a hastily organised vote following Lafta-Gareen’s ouster. Crisis Group expert Omar Mahmood says Monday’s attack was the largest and deadliest to date. Calm has since returned to Baidoa, but absent an initiative to address lingering grievances over the political transition in Southwest state, further violence is likely. 14 August 2026 IRAN - U.S. Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis attacked a merchant vessel Tuesday near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, killing six people aboard, as the U.S. fired two missiles at a cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman to enforce its renewed blockade of Iran-bound maritime traffic. The strikes came as both U.S. President Donald Trump and Iran claimed to have “total control” over the Strait of Hormuz. The Islamic Republic and Oman are in negotiations over a deal to partially reopen this crucial waterway. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says these consultations are part of a scramble by mediators to nudge the U.S. and Iran back into a truce, without which any bilateral understanding about the strait is unlikely to get much traction. Colombia retaliated with tariffs on Ecuadorian goods and a suspension of electricity exports. Ecuador then raised the fee for Colombian oil shipped through its pipelines tenfold from about $3 to $30 per barrel. Crisis Group expert Glaeldys González Calanche says the meeting indicates that the two capitals understand the dispute will hurt both economies as well as weaken both states’ ability to confront security challenges on the frontier. Rather than acting in isolation, the two should mount a coordinated cross-border response, which is likely to be more effective in fighting transnational criminal networks. IRAN U.S. President Donald Trump told Iran Wednesday that it risks "major destruction" if it fails to negotiate a nuclear deal with Washington. The ultimatum follows earlier warnings of U.S. intervention over the Islamic Republic's repression of protests. The U.S. has dispatched additional naval assets, airpower and defensive systems to the Middle East. Tehran – along with some of its non-state allies in the region – has threatened retaliation if attacked. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says Iran is unlikely to meet the White House's sweeping demands, which encompass nuclear, missile and regional concessions, raising the likelihood of confrontation at a time when the Islamic Republic already faces increasing diplomatic isolation, mounting economic problems and outrage at its brutal crackdown on dissent. SOUTH SUDAN The South Sudanese army announced Sunday it is launching a major offensive to recapture territory in Jonglei state that has been seized by opposition forces and allied militias since hostilities intensified in December. The UN warned this week that mass troop mobilisation and inflammatory rhetoric from senior commanders have significantly heightened the risk of violence against civilians. Crisis Group expert Daniel Akech says the escalation signals a clear slide toward full-scale war. The rapidly expanding conflict threatens to draw in neighbouring states, including Uganda, and to deepen South Sudan’s dangerous entanglement in the war in Sudan. 23 January 2026 DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO M23 rebels withdrew from Uvira, near the Burundian border, over last weekend, ending a tense month in which they controlled the South Kivu town. They had promised to pull out, likely due to U.S. pressure following a December summit in Washington between their main outside backer, the Rwandan president, and his Congolese counterpart. The Congolese army and allied Wazalendo militias re-entered Uvira this week, but in the interim chaos engulfed the town, with widespread looting and abuses against civilians, mainly by the Wazalendo. Of particular concern, says Crisis Group expert Richard Moncrieff, is the mounting ethnic tension in the area. The M23 insurgents, who portray themselves as defenders of the Tutsi people, took Uvira claiming that the Tutsi-related Banyamulenge living in town needed their protection. Primary responsibility for attacks on Banyamulenge residents lies with the Congolese authorities and their allies, but the rebels appear to have exposed these people to predictable retaliation after retreating. Another M23-aligned armed group, the Twiraneho, is involved in fighting around Uvira, also pointing to a pattern of inter-communal violence. GUATEMALA President Bernardo Arévalo declared a 30-day state of emergency Monday after inmates had taken more than 45 guards hostage at three prisons two days earlier. After the authorities regained control of one of the facilities, gang members outside jail killed ten policemen in retaliation. The state of emergency limits citizens' rights and gives state forces special powers such as making arrests without cause. It echoes the iron-fist approaches to public safety pursued by leaders in El Salvador and Ecuador. Crisis Group expert Renata Segura says Arévalo, who won the 2024 election touting a progressive reform agenda but has since lost popularity, listened to demands from Guatemalans for a decisive response to an uptick in violent crime. If the measure delivers immediate results, it could help the president’s political standing. UGANDA Tensions simmered this week after the 15 January elections, which saw President Yoweri Museveni win another term with 71.65 per cent of the vote. The leading opposition candidate, Robert Kyagulanyi of the National Unity Party (NUP), rejected the result, alleging widespread fraud. He remains in hiding after dodging a police raid – staged for reasons that remain unclear – on his residence. The president's powerful son, army chief Muhoozi Kainerugaba, said on social media Tuesday Kyagulanyi would be treated as an "outlaw/rebel" if he did not surrender within 48 hours. (He later deleted this and other inflammatory posts.) Meanwhile, authorities charged more than 100 NUP members with involvement in election day violence. An internet blackout has made details of the incidents difficult to verify. The official death toll is twelve, but both Kyagulanyi and Muhoozi have cited higher figures. The government says ten died when its forces were attacked at an opposition legislator's home, a version of events sharply contested by others who were present. Crisis Group expert Meron Elias says the opacity of events, along with Muhoozi’s threats, will likely keep the political temperature high following the polarising vote. 16 January 2026 CUBA The bodies of 32 Cuban soldiers killed during the 3 January U.S. raid in Venezuela arrived in Havana Thursday. Cuba is facing considerable uncertainty after U.S. President Donald Trump on Sunday urged its government to “make a deal” or face the consequences, vowing that the U.S. would cut the Venezuelan oil supply to the island nation, which is heavily dependent on these deliveries for its energy needs. Crisis Group expert Renata Segura says Washington appears to be calculating that a deepening economic crisis in Cuba will mobilise the masses to bring about the regime’s collapse. The Cuban regime retains a strong military and solid ties to Russia and China, however, and previously has not hesitated to crush dissent. GREENLAND Several European NATO members have deployed troops to Greenland, an autonomous territory of Denmark, to beef up infrastructure and carry out joint military exercises after U.S. President Donald Trump repeatedly stated that the U.S. intends to acquire the island, by force if necessary. Wednesday’s meeting among the U.S., Greenland and Denmark in Washington failed to resolve “fundamental disagreement” on Greenland’s future, according to the Danish foreign minister. With Europe already buffeted by Russia's full-scale war in Ukraine, says Crisis Group expert Olga Oliker, this crisis will have dire implications for the future of NATO and European security writ large if the U.S. does not back down. SYRIA Thousands demonstrated in the north east Tuesday against government forces’ expulsion of Kurdish fighters from Aleppo. Since the last Kurdish fighters left the city Sunday, fighting shifted eastward, raising the risk of sustained confrontation. In early January, the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) clashed with the Syrian army in Aleppo as negotiations to integrate Syria’s north east under central government control stalled. Crisis Group expert Nanar Hawach says Damascus cannot take the whole region militarily, but it will likely keep applying pressure on the SDF. The U.S., which supports both sides, has kept a ceiling on escalation thus far and should use its leverage to bring the parties back to the negotiating table. 9 January 2026 CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC Provisional results show that President Faustin-Archange Touadéra has secured a third term after general elections on 28 December. Two challengers – Anicet-Georges Dologuélé and Henri-Marie Dondra – have called for annulling the vote, alleging fraud, while the main opposition coalition boycotted the ballot, citing an uneven playing field. The disputed poll coincided with renewed violence in the south east. Fighters linked to the Azandé Ani Kpi Gbé (AAKG) – a Zandé self-defence militia – disrupted voting in Bambouti. Clashes then spread, including AAKG attacks on government forces around Zémio in early January. The AAKG was initially aligned with Bangui but later broke with the government after its rapprochement with a Fulani-led armed group that the militia accuses of encroaching on Zandé land. Crisis Group expert Fulbert Ngodji says the AAKG may be digging in to battle the state. Stability during Touadéra’s new term will hinge on promoting intercommunal dialogue in the south east, better integrating militias under army command, and reducing regional isolation through development and security reform. IRAN The falling value of Iran's national currency sparked demonstrations that since late December have grown into nationwide anti-regime unrest. The government has altered its subsidy policies but done little to dampen wider grievances. At least three dozen people have been killed as state forces crack down on protests that show little sign of slowing down. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says the Islamic Republic faces a major dilemma: it is neither willing nor able to adopt reforms that could meet expectations for political, social and economic change and on notice from U.S. President Donald Trump that outside intervention is possible if its repression intensifies. LEBANON Lebanon said it had passed a milestone in disarming Hizbollah, but the country’s fragile ceasefire deal with Israel remains imperilled. On Thursday, the Lebanese army announced that it had brought all weapons under state control in the southern area between the Litani River and the Israeli border. Israel immediately disputed the army’s assertion, saying Hizbollah retains military infrastructure in that region. Crisis Group expert David Wood says Beirut faces dangers ahead in any case. The army must soon move toward disarming Hizbollah north of the Litani, where the group refuses to comply – driving up the risk of internal discord. Yet Lebanese leaders also know that Israel will almost certainly respond to any hold-ups in disarming Hizbollah with severe military escalations, inflicting still more pain on their embattled country. AFP / Anthony Wallace Report 359 / Asia-Pacific 09 October 2026 20+ minutes Toward a Thaw in the Cambodia-Thailand Border Conflict Hostilities between Cambodia and Thailand ceased in late 2025, after two rounds of combat along the frontier. But the truce is under growing strain. To avoid more war, the two countries should restore normal diplomatic ties and resume work on demarcating their shared border. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print "> Download PDF Related Tags Thailand Cambodia What’s new? Fighting between Cambodia and Thailand over a border dispute killed at least 150 people and displaced almost a million more in 2025. Now, the ceasefire between the two countries is fraying, while diplomacy has stalled. Why does it matter? The 2025 combat was the costliest yet between the two countries and the worst confrontation ever between two members of the Association of South East Asian Nations. War could break out again if Bangkok and Phnom Penh do not improve relations. What should be done? Leaders in Bangkok and Phnom Penh should work to normalise diplomatic ties, reconvene the Joint Boundary Commission in order to resume the surveys that will let the sides demarcate the land border, when circumstances allow, and cooperate on a program of demining affected areas. Executive Summary After two rounds of fighting in 2025 over a longstanding territorial dispute along their 800km land border, a ceasefire between Cambodia and Thailand is under strain, threatened by heightened nationalism on both sides and mutual allegations of violations. Tensions between the two countries resurfaced early in 2025, erupting into combat that dwarfed earlier clashes in scale. When the shooting stopped on 27 December, Thailand had the upper hand, holding most of the contested areas as well as slivers of Cambodian territory. In May, Bangkok withdrew from a 2001 bilateral agreement on how to resolve overlapping maritime claims, leading Phnom Penh to initiate compulsory conciliation – a non-binding international legal proceeding – under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea. In turn, Thailand suspended participation in bilateral mechanisms on land border demarcation, leaving negotiations in limbo. To avoid more war, the two countries should put nationalist fervour to the side and overcome their mistrust, starting with restoring normal diplomatic ties and resuming efforts to jointly demarcate the land border. Following an exchange of fire in May 2025 that killed a Cambodian soldier, fighting broke out along the border in late July. With Malaysian mediation, backed up by U.S. President Donald Trump’s vow to suspend trade talks with both countries so long as hostilities continued, the two sides agreed to a ceasefire after five days of combat. Tensions simmered over the following months, however, with regular confrontations between troops and a series of landmine explosions that wounded sixteen Thai soldiers. The ceasefire collapsed in November, and a second round of hostilities ensued, displacing almost a million people on both sides before halting with another truce, brokered this time with China’s help near year’s end. The conflict is linked to domestic politics in both countries. Border tensions were pivotal in the disqualification from office of Thailand’s Prime Minister Paetongtarn Shinawatra in 2025. Her successor Anutin Charnvirakul, leader of the Bhumjaithai (Thai Pride) Party, took office that September, dissolved parliament in December and won in a general election the next February, in part by maintaining a hard line on Cambodia amid a wave of Thai nationalism. The episode evoked memories of the 2008 conflict between Cambodia and Thailand, when royalist opponents of Paetongtarn’s father, the controversial former Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra, fanned nationalist discontent over the border to undermine the Thaksin-aligned government of the day. Nationalist zeal has also appeared to bolster the government of Prime Minister Hun Manet in Cambodia, though further fighting could shake the unity of the ruling Cambodian People’s Party and the regime built by his father, and current senate president, Hun Sen. While the ceasefire has held thus far, the conflict continues through diplomatic channels, with Cambodia decrying Thai occupation of its territory. While the ceasefire has held thus far, the conflict continues through diplomatic channels, with Cambodia decrying Thai occupation of its territory. Thailand insists it is observing the ceasefire agreement, which provides for troops to remain in positions they held when it came into effect, and accuses Cambodia of attempting to internationalise the dispute. Compulsory conciliation on the overlapping maritime claims will take at least a year to conclude. In the meantime, Bangkok has declined to resume the technical work of a Joint Boundary Commission to survey and demarcate the land border between the countries, while cooperation on demining the frontier has been suspended since the 2025 fighting. Both sides are angry, with each portraying the other as the obstacle to resolving the conflict. Amid the mutual recriminations, it would be easy for a minor border incident to blow up into something bigger, including a third bout of major fighting. Ideally, a third party would mediate between Cambodia and Thailand to head off the possibility of escalation. But several factors impede movement toward dialogue. First, strident nationalism on both sides makes compromise appear hazardous. In Bangkok, the government seems content with the status quo and is following the military’s lead on border security. In Phnom Penh, senior leaders recognise the risks another round of fighting could pose to the government’s legitimacy, but they cannot appear to be bending on sovereignty or territorial integrity. Confrontation continues, for now, to bring political rewards to decision-makers on both sides, especially the Thai military, which has been able to polish a tarnished image. Secondly, while the conflict has been economically damaging to both countries, it has not been sufficiently costly to precipitate a thaw in the interest of resuming cross-border commerce. Both Thai and Cambodian leaders perceive the political costs of conciliatory moves as greater than the prospective benefits. Thirdly, international powers have limited leverage to push the two sides toward a deal. Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim, the rotating chair of the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) in 2025, took the lead in brokering the July ceasefire – with decisive help from Trump’s trade talks threat. But since that truce unravelled, the bloc has been unable to expedite resolution of the dispute. Current ASEAN chair the Philippines has used its good offices to bring the Cambodian and Thai prime ministers together, but it is in no position to spur dialogue. Preoccupied with the Middle East, the U.S. shows no interest in mediating. China would be able to convene talks, but it is unlikely to jeopardise its relations with either country by attempting to impose an agreement. Under these circumstances, immediate prospects for concerted efforts to resolve the border issue are poor. But until the dispute is resolved, the possibility of another war, with all the associated death, displacement and other human suffering, will remain. Both sides should dial down official rhetoric that casts the other as an enemy and seek areas of common interest, starting by normalising diplomatic relations and reposting ambassadors in the other’s capital. Though the Joint Boundary Commission has neither the mandate nor a mechanism to resolve the political impasse, its work of surveying and demarcating the border is a prerequisite for settling the dispute and should be restarted as soon as possible. Demining is a priority for both countries that should offer another politically acceptable platform for cooperation. Crucially, both border demarcation and demining are already stipulated in the ceasefire agreement. The alternative to honouring these truce terms that the two neighbours have agreed upon could be more bloodshed, which is highly unlikely to put this long-running border dispute to rest. Bangkok/Phnom Penh/Brussels, 9 October 2026 I. Introduction The border dispute between Cambodia and Thailand is hardly new, but the fighting that erupted between the two South East Asian neighbours in July and December 2025 was deadlier and more widespread than earlier clashes, killing at least 150 people and displacing roughly one million. 1 For background, see Crisis Group Asia Report N°215, Waging Peace: ASEAN and the Thai-Cambodian Border Conflict , 6 December 2011; and Matthew Wheeler, “ Border Dispute with Cambodia Sparks Political Disarray in Thailand ”, Crisis Group Commentary, 1 July 2025. See also “Situation Report 20 – Displacement Crisis as a Result of the Cambodia-Thailand Border Conflict”, World Vision International in Cambodia, 2 January 2026; and “Thai deadly border clashes displace over half a million in Cambodia”, France 24, 21 December 2025. By 27 December, when the parties reached the latest ceasefire, Thai troops had taken high ground in many locations along the 800km border, occupying contested areas as well as patches of Cambodian territory. 2 Given that portions of the border are undemarcated and disputed, its exact length is not known. Cambodia’s estimate is 817km; Thailand’s is 798km. Since then, the ceasefire has been tested regularly. Bangkok and Phnom Penh have made little progress toward delimiting the border or resuming normal diplomatic relations. The risk of a third round of war is real. In the wake of the 2025 fighting, bilateral relations are at a low ebb. Each side accuses the other of having started the conflict, while indulging in provocative rhetoric and actions that undermine prospects for resolution. Cambodia alleges that Thailand aims to annex parts of its territory seized in the December 2025 fighting. Thailand maintains that it is observing the ceasefire deal, which stipulates that troops remain in positions they held when the agreement entered into force. The territorial dispute extends out to sea as well. In May, Bangkok withdrew from a 2001 memorandum of understanding on overlapping maritime claims, leading Phnom Penh to initiate compulsory conciliation, a non-binding dispute resolution mechanism under the UN Convention of the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS). This report examines the roots of the conflict, its domestic political drivers and the current diplomatic impasse. It is based on research conducted since February in Bangkok and Phnom Penh, including interviews with officials of both governments, some of whom have retired but have direct knowledge of developments, as well as diplomats, analysts and journalists covering the conflict. Women made up about a fifth of the interlocutors. Research was also carried out in Siem Reap and Anlong Veng in Cambodia, as well as in the Thai border provinces of Buriram, Sa Kaeo, Si Sa Ket and Surin. The report uses both Khmer and Thai place names on first reference. It uses the Khmer name for the 11th century Preah Vihear temple, known in Thai as Khao Phra Viharn, in view of the 1962 International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruling that the temple is situated in Cambodian territory. 3 “Case concerning the Temple of Preah Vihear (Cambodia v. Thailand)”, International Court of Justice (ICJ), 15 June 1962. After two rounds of fighting in 2025 over a longstanding territorial dispute along the 800km land border, a ceasefire between Cambodia and Thailand is under strain, threatened by heightened nationalism on both sides. Source: Openstreetmaps; CSIS Asia Maritime Transparency Initiative / CRISIS GROUP II. The Weight of History The contemporary border conflict is a legacy of both colonialism and nationalist historical narratives, which elites in both Cambodia and Thailand have repeatedly exploited for domestic political advantage. A. Preah Vihear and Thailand’s “Lost Territories” In the 18th and 19th centuries, Siam and Vietnam vied for control of Cambodia, while Khmer kings sought room for manoeuvre by playing the larger powers against each other. 4 The Khmer Empire, renowned for building Angkor Wat, dominated mainland South East Asia from roughly the 9th to the 15th century. Siam gained suzerainty over what is now western Cambodia in 1794, but it did not actively colonise the area. 5 David Chandler, A History of Cambodia (Boulder, Colo., 2008), pp. 142-143; 183-184. France then established a protectorate over Cambodia in 1863, stopping the kingdom’s neighbours from swallowing it whole. In 1893, French gunboats dropped anchor in waters near the royal palace in Bangkok to press Siam to cede territories east of the Mekong River, as well as the eastern provinces of Chantaburi and Trat, to France. This event, known as the Pak Nam Crisis, marks the origin of a still-ubiquitous Thai historical narrative of “lost territories” sacrificed by King Chulalongkorn to preserve his domain from the encroachment of Western colonialism. 6 Thongchai Winichakul, Siam Mapped: A History of the Geo-Body 0f a Nation (Honolulu, Hawaii, 1994), pp. 111, 150-153; Shane Strate, The Lost Territories: Thailand’s History of National Humiliation (Honolulu, Hawaii, 2015). Franco-Siamese treaties of 1904 and 1907 established that the border between Siam and French Indochina would follow the watershed of the Dangrek Mountains. In 1908, Siam received a series of maps, drafted by a French expedition, depicting a border line. 7 The expedition that drafted the map was supposed to be a joint Franco-Siamese endeavour, but Siam did not send surveyors to participate. These maps, known as Annex I of the 1907 treaty, deviate from the treaty’s text; the border line departs from the watershed to place the ancient temple complex of Preah Vihear – a vestige of the Khmer empire – within French Indochina. Siamese officials did not detect the discrepancy until they made their own survey in 1934, but they raised no objection until much later. 8 Strate, The Lost Territories , op. cit., pp. 161-162. The 1:200,000-scale Annex I border maps remain the only legally recognised ones. In Thailand, Preah Vihear became a national cause under Field Marshal Phibun Songkhram, a strongman who governed the country from 1938 to 1944 and again from 1948 to 1957. In 1939, the Department of Education included the temple complex on maps of Thailand’s historical sites. During World War II, Thailand reclaimed Cambodia’s western provinces, encompassing the Preah Vihear complex. The Thai government promoted the temple as a symbol of territories earlier surrendered to colonial powers to retain Siam’s independence. 9 Ibid., pp. 162-163. As a condition for admission to the UN, Thailand then ceded the Cambodian provinces to France under the 1946 Washington Treaty, but it asserted Thai sovereignty over Preah Vihear after Cambodia gained independence in 1953. 10 Sok Udom Deth, A History of Cambodia-Thailand Diplomatic Relations, 1950-2020 (Glienicke, 2020), p. 26. In Thailand, press coverage of the [1958] negotiations stirred up nationalist sentiments, helping turn Preah Vihear [temple] into a popular issue. After years of wrangling, formal bilateral talks about the disputed temple began in 1958. In Thailand, press coverage of the negotiations stirred up nationalist sentiments, helping turn Preah Vihear into a popular issue. Similarly, Cambodia’s King Norodom Sihanouk promoted the historical monument as a national cause, portraying Thailand as a perennial threat to the nation’s sovereignty. 11 Strate, The Lost Territories , op. cit., pp. 165-166. Cambodia withdrew from negotiations in October 1959 and appealed to the ICJ to settle the dispute. In 1962, the court ruled that Preah Vihear was situated in Cambodian territory, reasoning that Siam’s failure to object to the Annex I map in the decades after it was issued signified acceptance. 12 “Case concerning the Temple of Preah Vihear (Cambodia v. Thailand)”, op. cit. In Thailand, the verdict inflamed popular opinion, helping entrench the idea of “lost territories” and national humiliation at the hands of Cambodia and colonial powers. 13 Strate, The Lost Territories , op. cit., p. 170. Satellite imagery of the Preah Vihear temple. Source: Google Earth / CRISIS GROUP B. Managing a Disputed Border The Khmer Rouge victory in Cambodia in 1975 opened a new chapter along the border. After Vietnam’s 1978 invasion of Cambodia, almost a million refugees fled to Thailand. Refugee camps became strongholds of armed groups, including the Khmer Rouge, resisting Vietnam’s occupation with Thai, Chinese and U.S. assistance. 14 Nicole Jenne, “The Thai-Cambodian Border Dispute: An Agency-centred Perspective on the Management of Interstate Conflict”, Contemporary Southeast Asia , vol. 29, n0. 2 (2017), p. 329. In the late 1980s, Thailand reoriented its regional diplomacy, seeking a change from “from battlefield to marketplace”. 15 Chatchai Choonhavan, Thai prime minister from 1988 to 1991, advanced this policy. Meanwhile, the 1991 Paris Peace Accords and the UN Transitional Authority in Cambodia brought relative peace and the prospect of economic development. In accordance with these changes, the two countries took steps to establish a new relationship, leading them to sign a bilateral agreement on border management in 1995. 16 “Agreement between the Government of the Kingdom of Thailand and the Government of the Kingdom of Cambodia on the Establishment of Border Committees”, Phnom Penh, 26 September 1995. This pact set up the General Border Committee (GBC), chaired by the countries’ defence ministers, and three Regional Border Committees (RBC), chaired by regional military commanders charged to “consider and agree on appropriate measures to promote cooperation in the maintenance of peace, order and stability in the border area”. 17 Ibid. The agreement empowered the RBCs to “solve specific problems that may arise” and promote cooperation and communication links “to enable immediate contact at all times”. 18 Ibid. The relevant commands are: Thailand’s 2nd Army Region and Cambodia’s 4th Military Region; Thailand’s 1st Army Region and Cambodia’s 5th Military Region; Thailand’s Chanthaburi-Trat Border Defence Command and Cambodia’s 3rd Military Region. The [Joint Boundary Commission] has ... succeeded in delimiting some 600km of the [Thailand-Cambodia] border, with roughly 200km outstanding. Five years later, Cambodia and Thailand signed a memorandum of understanding establishing a Joint Boundary Commission (JBC) to govern border surveys and demarcation. 19 “Memorandum of Understanding between the Government of the Kingdom of Thailand and the Government of the Kingdom of Cambodia on the Survey and Demarcation of Land Boundary”, 14 June 2000. This document – known as MOU 43 for the Buddhist year 2543 in which it was signed – provides for a five-step process, including identifying the 73 boundary markers installed between 1909 and 1919, jointly surveying the boundary and demarcating the border. In 2003, the two sides then agreed on Terms of Reference dividing the border into seven sectors. 20 “Terms of Reference and Master Plan for the Joint Survey and Demarcation of Land Boundary between the Kingdom of Thailand and the Kingdom of Cambodia”, p. 14. The JBC has since succeeded in delimiting some 600km of the border, with roughly 200km outstanding. 21 “Thai-Cambodian border row: Does 1:50,000 or 1:200,000 mapping give the edge?”, The Nation , 16 June 2025. In 2001, Bangkok and Phnom Penh signed a separate memorandum of understanding on overlapping maritime claims. Known as MOU 44, it provided for boundary delineation and joint development of hydrocarbons in a portion of the 26,000 sq km disputed area, which may contain as much as eleven trillion cubic feet of natural gas and between 300 and 500 million barrels of crude oil, with a combined value of some $300 billion. 22 “Memorandum of Understanding between the Government of the Kingdom of Thailand and the Government of the Kingdom of Cambodia regarding their Overlapping Maritime Claims to the Continental Shelf”, 18 June 2001; Supalak Ganjanakhundee, “Beyond scrapping the MOU: Navigating maritime disputes under UNCLOS”, Prachatai English , 1 June 2026. Appended to the document is a map depicting the two sides’ continental shelf claims and the resulting areas of overlap. This map has spurred criticism in Thailand as the Cambodian claim line appears to cross the island of Koh Kut, which the 1907 treaty had clearly identified as Siamese territory. C. Politics and Conflict The historical dispute over territory does not in itself explain why conflict erupted in 2025. Contemporary tension between the two countries is intimately linked to Thailand’s turbulent domestic politics, which for two decades has revolved around a contest for power between the tycoon-turned-politician Thaksin Shinawatra and his conservative opponents. 23 See Crisis Group Asia Reports N°274, Thailand’s Lengthening Roadmap to Elections , 10 December 2015; N°263, A Coup Ordained? Thailand’s Prospects for Stability , 3 December 2014; and N°192, Bridging Thailand’s Deep Divide , 5 July 2010; as well as Crisis Group Asia Briefings N°121, Thailand: The Calm before Another Storm? , 11 April 2011; N°82, Thailand: Calming the Political Turmoil , 22 September 2008; and N°80, Thailand: Political Turmoil and the Southern Insurgency , 28 August 2008. Thaksin also had close ties with Cambodia’s Hun Sen, who served as prime minister from 1985 to 2023, currently presides over the senate and still controls the ruling Cambodian People’s Party. That relationship crumbled in dramatic fashion in June 2025, with direct repercussions for bilateral relations. 1. Thailand Thaksin became prime minister in 2001. His Thai Rak Thai Party won support by delivering on popular policies but earned the enmity of conservatives and the military over alleged conflicts of interest and challenges to the prerogatives of the royal palace. Led by conservative royalists, the People’s Alliance for Democracy (PAD) took to the streets to call for Thaksin’s resignation in 2005. The military ousted him in a September 2006 coup, sending him into exile, but his proxy parties continued to win elections. The Thaksin/conservative divide was the fulcrum of Thai politics for more than a decade. In May 2008, under a Thaksin-aligned government, Thailand signed a joint communiqué with Cambodia supporting inscription of Preah Vihear temple as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The PAD promptly began using this issue as a cudgel against Thaksin, playing on the memory of the 1962 ICJ decision and the theme of lost territory, and portraying Thaksin’s purported business dealings in Cambodia as a threat to Thai sovereignty. 24 Crisis Group Report, Waging Peace , op. cit., pp. 4-5. Ever after, despite a lack of hard evidence of any conflict of interest, Thaksin’s opponents would accuse the Shinawatra family of “selling out” the national interest to Hun Sen. 25 Puangthong Pawakapan, State and Uncivil Society in Thailand at the Temple of Preah Vihear (Singapore, 2013), pp. 37, 62-64. With Preah Vihear [temple] ... a live political issue in Thailand, tensions increased on the border [with Cambodia]. With Preah Vihear again a live political issue in Thailand, tensions increased on the border. The two sides exchanged fire on six occasions between October 2008 and May 2011, claiming at least 34 lives. 26 Martin Wagener, “Lessons from Preah Vihear: Thailand, Cambodia and the Nature of Low-Intensity Border Conflicts”, Journal of Current Southeast Asian Affairs , vol. 30, no. 3 (2011), pp. 32-33. In April 2011, Cambodia requested that the ICJ interpret the 1962 verdict, particularly Thailand’s obligation to withdraw troops from the Preah Vihear temple or “its vicinity on Cambodian territory”. In July, the court issued a provisional ruling, including establishment of a demilitarised zone around Preah Vihear. In 2013, the ICJ affirmed Cambodia’s sovereignty over the promontory on which Preah Vihear is situated but referred delineation of the border in adjacent disputed territory to bilateral negotiations. “Request for interpretation of the Judgment of 15 June 1962 in the Case concerning the Temple of Preah Vihear (Cambodia v. Thailand) Request for the indication of provisional measures”, Summary of the Judgment, ICJ, 11 November 2013. In 2009, in a provocation to his political opponents, Thaksin accepted an appointment as an adviser to Hun Sen, who also offered refuge to his supporters fleeing a 2010 Thai army crackdown. Thaksin’s sister Yingluck, prime minister from 2011 to 2014, then took refuge in Cambodia after the Constitutional Court disqualified her from office, just before the military staged a coup. With the Thai military firmly in power and both Thaksin and Yingluck in exile, the pro/anti-Thaksin antagonism no longer defined Thai politics. But in 2023, the Thaksin-aligned Pheu Thai Party struck a bargain with its erstwhile conservative foes, joining forces to keep the progressive People’s Party from power after its massive general election victory. The deal allowed Thaksin proxy Srettha Thavisin to become prime minister and Thaksin himself to return home from fifteen years in exile. Hun Sen was Thaksin’s first visitor from abroad. 2. Cambodia Cambodia is ostensibly in transition from rule by Hun Sen to government by Hun Manet, who replaced his father as prime minister in 2023. During his 38 years as prime minister, Hun Sen consolidated power through a mix of co-optation and repression, while casting himself as Cambodia’s saviour. Beginning in 2017, a crackdown on dissent saw the main opposition party outlawed, scores of politicians jailed and driven into exile, and independent media suppressed. 27 Lee Morgenbesser, “Cambodia’s Transition to Hegemonic Authoritarianism”, Journal of Democracy , vol. 30, no. 1 (2019); Neil Loughlin, “Beyond Personalism: Elite Politics and Political Families in Cambodia”, Contemporary Southeast Asia , vol. 43, no. 2 (2021); “Cambodia: Hun Sen Extinguishes Media Freedom”, Human Rights Watch, 13 February 2023. Hun Sen remains extremely powerful, both as senate president and as the leading figure in the ruling Cambodian People’s Party (CPP). Hun Manet’s rise to the prime minister’s office is part of a generational succession designed to secure the Hun family’s pre-eminence by safeguarding the interests of other senior CPP figures; the sons of some of Hun Sen’s long-serving ministers took over their fathers’ posts at the same time. 28 Tea Banh, defence minister since 1993, handed down his position to his son Tea Seiha and Sar Kheng, interior minister since 1992, turned over his post to his son Sar Sokha. Hun Manet’s younger brothers also ascended to high-ranking positions. Will Brehm, “How did Hun Sen engineer a seamless succession in Cambodia?”, East Asia Forum , 9 September 2023. Unassuming and technocratic, Hun Manet appears focused on governance and economic reforms, but he governs in his father’s shadow, and it remains to be seen if he can keep Hun Sen’s coalition intact. 29 Crisis Group interview, former official, Phnom Penh, May 2026. See also Chheang Vannarith, “Hun Manet’s Worldview”, Southeast Asian Affairs 2025 (Singapore, 2025). While domestic political opposition is weak, Hun Sen appears worried about popular discontent. 30 Crisis Group interviews, diplomats and analysts, Phnom Penh, February 2026. The Hun family’s grip on power is not necessarily secure, as CPP factions weigh a post-Hun Sen future. 31 Crisis Group interviews, analysts, former official, Phnom Penh, February and May 2026. On 1 June, Hun Sen warned, “Only the ‘angels’ [CPP members] and their children have the right to govern this country”. 32 “Hun Sen warns extremists against ouster attempts”, Khmer Times , 3 June 2026. While Khmer nationalism has generally been the province of the CPP’s political opponents, confrontation with Thailand has offered Hun Sen an opportunity to burnish his own nationalist credentials and bolster his family’s political legitimacy during the period of generational succession. 33 Crisis Group interviews, analysts, Phnom Penh, February 2026. III. The Path to Conflict A convergence of heightened Thai nationalism, linked to conservatives’ antipathy for Thaksin, and escalatory actions by Cambodia, led to two rounds of fighting in 2025. A. The Resurgence of Thai Nationalism The unlikely bargain between Thaksin and conservative parties struck in 2023 to keep the progressive People’s Party from power set the stage for a revival of Thai nationalism anchored in anti-Cambodia sentiment. In February 2024, Prime Minister Srettha Thavisin agreed to open talks with Hun Manet on joint development of hydrocarbons in the maritime overlapping claims area, providing Thaksin’s opponents with a pretext to reopen the 2008 “lost territories” playbook. 34 “Thailand, Cambodia to discuss joint petroleum exploitation”, Bangkok Post , 7 February 2024. The refrain only grew stronger after Thaksin gave a speech that included a pledge to “unlock” the Gulf of Thailand’s oil and gas resources in August. 35 William J. Jones, “Thai nationalism rears its ugly head again”, East Asia Forum , 17 January 2025. Thaksin’s daughter Paetongtarn Shinawatra became prime minister in August 2024 and continued these nascent efforts, stirring the disquiet of conservatives and old PAD networks about MOU 44. 36 Thailand’s Constitutional Court removed Srettha Thavisin from office on 14 August 2024 for violating ethical standards in a cabinet appointment. Critics of the agreement argued that it jeopardised Thai sovereignty over the island of Koh Kut, conferred structural advantages upon Cambodia and reflected conflicts of interest on the Shinawatra clan’s part. 37 Tita Sanglee, “Doubt and Dissent: Thai Nationalist Views on the Thailand-Cambodia Maritime Dispute”, ISEAS Perspective , no. 9, 2025, p. 3. As a prominent Thaksin critic asked: “[F]or whose benefit is the Thai government rushing to negotiate within the old framework, given that [MOU 44] contradicts the 1973 Royal Decree [codifying Thailand’s continental shelf claim] and risks territorial loss, as in the Preah Vihear case?” 38 “‘Mom Korn’ points out that MOU 44 contradicts the royal decree of King Rama IX, risks losing territory and urges its immediate cancellation”, Thai Post , 25 October 2024 [Thai]. In June 2024, Paiboon Nititawan, deputy leader of the military-backed Phalang Pracharat Party (PPRP), petitioned the Constitutional Court to determine whether MOU 44 was illegal because parliament had not approved it. 39 “PPRP seeks ruling on MoU with Cambodia”, Bangkok Post , 14 June 2024. The court dismissed the petition in September of that year, on the grounds that Paiboon lacked the standing to bring such a case. 40 “Court verdict empowers Thai government to push energy deal with Cambodia”, Thai PBS World, 17 September 2024. The PPRP then held a press conference a month later alleging that joint development under MOU 44 could jeopardise Thailand’s sovereignty over Koh Kut, putting the government on the defensive. 41 “Thai territory bordering Cambodia is safe, says government”, Bangkok Post , 31 October 2024. Amid demands from the party and conservative activists to scrap MOU 44, Thailand’s defence minister visited the island to assert Thailand’s sovereignty. 42 “Thailand cannot scrap MOU 44 without Cambodia’s okay: Anutin”, The Nation , 4 November 2024; “Thai deputy PM makes case for Cambodia deal”, Bangkok Post , 9 November 2024. B. Border Tensions With maritime tensions simmering, friction increased along the land border. On 13 February 2025, a group of Cambodians visited the disputed Ta Muan Thom/Tamone Thom temple, reportedly escorted by Cambodian soldiers, and sang a patriotic song.
