The U.S. and UN Will Need More Patience to Resolve Western Sahara Conflict cmoore Fri, 10/09/2026 - 17:45 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List A United Nations Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO) Mil Mi-8 helicopter lands on the Moroccan side of the border crossing point between Morocco and Mauritania, in Guerguerat located in the Western Sahara. 25 November, 2020. AFP / Fadel Senna Commentary / Middle East & North Africa 09 October 2026 17 minutes The U.S. and UN Will Need More Patience to Resolve Western Sahara Conflict Talks between Morocco and the pro-independence Polisario Front over Western Sahara have hit a wall, with U.S. and UN representatives pushing for Rabat’s autonomy plan as the centrepiece of negotiations. If they are to broker a compromise, the mediators will have to slow down. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Also available in Arabic English Arabic Riccardo Fabiani Project Director, North Africa https://twitter.com/ricfabiani Related Tags Multilateral Diplomacy Western Sahara Morocco Mauritania For some time after October 2025, it seemed that the long diplomatic stalemate over Western Sahara might have been broken. This desert territory is claimed by Morocco but sought by the Algeria-based Polisario Front as the home of an independent state for the Sahrawi people. A UN Security Council resolution passed in October 2025 strengthened international backing for a Moroccan autonomy proposal while remaining vague enough to allow for the possibility of other outcomes. Working together with the UN envoy to Western Sahara, Washington used this narrow opening to bring Morocco and the Polisario back into direct discussions for the first time since 2019. Algeria and Mauritania, both neighbours of Western Sahara, also joined. Three rounds of talks in Washington and Madrid allowed the parties to explore practical elements of a possible settlement without forcing either Morocco or the Polisario to abandon its stance on Western Sahara’s sovereignty, autonomy and self-determination. But the opening is now in danger of closing. The U.S. and UN tried to move too fast, from exploratory discussions to negotiations centred on Morocco’s autonomy proposal, meeting with firm resistance from the Polisario, which insists on a self-determination vote. Meanwhile, a series of diplomatic and military incidents sullied what had been a constructive atmosphere. Washington has responded by applying increasing pressure on the Front, entertaining alternative Sahrawi interlocutors and considering changes to the diplomatic framework. Uncertainty about the U.S. position on the future of the UN Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO) adds another complication. The U.S. concededly has a difficult diplomatic task. It needs to show both resolve and a capacity for patience if it wants to coax the parties toward progress – and right now the balance is off. Why the U.S. decided to become so seized of this issue is unclear, but if the objective is a quick diplomatic win, then it is looking at the wrong file. Indeed, there is a significant risk that, if the administration persists in trying to force a quick settlement, it will risk deepening the mistrust that has long impeded progress in negotiations. Rather than searching for shortcuts, the U.S. and UN should seek to rebuild confidence among the parties, preserve an open negotiating framework and gradually create the political conditions under which substantive compromises might eventually become possible. Creating Space for Talks The Western Sahara conflict dates to 1975, when Spain withdrew from the territory and Morocco and Mauritania moved to divide it between them. The Polisario Front, backed principally by Algeria, launched an armed struggle for independence. Thousands of Sahrawis fled to Algeria. A UN-brokered ceasefire in 1991 envisaged a referendum on self-determination, but disagreements over who should be able to vote have prevented it from taking place. Morocco has instead promoted a plan that would devolve powers to an autonomous Western Sahara under Rabat’s sovereignty, while the Polisario continues to demand a route to independence. The ceasefire collapsed in 2020, though fighting has remained limited. That same year, during President Donald Trump’s first term, the U.S. recognised Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara, in exchange for Morocco’s normalisation of relations with Israel; during Trump’s second term, the administration has strongly endorsed Rabat’s autonomy plan. In October 2025, the UN Security Council agreed to renew MINURSO’s mandate for another year, with new language more explicitly supporting Morocco’s autonomy plan. As the penholder, the U.S. had tabled a first draft that called autonomy “the basis” for future negotiations and “the most feasible solution”; but consultations among Council members led to watered-down language. The final version’s ambiguously (and awkwardly) worded text says autonomy will be taken “as basis” for negotiations and represents “a most feasible solution”. The Council thus gave its strong backing for the autonomy plan, while leaving the door ajar for discussion of other proposals. While both the Polisario and Algeria said the resolution’s final version improved upon the first draft, they rejected it. While both the Polisario and Algeria said the resolution’s final version improved upon the first draft, they rejected it. The former reiterated its demand for a self-determination referendum to settle the conflict, while the latter – then an elected member of the Council – took the politically unsurprising but exceptionally rare step of not voting on the resolution to register its opposition to a reference to “Moroccan sovereignty” in one of its preambular clauses. Nonetheless, U.S. Senior Advisor for Arab and African Affairs Massad Boulos used the resolution’s ambiguity to press Algeria and the Polisario to return to negotiations. In the weeks after the Council vote, Boulos signalled to both actors that, though Washington clearly supported autonomy, the UN resolution did not preclude another solution if the conflict parties agreed to it. At the time, a Polisario official told Crisis Group that “Boulos’s language is more neutral than the UN Security Council resolution” – an expression of growing confidence in Washington’s role. Between January and February 2026, ministerial-level delegations from Algeria, Mauritania, Morocco and the Polisario gathered twice in Washington and once in Madrid, the first direct meetings between the conflict parties in seven years. The co-chairs were Boulos, U.S. Ambassador to the UN Michael Waltz and UN envoy Staffan de Mistura. These rounds differed from previous efforts in at least three ways. First, Washington was directly involved in the discussions, marking a break from its traditional role as the UN envoy’s external supporter, with U.S. officials both driving the conversation and giving de Mistura space to help do the same. Secondly, Algeria and Mauritania participated in the talks – though only as ostensible “observers”. For years, Rabat has wanted Algiers and Nouakchott involved in negotiations, claiming that the Polisario is an Algerian proxy and that, to be durable, any agreement will have to be part of a grand bargain with countries abutting Western Sahara. Algeria and Mauritania have countered that they are merely neighbours interested in the conflict’s resolution (hence their insistence on “observer” status). Thirdly, ahead of the talks and responding to a demand repeatedly put forward by the U.S. and its European partners over the years, Morocco expanded its four-page autonomy proposal floated in 2007 into a comprehensive 40-page blueprint to guide negotiations. The co-chairs insisted on confidentiality from the participants to protect discussions from political pressures at home. Though news broke that the four parties were talking, the contents of the three rounds have remained mostly secret, with Morocco’s expanded autonomy plan still under wraps. That said, diplomatic sources have told Crisis Group that the talks, which apparently touched upon organising elections and reintegrating Sahrawi refugees, among other things, went well overall. In a conversation with Crisis Group, a Polisario official was keen to stress that these exchanges were “a discussion, not a negotiation”. The open-ended format seemed to suit both sides, making it possible for them to re-engage with each other, however warily. From Progress to Stalemate The talks subsequently hit a wall, however. After the three meetings, the U.S. and UN repeatedly asked the Front to offer its comments on Rabat’s plan with the aim of kickstarting a more substantive discussion of how to end the conflict. The Polisario baulked, with an official explaining to Crisis Group that the Front “has not accepted the Moroccan autonomy plan as the basis for negotiations and the UN Security Council does not require us to accept it”. While this position should not have been surprising – the talks gained momentum only because of the ambiguity that the U.S. had managed to create around this key issue – U.S. and UN diplomats seemed both frustrated and bewildered by the Front’s attitude. A U.S. official noted that “Algeria showed much more flexibility than the Polisario” by encouraging the Front to respond to Morocco’s autonomy plan, rather than rejecting the proposal out of hand. Between May and June, relations between the parties – as well as between the U.S. and the Polisario – quickly deteriorated. On 5 May, after a long period of quiet, the Front fired rockets at the city of Smara, in Moroccan-controlled Western Sahara, wounding a civilian and damaging a number of buildings. The U.S., France and several other countries, along with the EU and UN, immediately condemned the attack, calling it an attempt to undermine negotiations . The next day, U.S. Ambassador to Morocco Duke Buchan III visited Dakhla, in Moroccan-controlled Western Sahara, reiterating the Trump administration’s recognition of Rabat’s sovereignty and criticising the Polisario. On 7 May, the Polisario issued a statement denouncing Buchan’s visit and justifying the Smara attack as legitimate resistance to colonialism. Things took a turn for the worse after an exchange of letters between Ambassador Waltz and Polisario leaders failed to restore mutual confidence. Things took a turn for the worse after an exchange of letters between Ambassador Waltz and Polisario leaders failed to restore mutual confidence. According to several U.S. and European diplomats, Waltz wrote to ask whether the Front’s leaders were still committed to a negotiated solution after Smara. The Polisario reportedly responded with a long missive about the dispute’s complexity that Washington saw as obfuscatory. At that point, a number of administration insiders turned against the group. Tensions escalated further when, on 7 June, Moroccan forces killed Lahbib Abdelaziz, son of former Polisario leader Mohamed Abdelaziz and a potential future leader of the Front. His killing shocked pro-independence Sahrawis, who complained that (in contrast to the outcry that followed the Smara attack) there was precious little international condemnation. Then, on 8 June, Sahrawi activist Naama Asfari – who was arrested in 2010 in connection with protests at Gdeim Izik – began a hunger strike , which lasted 47 days and ended only after Rabat granted him a transfer to a jail closer to his family. By late June, U.S. frustration with the Polisario had begun to show. On 30 June, Waltz met with a delegation of the Sahrawi Movement for Peace (MSP), founded in 2020 as a self-styled moderate alternative to the Polisario, expressing willingness to negotiate with Morocco over autonomy. Waltz praised the MSP as an organisation committed to “peace, compromise and a durable solution” that “the world should hear”. Another meeting between a U.S. embassy official and an MSP delegation followed on 28 July. With these steps, the U.S. was breaking with a well-established practice of recognising the Polisario as the representative of the Sahrawi people (even if there was some dispute over whether it should be considered the sole, exclusive representative) and raising the spectre that it might bypass the Front absent greater cooperation. The Front reacted dismissively. A Polisario official told Crisis Group that U.S. officials “should come on the ground and see who really represents the Sahrawis. The Polisario comes from the people and remains representative. The groups they want to promote are nothing”. Summing up the U.S. approach, a Western diplomat told Crisis Group that Washington believes the Polisario’s choice is between “the hard way and the harder way”, meaning that continued resistance by the movement to engaging with Morocco’s plan will bring more adverse consequences upon it. In another sign of tougher steps to come, and in parallel to the talks, a group of U.S. members of Congress introduced two bills that would require the Secretary of State to designate the Polisario as a foreign terrorist organisation (FTO) due to its alleged links with Iran and Lebanese Hizbollah. For legal and political reasons, it is hard to imagine these bills passing into law and being enforced, and the administration has expressed no support for them. But the administration could be working with Congressional allies to signal what might come next should the impasse persist. Searching for Alternatives Faced with a diplomatic deadlock ahead of the expiry of MINURSO’s mandate at the end of October, U.S. officials have been weighing other options, including replacing the Polisario with more flexible Sahrawi representatives, such as the MSP, in the talks. A Western diplomat observed that Washington could use the mandate renewal to try including new language that creates space at the negotiating table for the MSP and others (eg, elected Sahrawi officials who reside in Morocco) – for instance by referring to “Sahrawi representatives” rather than “the Polisario Front” when describing the concerned parties. That said, not all U.S. officials seem ready to drop the Front or give up on the current format. In a 25 September interview with France 24 , Boulos stressed that the U.S. was still hoping the Polisario would engage in talks, praised Algeria’s stance and highlighted that more work was needed to achieve a mutually acceptable settlement. The pro-Polisario media welcomed these remarks. In his 28 September speech to the UN General Assembly, Algerian Foreign Minister Ahmed Attaf reiterated his country’s rejection of any shortcut to a deal: “Algeria warns that any attempt to bypass this framework of reference or marginalise the holders of the inalienable right, the people of Western Sahara and their sole, legitimate representative, the Polisario Front, will not contribute to resolving the conflict; rather, it will further exacerbate tensions”. Meanwhile, Morocco has been assiduously currying favour with the Trump administration, even if it has not openly backed the idea of opening negotiations to other Sahrawi groups. In July, King Mohamed VI announced that the Tiznit-Dakhla road connecting Morocco to Western Sahara would be renamed the Donald J. Trump Highway as “a personal expression of my high regard”. On 15 September, Moroccan Foreign Minister Nasser Bourita, Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar and U.S. Ambassador Waltz agreed in New York on upgrading Israel-Morocco relations by appointing ambassadors and working toward a series of economic agreements to be signed by year’s end. In their official statement, the three countries reaffirmed Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara and support for the autonomy plan. “The tripartite agreement with the U.S. and Israel is an essential part of Morocco’s approach to Western Sahara”, a Moroccan expert told Crisis Group. “The diplomatic upgrade is a gesture addressed to Washington, as we need the U.S. on our side ahead of the next Security Council meeting”. According to Moroccan and European sources, Rabat is hoping that the MINURSO renewal will, among other things, include clearer backing for the autonomy plan as “the only basis” for resolving the conflict. MINURSO’s future remains up in the air. At this stage, MINURSO’s future remains up in the air. In October 2025, Washington tried to shorten the mission’s mandate to three months, hoping that more frequent Security Council involvement might increase pressure on the parties to reach a deal, thus allowing MINURSO to wind down, in line with the U.S. agenda of reducing spending on peacekeeping missions. Eventually, the U.S. settled for a twelve-month renewal in parallel with a strategic review conducted by the Secretary-General. Meanwhile, in anticipation of U.S. requests to trim peacekeeping spending, MINURSO underwent cuts , removing 23 civilian posts, reducing flying hours and slashing its own budget by 11.5 per cent. In an April Senate hearing , Waltz mentioned MINURSO as a mission that – in the Trump administration’s eyes – has outlived its purpose. Several European diplomats told Crisis Group that they suspected Washington would once again push for a major cut in the mission’s expenses or (less likely) its termination during the next renewal debate. MINURSO’s political mandate has changed beyond recognition since its inception, insofar as it presently plays only a marginal role in diplomacy. But European officials who spoke to Crisis Group share the conviction that its presence remains critical to avoiding escalation. In 2022, Morocco made clear that, should MINURSO withdraw from the UN buffer zone separating the territory held by Rabat from the Algerian and Mauritanian borders, the kingdom would occupy this strip of land. If that were to happen, the Polisario would likely attack Moroccan installations from Algeria or Mauritania, rather than using the buffer zone as its launchpad, as is now the case. In turn, Rabat might decide to pursue Polisario units into Algerian or Mauritanian territory, potentially dragging its neighbours into conflict. Rebuilding Confidence among the Parties With the October deadline for renewing the MINURSO mandate fast approaching, U.S. officials could be tempted to either strong-arm the Polisario into accepting Morocco’s autonomy plan or replace the Front with a more accommodating alternative. They may hope that this small organisation will eventually buckle under Washington’s pressure, fearful of the consequences of continued obduracy, which might range from being cast aside to being designated as an FTO, with the severe attendant sanctions. For an administration keen to secure quick deals to end wars, ending the Western Sahara conflict might look like low-hanging fruit. Taking this tack would be highly risky. Since the breakdown of the UN-organised referendum scheme in the early 2000s and, in particular, the resumption of hostilities in 2020, confidence between Morocco and the Polisario has been running low, a by-product of the conflict’s five-decade duration, the accumulation of failed diplomatic initiatives, competing legal and historical narratives, and repeated periods of military confrontation and political deadlock. The two sides continue to approach negotiations from fundamentally different premises: Morocco sees autonomy under its sovereignty as the sole viable end state, while the Polisario insists on a process that preserves the option of independence. In addition, since the 2021 diplomatic rupture between Algeria and Morocco, the conflict has been nestled within a regional dispute , further complicating efforts to resolve it. U.S. pressure alone is unlikely to yield a substantive breakthrough, certainly not without simultaneous confidence-building measures. U.S. pressure alone is unlikely to yield a substantive breakthrough, certainly not without simultaneous confidence-building measures. The Polisario regards self-determination for all practical purposes as an existential issue, meaning that it is more likely to dig in than concede in the face of coercion, with much of the cost of any standoff being borne by vulnerable Sahrawi refugees. In such a scenario, the risk of escalatory violence would also increase. For leaders on both sides to make difficult concessions, and for public opinion to accept them, at least some preliminary steps are needed. Otherwise, both will view negotiations as a zero-sum game, dimming prospects for a resolution. “We need a minimum of trust”, a Polisario official commented to Crisis Group. Against this backdrop, Washington should drop any illusion of reaching a swift deal. Instead, it ought to embrace a more patient approach that, for now, focuses on clearing the air among parties whose relations have soured. The co-chairs should look to four confidence-building measures that might create a better atmosphere for future talks. They should: First, press Morocco and the Polisario to allow Sahrawi families in Algerian refugee camps to visit Moroccan-controlled Western Sahara, and vice versa, resuming a program that was suspended in 2014. These exchanges would create regular, low-risk cooperation among Morocco, Polisario and the UN in service of a concrete humanitarian need, while reconnecting people divided by the conflict and helping reduce both mistrust and the political cost of engagement; Secondly, urge Morocco to release some or all the Sahrawi prisoners it has held since the 2010 Gdeim Izik protests – or at least to honour prisoners’ requests for transfer to jails closer to their families; Thirdly, push the Polisario to declare a unilateral truce in return. Even though the Front rejects returning to the 1991 ceasefire, it might be persuaded to temporarily suspend its attacks to avoid undermining talks; and Finally, arrange for U.S. and UN officials to visit the Sahrawi refugee camps in Tindouf, Algeria, meeting the Polisario leadership and holding town hall-style meetings with refugees to listen to their concerns. The co-chairs also should revise their diplomatic approach to get out of the current cul-de-sac. Rather than pushing the Polisario to respond to Morocco’s autonomy plan – which it rejects as a sole basis for negotiations – they should revert to the format of the three rounds held in Washington and Madrid, thus creating space for the parties to continue a less structured exchange of views on their respective plans. The co-chairs could facilitate these conversations and advance bridging proposals on the specific issues discussed. The most difficult questions relating to sovereignty should be left for the end. Over time, such an approach – pursued on the basis that “nothing is agreed until everything is agreed” – might eventually allow for more in-depth discussions. Algeria has made clear it would not participate in a dialogue that does not include the [Polisario] Front. Crucially, the U.S. should stop suggesting it might replace the Polisario with other Sahrawi representatives in the talks. Algeria has made clear it would not participate in a dialogue that does not include the Front. Besides, any settlement reached with such alternative groups would almost certainly lack popular buy-in and would fuel tensions among Morocco, the Polisario, Algeria and Mauritania. That said, the co-chairs might create a purely consultative parallel track bringing together other Sahrawis, from elected officials in Morocco to the MSP to civil society groups from the Tindouf camps – all of whom might have more political flexibility to put ideas on the table than Morocco and the Polisario. These Sahrawis could contribute their ideas on specific issues such as elections, natural resource management and refugee reintegration – as well as on the sovereignty-related endgame issues. For its part, the Polisario should engage more earnestly in the process. Whatever the Front thinks of the Trump administration’s pressure campaign, both the Polisario and Sahrawi refugees would benefit from seeing it defused. Showing some flexibility would have the dual advantage of helping stave off this threat while taking advantage of U.S. engagement to advance diplomacy. For example, the Polisario could present a new proposal based on a 2003 plan advanced by James Baker, the former U.S. secretary of state who was then UN envoy. Under that plan, which combined autonomy and self-determination, Western Sahara would have had five years of substantial self-rule, with an elected local executive and legislature, while Morocco would have retained responsibility for foreign affairs and defence. After that transitional period, the UN would have held a referendum on the territory’s final status. At the time, the Front accepted the plan, while Rabat rejected it. Such a counteroffer would at least provide the co-chairs with a document they could use in trying to bridge the gap between the two sides’ positions. Morocco should also find ways to show flexibility. While one concrete way to do that might be releases of Gdeim Izik prisoners, it will also need to set something of a different tone in negotiations, resisting the temptation to treat autonomy as an outcome that can be fast-tracked. A more durable settlement will require Rabat to accept a long, difficult negotiating process in which trust gradually is rebuilt and the terms of any eventual compromise are worked through with the Polisario, rather than presented as a fait accompli . Meanwhile, the UN Security Council should refrain from sunsetting MINURSO and ensure that any effort to streamline its mandate or reform the mission preserves its military monitoring component to manage the risk that fighting will spill into Algerian or Mauritanian territory. Washington may reasonably seek to review the mission’s costs and functions, but reforms that significantly weaken or eliminate this military role could remove one of the few remaining stabilising mechanisms in Western Sahara. Finally, Washington should maintain a balanced approach to regional diplomacy – engaging regularly with both Algeria and Morocco, as it has sought to do during the current diplomatic effort, rather than allowing its closer ties with Rabat to feed perceptions that it is taking sides in an increasingly polarised regional competition. Maintaining credible channels with both capitals could help contain bilateral tensions, limit the Western Sahara dispute’s entanglement in wider rivalries and protect the political space needed for an eventual negotiated settlement. Should U.S. diplomats instead choose to intensify pressure on the Polisario and its backers in hopes of forcing rapid acceptance of Morocco’s autonomy framework, they are likely to find – potentially at high cost to the parties and to the region – that a conflict more than five decades old is unlikely to be resolved through coercion alone. A Fateful Choice: Will This Election Change Israel? cmoore Mon, 10/12/2026 - 13:35 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List A Fateful Choice: Will This Election Change Israel? Online Event Tuesday, 20 October 2026 10am Washington, DC | 4pm Brussels | 5pm Tel Aviv Please register here if you would like to attend this online event. The Knesset elections on 27 October could be the most consequential in Israel’s short history. After four years of hard-right government under Benjamin Netanyahu, and three years of war on multiple fronts since the Hamas attack of 7 October 2023, Israelis head to the polls with starkly different hopes for their future. About a dozen political parties are expected to cross the threshold needed to enter the 120-seat parliament. Two main blocs, of nearly equal weight according to polls, face off against each other: an alliance of hard-right parties dominated by Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister and head of the Likud party, and an opposing camp led by Gadi Eisenkot, a former army chief of staff and head of Yashar, a centre-right party he founded last year. A third group, made up of parties that represent Israel’s Palestinian minority, is projected to capture a smaller but critical share of seats. Whichever bloc comes out on top, a question hangs over the vote: has the Israeli political “centre” shifted so much that even new leaders may not bring real change – at least, not on big issues that matter to the rest of the world, such as accommodating the 7.5 million Palestinians that live under Israeli rule? In this online event, Crisis Group brings together leading Israeli political analysts who will tackle this and other questions. It is not too late to avert disaster. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Related Tags Ethiopia Eritrea Horn of Africa Ethiopia and Eritrea stand perilously close to all-out war as heavy fighting inches close to their shared border. The threat of resurgent interstate conflict in the Horn of Africa follows several weeks of fighting between Ethiopia’s federal government and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), which launched an armed rebellion on 23 September. The Ethiopian military has gained the upper hand in those clashes, moving northward after capturing Tigray’s regional capital, Mekelle, on 3 October. Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of supporting the TPLF and deploying military personnel on its soil, a claim that has been backed up by media reports and other accounts, though it appears that Eritrea subsequently pulled its troops back toward the border in the face of an Ethiopian advance and reported drones strikes on its forces. The effects of these cross-border movements could be dire: they could trigger a full-scale war between Ethiopia and Eritrea that, in turn, could spiral into a wider conflagration along Eritrea’s Red Sea coast. A push at the highest political and diplomatic levels to prevent this budding confrontation is a matter of extreme urgency. The Resurgence of Conflict The risk of direct conflict between Ethiopia and Eritrea has risen sharply since late September as war has engulfed Tigray. On 20 September, the TPLF and six other groups announced a new “alliance for survival” aimed at toppling Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government, which they see as authoritarian and bent on centralising power. Two days later, Ethiopia conducted a large drone raid on sites in southern Tigray, where officials believed the TPLF was massing for an attack. On 23 September, the TPLF mounted large-scale offensives against the federal government. It was apparently trying to join forces with two of its allies, the Amhara Fano and Afar Revolutionary Democratic Unity Front, which commenced their own assaults on Ethiopian military positions near Tigray’s boundaries. This first wave of attacks made gains, but Ethiopian forces quickly regrouped. They have steadily pushed the Tigrayans back since then, recording a string of battlefield victories and capturing most of Tigray. On 3 October, federal forces and their allies took Mekelle without a fight. As the TPLF withdrew, the war’s front line shifted toward the group’s strongholds in the northern mountains, near the border with Eritrea. At the same time, tensions between Ethiopia and Eritrea reached fever pitch in the wake of reported Eritrean troop deployments to northern Tigray in support of the TPLF’s rear guard. For the first time since 2000, when Ethiopia and Eritrea ended their last war, the two neighbours now seem poised to engage in frontal combat. For the first time since 2000, when Ethiopia and Eritrea ended their last war, the two neighbours now seem poised to engage in frontal combat. Frictions between the two are neither sudden nor surprising, even if the present rift between them in some ways marks a radical turnaround. For more than a year, Addis Ababa has been denouncing Asmara, and more recently its allies in the Sudanese army, for backing rebel groups in Ethiopia, particularly the TPLF. This antagonism stands in sharp contrast to what prevailed during the last Tigray war, which raged between 2020 and 2022, when Ethiopia and Eritrea had become friends rather than foes. That conflict came on the heels of Abiy’s ascent to power, which in turn dethroned the TPLF, a pivotal force in national politics for decades, and set the stage for a power struggle between the federal government and the TPLF high command in Tigray. Eritrea, which had fought its previous war with Ethiopia from 1998 to 2000 while the TPLF was in charge in Addis Ababa, sought common cause with Abiy in confronting the group after Tigrayan forces attacked Ethiopia’s Northern Command in November 2020. A seesaw battle ensued, with Addis Ababa and its allies eventually beating back the TPLF ahead of the signing of the Pretoria peace agreement in November 2022. This agreement left the TPLF largely intact, however, and its commitment to fully demobilise its armed forces was never fully enforced. Eritrea, which was not involved in the Pretoria negotiations, had been pushing for the group’s complete elimination. Asmara was incensed at the outcome. In its view, its critical national interests had not been respected during the talks. Eritrea’s relations with Ethiopia subsequently began to deteriorate. Some say Abiy was quietly courting the TPLF in order to establish a new alliance with it against Eritrea in the acrimonious aftermath of the peace deal. TPLF leaders apparently rebuffed these advances. Abiy also began to argue in public that Ethiopia needed to restore sovereign access to the sea. He said Ethiopia had a historical claim to the Red Sea coastline, which it had lost when Eritrea seceded in 1993. Since then, Ethiopia, the world’s largest landlocked country by population size, has been relying almost exclusively on Djibouti to export goods by sea. Officials in Abiy’s government have stressed that Ethiopia will not be satisfied merely with access to a wider range of ports, a course some have suggested it pursue, but needs a sovereign seaboard with a naval base. Asmara has viewed this rhetoric as a threat to seize Eritrea’s coastline, especially its southern port of Assab, by armed force. With bilateral relations souring, Eritrea and the TPLF began to explore establishing a common front against Addis Ababa. With bilateral relations souring, Eritrea and the TPLF began to explore establishing a common front against Addis Ababa. Asmara appears to have seen Tigray in the TPLF’s grip as a potential geographic buffer between it and the Ethiopian heartland, as well as a military counterweight to Addis Ababa. The TPLF, for its part, was keen to break the encirclement it endured in the 2020-2022 war. As a sign of their strengthening ties, Eritrean and Tigrayan authorities promoted new cross-border “people-to-people” exchanges known as tsimdo (“engagement” in Tigrinya), providing further ballast for their switch from adversaries to allies. Meanwhile, the 2022 peace deal began to fray. The TPLF complained that the government had failed to resolve major issues stemming from the conflict, including the status of disputed territories occupied by Amhara forces during the war and the return of displaced people to their homes in these areas. Little effort was made to remedy the antipathy between the TPLF and Abiy: Addis Ababa never reintegrated Tigray back into the national political federation, with the region remaining without representation in parliament or other institutions in the capital. In March 2025, the TPLF ousted the first post-war interim Tigray administrator, Getachew Reda, who had been a lead negotiator in the Pretoria peace negotiations for the TPLF and was chosen ahead of TPLF chairperson Debretsion Gebremichael. The group claimed that Getachew was too close to the federal government and had not defended Tigray’s interests sufficiently during his time in office. (Getachew fled to Addis Ababa, where he joined Abiy’s administration.) Abiy then appointed Tadesse Werede, a top Tigrayan general, in Getachew’s place, but the relationship between Tigray’s new ruler and the TPLF also began to worsen. In May 2026, the TPLF retook power in Mekelle, dismantling the interim administration, reinstalling its leader Debretsion as regional president and placing Tadesse under house arrest. The federal government responded by tightening its economic restrictions on the region and launching a campaign of airstrikes inside Tigray. In August, a major clash broke out between TPLF and federal ground forces before quickly subsiding. Shuttle diplomacy by the African Union and others aimed at restarting negotiations failed to gain traction. Simultaneously, mediators found their efforts thwarted by rising hostility among powers across the Horn. Addis Ababa began to denounce Asmara for trying to coordinate a transnational alliance against it, and accused the Sudanese army , an ally of Eritrea and Egypt (another Ethiopian foe), of supporting meetings of a nascent alliance of opposition groups in eastern Sudan. Ethiopia also complained that Sudan was harbouring a group of Tigrayan troops, known as Army 70, in Sudanese territory, where they were said to have stood alongside the army in fighting its enemy, the Rapid Support Forces (RSF). Ethiopia, on the other hand, began allowing the RSF to base itself in its Benishangul-Gumuz region close to the Sudanese border, from where it could launch attacks into Sudan’s Blue Nile state. Ethiopia’s relations with the Sudanese army, which had continued to function despite the chill between them, became icy as a result. Sudan has also claimed that drones attacking Khartoum were dispatched from Ethiopian territory. Neighbours at Loggerheads This mosaic of enmities and alliances has come into sharp relief since war broke out in Tigray. As hostilities have intensified, Ethiopia and Eritrea have edged ever closer to conflict. Ethiopia considers Eritrea to be masterminding the TPLF’s war effort. Soon after fighting broke out, Ethiopian federal officials and Afar’s regional president accused Eritrea of deploying forces in the Afar region. On 1 October, Ethiopia expelled all Eritrean diplomats from the country, accusing Asmara of “direct and indirect acts of hostility and belligerence”. All diplomatic ties between the two states have since been severed. After Ethiopian federal forces began advancing north of Mekelle, the first reports emerged of alleged Eritrean deployments in northern Tigray, seemingly with the aim of bolstering the TPLF’s defensive lines. Several media reports indicated on 7 October that Eritrean units had passed through Adigrat, 30km south of the Ethiopian border. Accounts also suggest that Eritrean forces took up positions south of Adigrat in the Edaga Hamus area. A day later, after reported drone strikes on Eritrean vehicles, some of its forces reportedly withdrew to the border. With Ethiopian forces currently approaching the frontier at several points, the two armies are positioned in alarmingly close proximity. Asmara’s apparent gamble to intervene more directly in the war, even if the incursion was brief, could well backfire. On 9 October, Ethiopia wrote a letter to the UN Security Council saying it was “taking measures” of self-defence in response to Eritrea’s deployment of infantry and mechanised units across the border and occupation of Ethiopian territory. The letter also accused Eritrea of “harbouring, supporting, financing, arming and directing armed insurgent groups operating within Ethiopia”. On 10 October, Eritrea responded with its own letter, accusing Ethiopia of declaring a “war of aggression” against it three years ago and using self-defence as a pretext for acts of war. The Security Council has scheduled a closed-door session to discuss the crisis on 13 October. A standoff along the two countries’ frontier would be an ominous turn of events. A standoff along the two countries’ frontier would be an ominous turn of events. The last major interstate conflict in the Horn of Africa, in which hundreds of thousands perished in trench warfare, was fought along precisely the same border. One flashpoint could be Eritrean military positions inside Ethiopian territory; another could be disputed territory along the border. Should Eritrean forces fully withdraw to their side of the border, Ethiopia could point to Eritrea’s apparent incursion and alleged harbouring of TPLF fighters as justification for seeking to cross into Eritrea. Even if Ethiopia stops short of a land invasion of Eritrea (and Ethiopian officials maintain that they have no intention of fighting a war on Eritrean soil), aerial warfare using drones and other long-range strike weapons could cause devastating harm. Ethiopia possesses the larger air force and drone arsenal, and it could try to quickly overwhelm Eritrea’s air defences. Should the two states lock horns, war could also extend across the region. The Sudanese army and Egypt look primed to jump to Eritrea’s defence, though it is uncertain how much support they would be willing or able to give. On the other side, the United Arab Emirates could be expected to back Ethiopia with more arms transfers. Saudi Arabia is keen to prevent a new front from emerging along the Red Sea, especially one involving the UAE, and has tried in the past to de-escalate tensions between Ethiopia and Eritrea. On this occasion, however, Riyadh might be tempted to throw its weight behind Eritrea should a larger conflict erupt, given that its own Red Sea security would be at stake. That said, Saudi Arabia is also embroiled in a fresh round of fighting in Yemen and may not want to rally to the side of what might be a losing cause. Halting the Slide to War Pulling Ethiopia and Eritrea back from the brink of war should be the priority for all those interested in preventing a deadly chain of interconnected conflicts from snaking across the Horn of Africa and Red Sea regions. Capitals such as Washington, Nairobi, Pretoria, London, Paris, Rome, Riyadh, Ankara and Abu Dhabi should press both sides to avoid escalation. In particular, they should urge Abiy to refrain from advancing into Eritrean territory. They should also appeal to Asmara to respect Ethiopian sovereignty and withdraw any remaining troops from Ethiopian territory, should they still be stationed there. Despite their rift, Saudi Arabia and the UAE could also use this moment to work together to staunch a new conflict along the Red Sea, which could otherwise cause even more trouble in their bilateral relations. Should efforts to avert an outright war prevail, diplomats should not desist until they manage to achieve a durable de-escalation of tensions between the two capitals. The heart of any settlement between the two countries is likely to be respect for each other’s sovereignty and restoration of diplomatic ties. In focusing on calming regional tensions, mediators should not forget the dispute between the Ethiopian government and the TPLF, should the latter manage to avoid complete collapse following its reversals. African leaders still look best placed to restart the Tigray peace track, even if neither federal officials nor TPLF leaders appear ready for direct talks any time soon. Prior to the start of hostilities, former Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo, who oversaw the Pretoria negotiations that ended the last Tigray war, had been acting as the African Union’s peace envoy for the region. He visited Addis Ababa and Mekelle several times earlier in the year but had little success in bringing the two sides together. Efforts should be made to reactivate Obasanjo at the earliest opportunity. Other African leaders or ex-leaders could also be dispatched, such as South African President Cyril Ramaphosa, who made a quick stop in Addis Ababa on 5 October to speak with Abiy, or former Kenyan President Uhuru Kenyatta, who also played a key role in the Pretoria negotiations in 2022. The U.S. or European powers could also play a part behind the scenes in trying to rekindle peace talks. At a minimum, all sides should press the federal government and the TPLF to abide by humanitarian commitments under international law. The UN Security Council, which as noted will discuss the crisis on 13 October, should make a clear call for both sides to respect the UN Charter and instruct the Secretary-General to undertake urgent diplomacy to prevent a new war between Ethiopia and Eritrea. Another war in the Horn of Africa may lie around the corner. Outright conflict between Ethiopia and Eritrea would likely spread to the Red Sea, disrupting the African side of this strategic waterway. It could also prove to be yet another front in the Horn that is easy to open and hard to close, especially once it becomes entangled in the mesh of disputes among neighbours and across the region. The best time to stop the looming Ethiopia-Eritrea war is now, before any more damage is done. Türkiye: End Internet Censorship. Click to expand Image Tags, with “Access blocked” and the name of blocked accounts belonging to journalists and media outlets, LGBT and women’s rights groups, and other rights defenders, are tied to the gates of Turkey’s Constitutional Court, to protest the Turkish authorities’ blocking of hundreds of social media accounts and websites. Ankara, October 7, 2026. © 2026 Yıldız Yazıcıoğlu (Istanbul, October 12, 2026) – The Turkish authorities over the last month have substantially escalated internet censorship, Human Rights Watch said today, along with ARTICLE 19, the Freedom of Expression Association, and 18 other organizations. Social media platforms should take meaningful steps immediately to uphold their human rights responsibilities and avoid contributing to suppressing independent media and violating the right to freedom of expression. The Turkish authorities should stop issuing blocking orders to restrict content and accounts on social media and websites in violation of the right to freedom of expression. The following is the groups’ statement: ARTICLE 19, Freedom of Expression Association (İFÖD), Human Rights Watch, and the undersigned human rights and media freedom organisations are deeply concerned by the severe escalation of internet censorship in Türkiye in the past month. We urge social media platforms to take meaningful steps immediately to uphold their human rights responsibilities and avoid contributing to the suppression of independent media and violations of the right to freedom of expression. We call on the Turkish government immediately to cease the use of blocking orders and other restrictive measures that violate the right to freedom of expression, and to ensure that any restrictions on online content fully comply with Türkiye’s obligations under international human rights law. In the month of September 2026 alone, İFÖD documented Turkish authorities and courts ordering the blocking of access to at least 1,270 accounts on the social media platform X, which had a combined following of 35 million. X complied with at least 90 percent of the orders by geo-blocking them (withholding access to them in Türkiye only). In many cases, the accounts were blocked in the context of an ongoing and wide-ranging crackdown on associations and activists defending the rights of LGBTQ+ people. In other cases, the authorities cited unspecified “national security and public order” grounds. Accounts withheld include news outlets such as soL Haber and Mezopotamya Ajansı; rights organisations including Amnesty Türkiye and the Media and Law Studies Association (MLSA); LGBTQ+; and women’s rights organisations such as Kaos GL and the Federation of Women’s Associations, as well as those of numerous journalists and academics. X also withheld the accounts of İFÖD, its co-founder, Yaman Akdeniz, and its Engelliweb account, which monitors and documents internet censorship in Türkiye. This account plays a critical role in enabling civil society, journalists, and the public to monitor and track websites, social media accounts and content subjected to access restrictions. Blocking T24, one of Türkiye’s biggest and oldest remaining independent news outlets, is particularly troubling. On 29 September, access was blocked to the T24 website and X account with 1.9 million followers, with a court order citing 118 news articles published on the site. The order claimed that the content was “aimed at disrupting and weakening the Turkish family structure” and of a nature “that would adversely affect the developmental process of young and underage individuals concerning sexual orientation and gender identity.” The order cited preventing crime and protecting public order as grounds for the measure but provided no explanation about how the cited content posed a threat to either objective or why blocking an entire news website and social media account was necessary and proportionate. The website has been inaccessible in Türkiye since 30 September. T24 changed its X handle in an attempt to prevent the account from being withheld in Türkiye, then changed it again, after another order blocked access to its second handle. Bianet, another online news outlet which focuses on human rights, also changed its X handle to escape censorship after its account with 400,000 followers was blocked. The court order blocking access to T24 was taken in the context of the “my family is safe” criminal investigations – a crackdown on LGBTQ+ people which targets activists, associations and a journalist advocating for their rights. The websites and social media accounts of at least 96 organizations and individuals were blocked on the same grounds. While most of the cases concern X, Meta has also withheld access to the Instagram and Facebook accounts of several media and civil society organisations, including, Kısa Dalga, Kaos GL, and the Civic Space Studies Association as part of the same operation. Türkiye’s long-standing abuse of Article 8/A of its Internet Law Most of the blocking decisions in September and October invoked Article 8/A of Türkiye’s Internet Law. Article 8/A, used as a tool for internet censorship since its introduction in 2015, provides that online content deemed a threat to national security, public order or presenting a risk on other grounds listed in the article can be removed or blocked on orders of the executive in urgent cases, subject to review later by a Criminal Peace Judgeship, the court assigned such cases. Major examples include blocking access to Wikipedia for 2.5 years in 2017, and to Türkiye’s leading user-generated online discussion platform Ekşi Sözlük for a year in 2023. The Constitutional Court eventually restored both, finding that blocking the entire sites had violated freedom of expression. The use of Article 8/A intensified sharply from 2025, with few safeguards or independent oversight and limited redress for those affected. The Constitutional Court has not ruled on any restrictions under Article 8/A since 2023. Concerning developments aimed at expanding censorship There is no indication that this pressure will ease. On the contrary, the government is taking further measures to accelerate and centralise internet censorship. On 31 July, Law No. 7590 transferred the powers previously exercised by the Information and Communication Technologies Authority (ICTA) contained in the Internet Law, to the Cybersecurity Directorate. This includes the authority to block sites on the request of the presidency or relevant ministries based on Article 8/A. This transfer of authority is troubling. The Cybersecurity Directorate is directly attached to the presidency, consolidating executive control over information and serving as the command centre for Türkiye’s censorship regime. Separately, on 24 September, the justice minister announced the establishment of new “Digital Space Security and Countering Disinformation Bureaux,” where specialised public prosecutors will closely monitor “criminal content and activities encouraging crime on digital platforms” including ‘spreading disinformation.” They are tasked in particular with identifying suspects and initiating criminal proceedings to intervene “more swiftly.” Social media platforms should take urgent action to uphold their human rights responsibilities The conduct of social media platforms forms an essential part of internet censorship in Türkiye. In September and early October, account holders reported receiving only a notification from platforms stating that their account had been withheld in Türkiye under Article 8/A, without any reason or explanation why or how the article had been applied. Some were unable to access the underlying blocking orders even after repeatedly requesting them from the platforms. Without access to the orders, users cannot examine the legal basis for the restriction or even identify to which Criminal Judgeship of Peace to submit their objections. Even when users were able to obtain the orders, the orders often failed to identify the specific content allegedly justifying the blocking of the entire account. Neither X nor Meta have provided public explanations about their responses to the September-October censorship waves. Human Rights Watch wrote to the two platforms requesting comment on their compliance with Turkish courts’ recent blocking orders. Neither platform had responded by the time of publication. Under the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, companies have a responsibility to respect human rights by avoiding causing or contributing to adverse human rights impacts and by addressing impacts directly linked to their operations, products, or services. This responsibility should also inform social media platforms when they respond to government requests that violate international human rights law, and in particular freedom of expression. We therefore urge X, Meta, and any other platform faced with such orders by the Turkish government to also follow these recommendations: Resist complying with arbitrary 8/A requests Refuse to comply with account blocking requests under Article 8/A of the Internet Law unless Turkish authorities identify the specific content at issue and provide sufficient reasoning and evidence demonstrating that the content gives rise to a clear, serious and imminent danger to the right to life and property, national security and public order, public health or other ground listed in the provision. Where account blocking orders provide sufficient information to enable a meaningful assessment, assess them against international human rights law and resist complying with blocking orders that restrict access to protected expression. This includes but is not limited to legally challenging such orders. Where relevant, limit restrictions in scope and duration, for example by restricting access only to the specific content identified in the order rather than withholding the entire account. Ensure transparency Immediately notify users when their accounts are withheld in Türkiye and provide them with the orders on which the restriction is based. This allows account holders to take necessary steps to challenge the orders. Provide transparency concerning account blocking measures, at least by publicly sharing the number of orders received, the number of orders complied with, and publishing case studies. This information is essential for enabling public scrutiny of government censorship and platforms’ role in it. Engage with Turkish civil society Meaningfully engage with Turkish civil society to understand the human rights implications and broader impact of platforms complying with account blocking measures, including the significance of the accounts targeted and the potential consequences of withholding them in Türkiye. Urgently review appeals to restrictions Review user appeals to account restrictions imposed in Türkiye in September and October 2026 and immediately restore access to accounts if the underlying orders fail to meet the requirements of identifying the specific content at issue, establishing a link between that content and the alleged threat to national security, public order and other grounds listed in Article 8/A, and providing adequate reasoning demonstrating that blocking the entire account is necessary and proportionate. We call on Turkish authorities to take urgent steps to end internet censorship and uphold freedom of expression, including by Immediately halting new restrictions on online content that violate freedom of expression, media freedom, and access to information as protected under international law and Türkiye’s human rights obligations.Restoring access to content which has been restricted in violation of international law and Türkiye’s freedom of expression obligations Signatories: ARTICLE 19 Freedom of Expression Association (İFÖD)Human Rights WatchAmnesty International Association of European Journalists (AEJ)Balkan Investigative Reporting Network (BIRN)Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ)Çağdaş Gazeteciler Derneği (ÇGD, Progressive Journalists Association)Foreign Media Association (FMA Turkey)IFEXInternational Press Institute (IPI)Media and Law Studies Association (MLSA)Norwegian Helsinki Committee (NHC)Osservatorio Balcani Caucaso Transeuropa (OBCT)P24 Platform for Independent JournalismPEN AmericaPEN DenmarkPEN InternationalPEN NorwaySouth East Europe Media Organisation (SEEMO)Turkey Litigation Support Project (TLSP)

Philippines: Flood Control Project Disregards Rights. (Manila) – Philippine authorities disregarded the rights of residents who were removed from a small island in Pampanga province for a flood control project and relocated to a site with chronic flooding and few livelihood opportunities, Human Rights Watch said today. In 2022, the Macabebe, Pampanga government relocated 90 families without adequate consultation and information from Pulo Island on the Pampanga River. The relocation site, in the town of Macabebe, is a low-lying area that was formerly a fish pond that floods throughout the year, causing residents to struggle to access services and work. Although the Pulo community wanted to stay together, some family members have since left because of the effects of the flooding on their lives and livelihoods. “Philippine authorities in Pampanga have threatened the safety and livelihoods of Pulo Island residents by relocating them to a low-lying area as part of a flawed flood control project,” said Lian Buan, Southeast Asia researcher at Human Rights Watch. “The Philippine government should consult the community to find a better solution and ensure that future relocations related to flood control projects respect affected people’s rights.” Play Video Pampanga province in the Philippines’ northern island of Luzon experiences the country’s most severe flooding, which is exacerbated by storms, sea-level rise, and limited dam capacity, and is likely to worsen as climate change accelerates. From 2015 to 2025, floods and sea-level rise displaced 6.6 million people in the Philippines. The Philippine government has adopted a national policy for moving entire communities, called planned relocation or resettlement. However, the authorities responsible for moving the Pulo Island community did not follow national or international standards to protect affected people’s rights. Planned relocations, according to the United Nations Guidance on Protecting People from Disasters and Environmental Change through Planned Relocation, should be a measure of last resort to protect life and health, and based on consultation with affected communities or at their request. One of the community boats used to ferry people during the day’s most flooded time at the Pulo relocation site, July 12, 2026. © 2026 Lian Buan/Human Rights Watch Some residents built elevated houses anticipating frequent flooding, July 13, 2026. © 2026 Lian Buan/Human Rights Watch Aidaliza Aquino supports her husband, Eduardo Aquino, who uses a walker for mobility, at the Pulo relocation site in Barangay Candelaria, Macabebe, Pampanga, Philippines, July 13, 2026. © 2026 Lian Buan/Human Rights Watch The river tide reached 1.6m during the high point of flooding at the Pulo relocation site, July 14, 2026. © 2026 Lian Buan/Human Rights Watch Human Rights Watch interviewed 35 residents of the Pulo relocation site in Pampanga’s Barangay Candelaria, Macabebe, between July and August 2026, as well as 9 authorities in Pampanga, and climate change experts. Human Rights Watch also analyzed satellite imagery of Pulo Island and the relocation site, and employed photogrammetry—using a camera to obtain precise measurements—to determine the difference in elevation between the relocation site and the dike. Between 2020 and 2023, the Pampanga municipal government and the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) dredged Pulo Island and relocated the island’s residents. Human Rights Watch found that the relocation did not involve adequate consultation, access to information, or the selection of a suitable site. “They removed us [from Pulo Island], and they put us in a place where we feel we were thrown here like trash,” said a 48-year-old mother of two children. Ria Clarin looks out to water surrounding her house, her daily view since moving to the Pulo relocation site, July 13, 2026. © 2026 Lian Buan/Human Rights Watch Ria Clarin’s house is unfinished because floodwater occasionally enters her house despite added elevation at the Pulo relocation site, July 13, 2026. © 2026 Lian Buan/Human Rights Watch Maria Mallari’s home at the Pulo relocation site was built without elevation, allowing flood waters to enter her home every day, July 14, 2026. © 2026 Lian Buan/Human Rights Watch Residents like Evangeline Bansil have a pair of rain boots for daily wear due to flooding at the Pulo relocation site, July 13, 2026. © 2026 Lian Buan/Human Rights Watch The community boat that ferries people across the flooded Pulo relocation site, July 13, 2026. © 2026 Lian Buan/Human Rights Watch Public works department engineers told Human Rights Watch that the late mayor of Macabebe, Anette Balgan, had requested the dredging—excavating sediment, soil, and other material from the bed of the Pampanga River—and to relocate the community. They said that removing the island would increase the river’s capacity and prevent flooding in the area, making the relocated residents and communities along the river safer. Beginning in 2018, government officials held several meetings with the affected families, some in the local Kapampangan language. None of the residents interviewed by Human Rights Watch felt they were given a choice about the relocation. Community members said they were informed about the relocation site in 2021, and expressed concerns about its suitability during meetings with authorities. The relocation site is below a dike, an elevated ridge built parallel to the river bank to prevent floodwaters reaching nearby residential areas. A road runs along the top of the dike beside the relocation site and serves as the main route to the town. “They did not present any other solutions,” said the 48-year-old mother. “There were no options.” Longtime residents said they felt pressured to move without understanding the reasons, or the compensation and assistance being provided. Residents were required to demolish their own homes to receive compensation. Many feared that if they did not demolish their houses quickly enough, the funding allocated would run out, based on rumors spread in the absence of official information. Some said they felt intimidated by the authorities. “The personnel on site were slightly harassing us too, telling us that we are obligated to leave, that we have no choice, and that they will tell on us to higher authorities,” said a 57-year-old farmer. Evangeline Bansil and Rina Tolentino wade through thigh-deep flood waters, July 14, 2026. © 2026 Lian Buan/Human Rights Watch The level of the river reached 1.6m during high tide at the Pulo relocation site, July 14, 2026. © 2026 Lian Buan/Human Rights Watch A resident looks out to water, her daily view in the Pulo relocation site, July 14, 2026. © 2026 Lian Buan/Human Rights Watch Maria Luz Suñga stands in front of her home at the flooded Pulo relocation site, July 14, 2026. © 2026 Lian Buan/Human Rights Watch A man carries a boy on his back as they wade through floodwater around the Pulo relocation site, July 14, 2026. © 2026 Lian Buan/Human Rights Watch Many of the families are related and wanted to stay together. The UN Guidance provides that planned relocation should “maintain social cohesion and kinship ties.” A massage therapist, 44, said an official became angry when she posed questions about the suitability of the relocation site: “The engineer pointed at me and said they studied engineering and would not risk their licenses over the project [if it weren’t suitable].” Community members said that in response to their concerns, local authorities told them the site would be raised to the same height as the road dike to protect them from flooding. However, the embankment works never reached that elevation, and the site remains below the dike. One engineer who worked on the relocation said that the road dike design does not allow raising the site to the same level. Human Rights Watch visited the relocation site from July 12 to 14, at the beginning of the rainy season, when at high tide the floodwater was knee- to thigh-deep. Human Rights Watch observed children wading through floodwaters, and older people who could not leave their homes while they were flooded. Residents, who described similar flooding year-round, needed to wade through flooded areas to reach the dike road. Click to expand Image The main street at the site where the Pulo Island community has been relocated lies 1.9 meters below the dike road. On the day Human Rights Watch visited, when there was light rain, the street was flooded 20 centimeters deep. Analysis and graphics © 2026 Human Rights Watch The Department of Human Settlements and Urban Development, which would normally have been involved in the relocation project, told Human Rights Watch that, pending further on-site assessments, the “reported physical characteristics of the site raise concerns regarding its suitability for permanent housing.” The Philippines is obligated under international human rights law to respect, protect, and fulfill everyone’s economic, social, and cultural rights. This includes protecting people from reasonably foreseeable climate change risks, including flooding and other impacts. The relocation of Pulo Island residents was inconsistent with international standards as reflected in the UN Guidance. The Commission on Human Rights told Human Rights Watch that had the project been referred to them, they could have helped ensure that rights-based processes were followed. The commission also said it will conduct a fact-finding investigation into the matter. “Communities in the Philippines living in flood-prone areas are already facing the consequences of climate change and shouldn’t have to suffer further from botched government relocations,” Buan said. “Donors supporting the Philippine response to the effects of climate change should press the government to ensure that every aspect of relocation meets international human rights standards.” For more details and accounts about the planned relocation in Pampanga, please see below. Relocation from Pulo Click to expand Image Satellite imagery showing the progressive removal of Pulo Island beginning in 2021 through dredging by the Department of Public Works and Highways. Images © 2026 US NARA, Airbus, Vantor, Google Earth. Analysis and graphics © 2026 Human Rights Watch Pulo is a 24-hectare island on the lower Pampanga River in Macabebe, Pampanga province, about 60 kilometers north of Manila, the Philippine capital. Most families had lived there for generations in a roughly three-hectare area in the northwest corner of the island. Families who lived there recalled rich agricultural land with abundant fruit and vegetables, and fish ponds. Few owned the land on which their houses stood, but many were farmer tenants or “share tenants,” for whom the landowner provides the capital and the tenant provides labor, and both share in the harvest. Residents did not pay rent, but they paid the property tax that the local government collected annually on residential lands. Under the Philippine Right-of-Way Act, those without legal claims on the land are still entitled to compensation for their structures. Macabebe is part of the Pampanga Delta, the portion of Pampanga, Bulacan, and Bataan provinces composed of low swampy lands prone to flooding. In the early 1990s, the Japan International Cooperation Agency funded the Pampanga Delta Development Project Phase I (PDDP I/Delta I), under which 1,851 households were to be resettled, but the project was never completed. The Pulo Island residents opposed being relocated by the project and remained. Two engineers from the flood control cluster of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH), Tomas Edison Olalia and Alvin Diaz, told Human Rights Watch that the removal of the island was “already long overdue” because it had been proposed under the earlier project. Since 2011, the Philippine government has spent Php 1.93 trillion (US$30 billion) on flood control projects across the country through the department. Almost one third, or Php 545 billion ($8.7 billion), was spent between July 2022 and May 2025, during the administration of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., amid allegations of massive corruption in flood control projects. At least 45 public officials have been charged in the anti-graft court in connection with various flood-control projects, most of them DPWH officials.The officials interviewed have not been implicated, nor did Human Rights Watch investigate corruption in the Pulo Island project. In 2019 and 2020, the department’s flood control cluster awarded two contracts worth Php 157 million ($2.6 million) to remove Pulo Island through its yearly flood mitigation program, according to contracts and budget line items. DPWH officials told Human Rights Watch that the project was initiated by then-Mayor Balgan. In separate letters sent by the former mayor to the agency and the agency to the residents, the community was termed “informal settler families” who needed to be removed from a “danger zone.” Under Philippine law, informal settler families occupy land without consent, or live in places considered “danger areas.” Olalia and Diaz, the engineers involved in the project, said Balgan requested the island’s dredging under a 2017 policy that instructs local government to “immediately commence the removal of illegal structures in all danger areas,” and communicated directly with now retired DPWH project manager Isabelita Manalo. Danger areas included “river banks, shorelines, creeks, waterways, esteros (estuaries) ... which when occupied for residential purposes actually pose danger to the life, safety and property of either the concerned residents, or of the general community.” Other Philippine agencies were not involved in the project, based on interviews with officials and written responses sent to Human Rights Watch by the Department of Human Settlements and Urban Development and the Commmission on Human Rights. “This was an isolated case,” said Olalia, referring to the lack of involvement by other government departments. “We just responded to the request of the LGU [local government unit] because it had a valid reason; the island was in a danger zone.” The Department of Human Settlements and Urban Development is normally the lead agency for planned relocation, along with the National Housing Authority, which are responsible under the National Resettlement Policy to check the feasibility of the relocation site and can provide financing for new houses. When informal settlers are affected by a resettlement, the Presidential Commission on Urban Poor should monitor the situation, according to the Department of Interior and Local Government’s resettlement guidelines. The Commission on Human Rights also has an oversight role in such cases, as its internal rules require the agency to “ensure strict compliance to the Commission on Human Rights Advisory on the Right to Adequate Housing and Humane Treatment of Informal Settlers.” In addition, the interior department’s resettlement guidelines require oversight by a local inter-agency committee or a local housing board. Human Rights Watch sent right of reply letters outlining the findings on September 21 and received responses from the human settlements department and the Commission on Human Rights. The DPWH, the municipal office in Macabebe, and the Presidential Commission on Urban Poor did not reply. “There was no check and balance,” said Ferdinand Zambrano, the project development officer at the local Department of Human Settlements and Urban Development office. The current mayor, Leonardo Flores, is Mayor Balgan’s brother. Flores’ office referred Human Rights Watch to Jomel Cruz, the disaster risk reduction officer, who was the municipal administrator during that time. Cruz said that there are no documents pertaining to the project among the files turned over by the former administration. The relocation site may be further affected by the planned Pampanga Delta Development Project Phase II (PDDP II or Delta II), which is undergoing feasibility studies, according to plans seen by Human Rights Watch that show Macabebe within the PDDP II project area. Key Human Rights Issues Relating to Planned Relocation Click to expand Image Graphic © 2026 Human Rights Watch International human rights law on planned relocations derives from various human rights treaties that the Philippines has ratified, notably the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights. It is also reflected in international standards and guidance, such as the UN Guidance on Planned Relocation and the UN special rapporteur on internally displaced persons Report on Planned Relocation, to help governments plan and carry out relocations of communities at risk in a rights-respecting manner. Consultation Under international human rights law, planned relocation and other government action that directly affects protected economic and social rights—particularly housing, land, relocation, eviction, water, or livelihoods—needs to be preceded by meaningful, informed, and participatory consultation with affected communities as an important procedural safeguard. Such consultation requires timely and accessible information, an opportunity to express views, and genuine consideration of those views. UN guidance and human rights standards establish that national and local governments need to ensure that planned relocation is a measure of last resort, and ensure that affected communities are meaningfully involved in decisions about a potential move. The UN Guidance says there needs to be some “flexibility to accommodate persons who may choose not to participate in the relocation,” and an opportunity for affected residents “to propose alternative options.” All members of the relocated community interviewed by Human Rights Watch said their concerns and questions about relocation were not given due consideration. What happened was not consultation but an “imposition,” said an 81-year-old woman. During meetings held by officials, including in the local language, residents said their opposition was merely noted. “They simply gave out forms for us to sign and promised us a relocation,” said Jenny Datu, 50. DPWH officials acknowledged that their staff did not conduct detailed consultations with residents, saying that their role was limited to technical assistance on the project. Pulo Island’s former residents said they ultimately agreed to move because officials said they could have a relocation site that would allow the community to stay together. In 2021, residents received “Agreement to Demolish and Remove Improvements” forms that were in English, which is not their preferred language. Some residents said they were frustrated that they received no assistance from anyone, such as a lawyer, to discuss the form. “We had no choice,” said Mary Grace Liguid, 38. “People just arrived measuring our houses, our lands. We had no choice but to agree, because you can’t be left there.” Right to Information The right to receive information, set out in article 19(2) of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, is a core component of a human rights-based approach to planned relocation. Information should be provided in a clear and accessible manner, and should include anticipated disaster and climate risks as well as the social, physical, and economic impacts of the relocation. The UN Guidance provides that adequate, advanced, up-to-date, and accessible information on the rationale for relocation, as well as alternatives considered, is essential to minimize the risk of forced evictions. Residents said they were told various reasons for their removal from the island, including that the island was blocking the flow of the river, which is the reason stated in government documents. Community members also said they were told the island was shaped like a cone, being eroded from underneath, and could collapse at any time. “They scared us that our island was running out of soil, and we will be washed away,” said a 46-year-old man. Olalia and Diaz said this information about the island being eroded did not come from their office. The current municipal engineer of Macabebe said the local government would have no capacity to come up with such an assessment. Satellite imagery analysis by Human Rights Watch shows that, in the 36 years preceding their removal, the surface area of the island reduced by 5.2 percent, from 25 hectares in 1984 to 23.7 hectares in 2020. Relocated residents said they could not recall being given the opportunity to discuss any risk assessment with government officials. None could recall any discussion about ways they could stay on the island. A lack of information and community concerns about compensation also caused delays, as documented by DPWH itself. “Unless the people paid for the houses to be demolished, they will not transfer to the designated relocation site,” said a 2021 department order, rescheduling that phase of the dredging, which was only completed between 2022 and 2023. The payment arrangement left residents with no choice but to demolish their homes. Once they signed the demolition forms, they could receive 70 percent of the assessed value by traveling to Metro Manila to cash their compensation check. They were expected to immediately demolish their homes upon receiving the partial payment and would only receive the remaining 30 percent after providing photos and videos of their demolished homes. Most of the residents interviewed said they felt rushed to demolish their homes and cited rumors of allocated funds running out. “We were panicking,” said Esmeralda Tubig, a 46-year-old daycare teacher. “First of all, you’d demolish your house without complete payment, then you have your daily life to think about. We didn’t know where we’d get our livelihood, then suddenly we also did not know where we’d live.” More than a dozen residents said they also felt intimidated by local officials. “It was raining heavily that time, and they wanted us to start demolishing our houses,” said a 61-year-old construction worker. Residents said that they never received other forms of compensation, including for their crops.
